summary: The paper proposes a sensible paired-transcript design (same audio, same prompts, reference vs. ASR windows, McNemar on discordant pairs) and is unusually candid about partial role separation among generator, verifier and answerer models. However, several stated controls do not control what they claim, and the design as executed cannot support several headline claims. Most seriously, the QA item set is built from "knowledge-error keywords" (i.e., terms an ASR system already misrecognized), so the reference-vs-ASR gap is a conditional estimate, not "how much of the recording's knowledge remains accessible"; the abstract's claim that QA gaps are largest for knowledge-intensive material/topics is never tested (the lower/higher knowledge-intensity labels are defined but never used); the ground-truth verification filter uses two of the three answerers on the same reference window, so the "verified" subset mechanically inflates reference accuracy and Cohen's h; and the L1/L2 comparison is confounded with venue/topic (NIH biomedical talks dominate the L2 group) with no speaker-level clustering or statistical test. Several text claims are contradicted by the paper's own figures (BWER is below WER for Whisper-M in every domain; Whisper-L with WER 0.197 yields higher QA accuracy than Wav2Vec2-L-s with WER 0.164; text reference accuracies of 99.3/98.3/97.9% vs. Figure 4's 95.4/94.0/93.5%). Missing controls (closed-book baseline, per-topic QA breakdown, per-model tests, ASR-window alignment procedure) and undisclosed selection rules (M3AV speakers chosen to hit a 75/25 L2/L1 split; 148 EdX videos excluded on a vague criterion) further limit internal validity.
strengths: Paired design holds audio, prompts, questions and window position fixed across the reference and ASR conditions, and analyzes only within-item discordance (McNemar exact test on toward/away counts, Table 3), which is the right test for this structure; the reported p-values reproduce exactly from the toward/away counts (e.g., 160/37 -> 9.9e-20; 14/6 -> 5.8e-2).

Question generation is conditioned on the reference transcript rather than ASR output (p.3, 'Generation uses the reference transcript rather than an ASR output. This prevents recognition errors from contaminating the answer key'), and the generator (Gemini) is never an answerer for the same item.

The authors explicitly disclose the incomplete role separation ('role separation is guaranteed against the generator but not fully among verifier and answerer roles', p.4) rather than overclaiming three-way independence.

The open-ended variant reuses the identical stem and window and only withholds options (p.4, 'Open-Ended Question Variant'), which is a clean manipulation of answer format holding item content constant, and it reveals that MC understated the gap (Table 4: 10.3-14.0 pt vs 2.7-4.7 pt).
Substitution vs. deletion error typing of discordant items (Table 3) links QA failures back to the ASR error mechanism, which supports interpretability of the downstream failures.

Breadth of systems: seven ASR checkpoints from two families and three QA LLMs (commercial and open-weight) with deterministic decoding and cleared history between items (p.4, 'Prompt and Temperature').

findings.title: Headline claim about QA gaps across topics / knowledge-intensive material is never tested; knowledge-intensity labels are defined but unused
findings.location: Abstract (p.1); Methodology 'Recording Corpus' (p.2); Conclusions (p.7); Figures 3-4 and Tables 3-4 (pp.5-6)
findings.description: The abstract states 'substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material' and the Conclusions repeat 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'. The Methodology defines a per-segment lower/higher knowledge-intensity label ('segments are classified as lower or higher in knowledge intensity based on the concentration of domain-specific terms...') and says it is 'verified ... via an automated in-audio explanation check applied to candidate keywords within the M3AV subset' (so EdX segments are never verified and the check itself is undefined). Yet no QA result in the paper is broken down by topic or by knowledge-intensity level: Figure 4 and Tables 3-4 pool all items; the only per-topic result (Figure 3) is ASR error for Whisper-M, not QA. The operationalization of 'knowledge intensity' therefore never enters any analysis, and the central RQ2 claim about topic/knowledge-intensity dependence has no evidence in the paper.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material'; p.2: 'segments are classified as lower or higher in knowledge intensity ... verified during keyword annotation ... via an automated in-audio explanation check applied to candidate keywords within the M3AV subset'; Figures 3 (Whisper-M CER/WER/BWER by domain, no QA) and 4 (QA accuracy by ASR system only, no topic axis).
findings.suggested_fix: Report QA accuracy and toward/away discordance per topic family and per knowledge-intensity level (lower vs higher) for both corpora, with a test of the interaction; define the 'in-audio explanation check' and apply it (or a human check) to EdX as well; otherwise remove the topic/knowledge-intensity claims from the abstract and conclusions.

findings.title: QA items are pre-selected on ASR keyword errors, so the measured gap is conditional on ASR failure and the keyword stage is not reference-only as claimed
findings.location: p.3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis' and 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation'; p.4 'Datasets'; Figure 1 (p.2); Table 3 (p.5)
findings.description: The item set is built from '1,113 knowledge-error keywords', the filtering pipeline operates on '(reference, ASR output) candidate pairs' ('rejects candidate pairs that are purely spelling or inflectional variants ... keeping only pairs where the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept'), and the question-generation stage 'specifically targets substitution and deletion errors on content words'. Every one of the 197 discordant items in Table 3 carries a Whisper-M substitution or deletion type (137+29+23+8 = 197), which implies every item is a Whisper-M keyword error. Consequences: (a) the abstract's claim that QA performance 'estimates how much of the recording's knowledge remains accessible after transcription' is not what is measured; the 3.7-pt pooled gap (Figure 1: 94.3% vs 90.6%) is P(QA fails | ASR corrupted the keyword), an upper-bound conditional quantity, and the unconditional learner-facing effect is much smaller; (b) the seven-system comparison in Figure 4 is run on an item set selected by one system's errors, which biases the cross-system comparison in an undetermined direction; (c) the claim that generation 'prevents recognition errors from contaminating' the pipeline holds for the answer key but not for item selection, which is ASR-driven.
findings.evidence: p.4: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords (457 EdX, 656 M3AV) surviving keyword triage'; p.3: 'keeping only pairs where the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept'; p.3: 'The downstream question-generation stage specifically targets substitution and deletion errors on content words'; Table 3: all 197 discordant pairs classified as Substitution (166) or Deletion (31) 'over the Whisper-M ASR transcript'.
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly which ASR system's errors define the item set. Add an unconditional item set (keywords sampled from the reference regardless of ASR outcome) so the absolute accessibility loss can be reported; or reframe all claims as conditional on a keyword error. For cross-system comparison, either build items from the union of errors and report per-system error status for each item, or restrict Figure 4 to the system that defined the items.

findings.title: 'Topic-specific vocabulary is harder than function words' and 'BWER exposes disparities WER understates' are contradicted by the paper's own Whisper numbers
findings.location: p.5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains'; Figure 3 (p.5); Table 2 (p.4)
findings.description: For Whisper-M, BWER is at or below WER in every one of the eight domains in Figure 3 (CS 0.072 vs 0.081; Eng 0.074 vs 0.093; Hum 0.047 vs 0.047; Sci 0.043 vs 0.044; SocSci 0.046 vs 0.046; IPP 0.039 vs 0.067; MLS 0.035 vs 0.056; NIH 0.061 vs 0.083), and in Table 2 BWER < WER for all four Whisper checkpoints on both corpora (e.g., Whisper-M EdX 0.064 vs 0.074). Since EdX BWER is 'approximated as all non-function words', BWER < WER on EdX means content words have a LOWER error rate than function words for Whisper-M, the opposite of the stated interpretation. BWER > WER only for the Wav2Vec2 family. Separately, the EdX BWER definition ('all non-function words') does not isolate rare/technical vocabulary at all, so the EdX BWER is not the 'stricter measure' the text describes and is not comparable to the slide-OCR-based M3AV BWER placed beside it in Table 2/Figure 3.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'We observe that topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words'; p.5: 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates'; Figure 3 bar labels (WER 0.081 vs BWER 0.072 for CS; 0.093 vs 0.074 for Engineering; 0.083 vs 0.061 for NIH); Table 2 Whisper-M EdX WER 0.074 / BWER 0.064; p.3: 'for EdX, approximated as all non-function words in the reference'.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the claims to the Wav2Vec2 family or retract them; define a genuine technical-term list for EdX (e.g., the triaged keyword set itself) so EdX BWER is comparable to M3AV; report BWER on the keyword set actually used for QA.

findings.title: L1/L2 disparity confounded with venue/topic and speaker clustering; no cross-tabulation, no test, unspecified aggregation
findings.location: Figure 2 (p.5) and accompanying text; Table 1 (p.4); Table 5 (p.6); p.3 L1/L2 labelling
findings.description: RQ1 is answered by Figure 2 alone. The L2 group is not comparable to L1 in content: M3AV topic families are venues (NIH/IPP/MLS), and the human-study sample shows NIH alone supplies 168 of 235 clips (71.5%) while L2 supplies 196/235 (83.4%); NIH also has the highest accentedness (4.2) and BWER (0.36) in Table 5. The paper never cross-tabulates L1/L2 by topic, so 'L2 speakers show consistently higher error rates' cannot be separated from 'biomedical NIH talks have denser terminology'. EdX's 1,380 videos come from only 27 instructors, so the effective L1/L2 sample is a handful of speakers; Figure 2 gives no confidence intervals, no speaker-level or mixed-effects analysis, and does not say whether WER is micro-averaged over words (letting prolific instructors dominate) or averaged over recordings/speakers. The inference that 'No system reverses this ordering ... indicating the L1/L2 disparity is a property of the recordings and speakers rather than an artifact of any one ASR system's training distribution' does not follow: all seven systems share English-dominant training data, so agreement among them cannot rule out shared training bias. Finally, the 'gap narrowing for the strongest Whisper models' holds only in absolute terms; the L2/L1 WER ratio is essentially constant (Whisper-S 1.40, Whisper-M 1.43, Whisper-L-t 1.38, Wav2Vec2-B 1.40, Wav2Vec2-L 1.39, Wav2Vec2-L-s 1.29), so 'recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap' is not supported in relative terms.
findings.evidence: Figure 2 labels: L1/L2 WER 0.058/0.081 (Whisper-S), 0.056/0.080 (Whisper-M), 0.135/0.174 (Wav2Vec2-L-s), 0.196/0.275 (Wav2Vec2-B); Table 5: NIH n=168, Acc 4.2, BWER 0.36; L2 n=196 of 235; Table 1: EdX 1,380 videos from 27 groups; p.5: 'with the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.'
findings.suggested_fix: Report an L1/L2 x topic cross-tab with per-cell WER/BWER; fit a mixed model with speaker random effects (or at minimum aggregate to speaker level) and report CIs; state the averaging unit; report relative as well as absolute gaps; soften the 'property of speakers rather than training' inference.

findings.title: Ground-truth verification by two of the three answerers on the same reference window creates a selection artifact that inflates verified-subset reference accuracy and Cohen's h
findings.location: p.3-4 'Question Construction' third check; p.4 'ASR and QA LLMs'; Table 3 (p.5); p.5-6 text on h=0.140 vs 0.190; Figure 4 vs text (p.5)
findings.description: An item is retained in the GT-verified subset 'only if both judges [GPT4o and Llama3] independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage'. This is operationally the same task as the reference-condition QA for those two models, so the verified subset is selected on GPT4o/Llama3 answering correctly from the reference window. Effects visible in the data: (i) the 'away' share of discordant pairs (reference wrong, ASR right) drops from 37/197 = 18.8% on the full set to 12/101 = 11.9% on the verified set, exactly as expected when items with reference-condition failures are filtered out; (ii) the net pooled drop actually falls from 123/3321 = 3.7 pt to 77/2439 = 3.2 pt, yet Cohen's h rises from 0.140 to 0.190 -- h(0.943,0.906) = 0.141 reproduces the full set, while h = 0.19 requires reference accuracy near 0.99, i.e., the arcsine transform magnifies a smaller gap because the filter pushed reference accuracy to the ceiling. The paper presents h=0.19 as a stronger effect without noting this. (iii) The text says 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)' while attributing this to Figure 4, whose reference bars read 0.954/0.940/0.935 (mean 0.943, matching Figure 1's 94.3%); the 99.3/98.3 figures are consistent with the ceiling induced by the verification filter on the verified subset. Qwen2.5, the only answerer not used as verifier, is not analyzed separately.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage'; Table 3: Full toward/away 160/37, h 0.140; GT-verified 89/12, h 0.190; p.6: 'h = 0.190 on the ground-truth-verified subset'; p.5: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%)' vs Figure 4 bar labels 0.954/0.940/0.935; Figure 1: 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%, ASR (Whisper) 90.6%, Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'.
findings.suggested_fix: Use verifiers that are not answerers (or exclude verifier models from the verified-subset analysis and report Qwen2.5 alone on it); report per-model reference and ASR accuracies for both subsets in the main text; reconcile the 99.3/98.3/97.9 figures with Figure 4; discuss the ceiling effect when comparing h across subsets.

findings.title: No closed-book / no-context control; the 'dependency check' is a generation instruction, not a verification
findings.location: p.3 'Each generated item passes three checks' (first check); p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'; Table 4 (p.6); Limitations (p.7)
findings.description: The first check ('distractors must be indistinguishable from the correct answer to a reader without access to the local window') is 'built into generation itself', i.e., it is a prompt constraint on Gemini with no independent test that items are actually unanswerable without the window. The answerability judges only see the marked answer plus the reference window, so they never test distractor quality or prior-knowledge answerability. The paper itself shows the MC items are partially solvable by elimination: reference-condition accuracy falls from 0.94-0.95 (MC, Figure 4) to 0.77-0.84 (open-ended, Table 4), and the text admits 'a QA LLM can sometimes eliminate distractors using its internal comprehensive capability without needing the gold reference'. The standard control -- answering each item with no transcript (or with a shuffled/unrelated window) -- would quantify this leakage directly and would also calibrate how much of the ASR-condition accuracy (90.6%) is prior knowledge rather than transcript-supported recovery. Limitations acknowledge the risk ('QA models may rely on pretrained knowledge') but the design does not measure it.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'a dependency check is built into generation itself: distractors must be indistinguishable ... so the item cannot be answered from general knowledge of the topic'; p.6: 'the multiple-choice format may understate the true accessibility gap, since a QA LLM can sometimes eliminate distractors using its internal comprehensive capability without needing the gold reference'; Table 4 ref accuracies 0.803/0.773/0.843 vs Figure 4 ref 0.954/0.940/0.935.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a no-context (closed-book) condition and a mismatched-window condition for every item and report accuracy; exclude or down-weight items solvable closed-book; report the reference-vs-ASR gap on the remaining items.

findings.title: M3AV L1/L2 labels partly inferred from name origin/affiliation, contradicting the stated procedure; M3AV speakers selected to hit a target L2/L1 ratio with undisclosed rule
findings.location: p.2-3 'L1/L2 speaker status'; p.4 'Datasets'; Table 1 (p.4)
findings.description: The Methodology states 'L1/L2 speaker status is established through biographical research rather than assumed from name or accent alone', but for M3AV 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup'. The size of the verified subset is never given (only 'e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers' were excluded as unresolvable), so for an unknown fraction of M3AV speakers the label rests on name origin -- exactly the proxy the paper disavows. The biographical proxies used (PhD institution/country, year of US arrival, years of US residence) also misclassify English-L1 speakers educated outside the US and L2 speakers educated in the US. Moreover, the M3AV sample was chosen 'targeting the same overall 75%/25% L2/L1 composition as EdX' (achieved: 92/123 = 74.8% vs 1037/1380 = 75.1%), and there were 228 NIH candidate speakers but only 123 M3AV videos across three venues, so a large, undescribed down-selection occurred, conditioned on the very variable under study. Which speakers/talks were kept, and by what rule, is not stated; this makes the M3AV L1/L2 comparison and its venue composition (NIH-dominated) non-random by construction.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'rather than assumed from name or accent alone'; p.3: 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers'; p.3: 'e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers'; p.4: 'targeting the same overall 75%/25% L2/L1 composition as EdX'; Table 1: M3AV 123 videos, L1 31, L2 92.
findings.suggested_fix: Report how many M3AV speakers were biographically verified vs. name-inferred, with inter-annotator agreement on the label; report the full selection procedure from 228+ candidates to 123 talks (and its stratification by venue); consider a sensitivity analysis restricted to verified speakers; define L1 explicitly (native English regardless of variety?).

findings.title: Cross-family QA ordering contradicts the claim that transcript quality (WER) drives QA loss; Figure 4 bars are not individually identified
findings.location: Figure 4 (p.5) and text 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' (p.5); Table 2 (p.4)
findings.description: The text claims 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2, indicating that transcription variability among ASR systems is what drives the downstream QA accuracy loss.' But Whisper-L has a higher WER than Wav2Vec2-L-s on both corpora (EdX 0.197 vs 0.164; M3AV 0.168 vs 0.174 roughly tied) and higher BWER on EdX (0.145 vs 0.167 is lower, but CER 0.148 vs 0.070 far higher), yet every Whisper bar in Figure 4 exceeds every Wav2Vec2 bar for all three QA models (GPT4o: min Whisper 0.926 > max Wav2Vec2 0.906; Llama3: 0.892 > 0.866; Qwen2.5: 0.899 > 0.869). Within the Whisper group, if bars follow the Table 2 order (S, M, L-t, L), the worst-WER checkpoint (Whisper-L) would have the highest QA accuracy (0.945 for GPT4o). The figure only labels 'Whisper family' and 'Wav2Vec family', so the reader cannot check which bar is which; either way the WER-drives-QA claim fails across families. A plausible reason is that Whisper-L's WER is inflated by 'hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio' occurring outside the ±100-word windows, which means whole-recording WER is not the right predictor for window-level QA and the family difference (Whisper vs. wav2vec2 CTC without an LM producing non-words) is a confound the design cannot separate from error rate.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'; Table 2 WER: Whisper-L 0.197 (EdX) vs Wav2Vec2-L-s 0.164; Figure 4 bar labels: GPT4o Whisper bars 0.933/0.926/0.944/0.945 vs Wav2Vec2 bars 0.895/0.905/0.906; p.5: 'driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio'.
findings.suggested_fix: Label each bar by checkpoint; compute WER/BWER on the exact ±100-word windows used for QA and correlate window-level error with item-level QA failure; discuss the family-level confound; fix long-form decoding (chunking/VAD, no-repeat constraints) so Whisper-L/L-t results reflect model capability.

findings.title: McNemar tests pooled across three QA models on the same items violate pair independence; no per-model tests reported
findings.location: Table 3 (p.5); 'Evaluation Metrics' (p.4); Figure 1 (p.2); p.6 open-ended test
findings.description: The Evaluation Metrics section says 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements', but Table 3 gives a single row per question set labelled 'for all QA LLMs', with N=1,107 items and 197 discordant pairs; the pooled net drop 123/(3x1,107) = 3.7 pt reproduces Figure 1's 94.3% vs 90.6% and h(0.943,0.906) = 0.141 reproduces h=0.140, confirming that the three models' answers on the same 1,107 items were pooled into 3,321 pairs. The same item answered by three models yields correlated pairs (the same corrupted keyword breaks all three), so the exact binomial on discordant counts overstates evidence; the 'N=1,107' label is also misleading about the number of trials. The open-ended test ('toward=140, away=33, n=173' from 300 items x 3 models) has the same issue.
findings.evidence: Table 3 caption: 'for all QA LLMs over the Whisper-M ASR transcript'; Table 3 'Full (N=1,107) All 160 37'; Figure 1: 'Reference 94.3%, ASR 90.6%, Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points, p = 9.9 x 10^-20'; p.4: 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report McNemar per QA model (as the Methods promise) and, if pooling, use an item-clustered test (e.g., item-level majority/any-failure indicator or a GEE/mixed logistic model with item random effects); state the number of pairs actually tested.

findings.title: ASR-side window construction and alignment to the reference ±100-word window are not described
findings.location: p.3 'Question Construction'; p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'
findings.description: Questions are generated from 'the keyword and a ±100-word window of surrounding context' in the reference, and QA uses 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window'. Nothing says how the ASR window is located: by word offsets (which shift after deletions, insertions or Whisper repetition loops), by timestamps (which are 'removed before comparison'), or by alignment to the reference. If ASR windows are misaligned or truncated relative to the reference window, part of the reference-vs-ASR gap is attributable to missing context rather than keyword corruption, and deletion-type items (where the keyword has no anchor in the ASR text) are especially vulnerable. The 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic' for multiword terms is mentioned but not specified.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'The keyword and a ±100-word window of surrounding context are provided to the generator'; p.4: 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window as context for QA LLMs'; p.3: 'Timestamps and formatting are removed before comparison'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the alignment procedure (e.g., word-level alignment of ASR to reference, then take the aligned span); report window length statistics for ASR windows; run a sanity check where the reference window is replaced by a length-matched reference window with only the keyword corrupted, to isolate the keyword effect from window-alignment effects.

findings.title: QA item set is dominated by M3AV (59% of keywords from 9% of videos) with a different keyword source than EdX, so RQ2 mostly reflects NIH-style talks
findings.location: p.4 'Datasets'; p.3 BWER definition; Table 1 (p.4)
findings.description: The ASR evaluation is 91% EdX (1,232 of 1,355 videos), but the QA item set is 59% M3AV (656 of 1,113 keywords). M3AV keywords are anchored in slide OCR text released with the corpus whereas EdX has 'no equivalent visual ground truth', so the two corpora contribute items generated under different keyword-source regimes. Combined with the venue/L2 confound (NIH dominates M3AV), the pooled QA results in Figure 4 / Tables 3-4 are largely a statement about biomedical academic talks, not about the EdX lecture corpus that motivates the accessibility framing. The paper never reports QA results per corpus.
findings.evidence: p.4: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords (457 EdX, 656 M3AV)'; p.4: 'leaving 1,232 EdX and 123 M3AV videos (1,355 total) in the ASR evaluation'; p.3: 'for M3AV, drawn from slide OCR text released with the corpus; for EdX, approximated as all non-function words'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report QA accuracy, discordance and h separately per corpus (and per venue/subject); explain why M3AV yields ~10x more keywords per video and whether keyword identification used slide OCR for M3AV but not EdX.

findings.title: Human-study QA follows a different protocol (questions from ASR output of ≤25-word clips, no ±100-word window) and Table 7 conditions on the outcome without a test
findings.location: p.7 'Relationship to ASR Performance' final paragraph; Table 7 (p.7)
findings.description: The main pipeline generates questions from the reference transcript with a ±100-word window. For the human-study clips, 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria' -- i.e., questions were generated from ASR output, which the Methodology says is avoided because it contaminates the answer key -- and the clips are '25 words or less', so no ±100-word window exists. It also says 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions', although in the main pipeline Gemini, not the QA LLMs, generates. Table 7 then splits the 194 clips by whether QA was 100% correct and reports 84% vs 91% L2 with no statistical test; the base L2 rate in the clip sample is already 83.4% (196/235), the 'QA 100% Correct' rows are tautological (1/1/1), and conditioning on the outcome cannot support the causal-sounding conclusion that 'L2 speakers are more likely to have lower QA LLM accuracy'.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria, but given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less, the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples'; Table 7: percent_L2 84 vs 91, Acc 3.8 vs 4.3; p.3: 'Generation uses the reference transcript rather than an ASR output. This prevents recognition errors from contaminating the answer key.'
findings.suggested_fix: Generate clip questions from the reference, state which model generated them, and report a test (e.g., Fisher exact on L2 x QA-failure, or logistic regression of QA failure on accentedness with speaker clustering); or drop Table 7's causal framing.

findings.title: Leak (specificity) filter removed at most 6 of 1,113 items, implausibly few for a filter that bans the keyword and its variants from stem and options
findings.location: p.3-4 'Question Construction' second check; p.4 'Datasets'
findings.description: The counts imply the leak filter almost never fired: 1,113 keywords -> 1,107 questions 'after leak-filtering', i.e., ≤6 rejections including generation failures, before 294 (26.6%) were then removed by answerability verification. Given that question types include 'concept identification' and 'definition completion' where the natural correct option is the keyword itself, a filter rejecting 'any question whose stem or options contain the literal target keyword, its ASR-mishearing, or an obvious variant of either' should have substantial attrition unless the generator was already instructed to paraphrase (as in the Figure 1 example, where 'excision' is paraphrased as 'Removal of damaged segments via specialized enzymatic pathways'). If the filter is nearly inert, the paper should say so and report how paraphrase-based correct options were prevented from being answerable from general knowledge (the paraphrase itself encodes the concept). Note also the tension between the keyword-priority criterion 'it recurs across the explanation' and the framework's premise that single-occurrence terms are the vulnerable ones: a recurring keyword inside a ±100-word window can be recovered from its other occurrences even when one is corrupted.
findings.evidence: p.4: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords ... yielding 1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification'; p.3: 'any question whose stem or options contain the literal target keyword, its ASR-mishearing, or an obvious variant of either is rejected'; p.3: 'it recurs across the explanation or connects the recording to likely course materials'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the number of items rejected by each check separately; give several full example items (stem, options, keyword, ASR mishearing) in the main text; report how often the keyword occurs more than once within the window and whether QA failure rate differs for single- vs multi-occurrence items.

findings.title: Whisper decoding language fixed to English 'additionally' for EdX after observing an improvement; unclear which run Table 2 reports and post hoc choice interacts with L1/L2
findings.location: p.3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'
findings.description: 'For EdX, Whisper models are additionally run with decoding language fixed to English (language="en") rather than automatic language detection, following an observed accuracy improvement on lecture audio with accented and code-switched speech; M3AV transcription fixes English decoding throughout.' 'Additionally run' implies two EdX runs exist; Table 2 / Figure 2 do not say which is reported. The choice was made after observing results on the evaluation data, and language auto-detection failures disproportionately affect accented (L2) speech, so the reported L1/L2 gap for Whisper depends on this decision and is not comparable to wav2vec2 (which has no such setting).
findings.evidence: p.3: 'Whisper models are additionally run with decoding language fixed to English ... following an observed accuracy improvement on lecture audio with accented and code-switched speech'.
findings.suggested_fix: State which configuration underlies every table/figure; report both configurations' L1 and L2 WER so the reader can see how much of the Whisper L1/L2 gap depends on language forcing.

findings.title: Whisper-L/L-t deficits attributed to long-form decoding artifacts, yet the seven-system comparison and 'L1/L2 property of speakers' inference are drawn from these uncorrected runs
findings.location: p.5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains'; Table 2 (p.4); Figure 2 (p.5)
findings.description: The authors state that Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t underperform because of 'hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit'. This is a pipeline artifact (chunking/long-form decoding settings) rather than a model property, but the affected numbers are retained in Table 2 and Figure 2 and used to argue that the L1/L2 ordering is consistent 'across every ASR system'. Whisper-L also shows the largest L2/L1 ratio (1.61), which may itself be a hallucination artifact rather than an accent effect.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'Inspection of individual transcripts shows this is driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit'; Figure 2: Whisper-L L1 0.133 / L2 0.214.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-run Whisper-L/L-t with standard long-form mitigation (VAD-based chunking, condition_on_previous_text=False, compression-ratio filtering) or exclude them from claims about model capability and L1/L2 consistency.

findings.title: Corpus counts and exclusion criteria are inconsistent or vague; post-exclusion L1/L2 split not reported
findings.location: Table 1 (p.4); p.2 'Recording Corpus'; p.4 'Datasets'; p.3 L1/L2 paragraph
findings.description: Table 1 lists 1,380 EdX videos (343 L1 / 1,037 L2) and '27 courses', while the text says 148 EdX videos were excluded, leaving 1,232, and refers to '27 unique instructors' (courses and instructors are conflated). The L1/L2 composition after exclusion is never given, and the exclusion criterion 'instructor groups whose presentation format was inconsistent with the rest of the corpus' / 'two instructor groups with an inconsistent presentation format' is not operationalized; with only 27 instructors, removing two instructor groups (plus 'multi-speaker cross-talk' and 'non-English content') could materially shift the L1/L2 balance, and whether the excluded instructors were L1 or L2 is not disclosed. Table 1 also reports 'Domains 3' for M3AV, which equals its venue count, confirming that topic and venue are the same variable for M3AV.
findings.evidence: Table 1: 'EdX 1,380 27 courses 5 343 1,037'; p.4: 'leaving 1,232 EdX and 123 M3AV videos'; p.3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors'; p.2: 'material from instructor groups whose presentation format was inconsistent with the rest of the corpus (148 EdX recordings excluded on this basis)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report Table 1 after exclusion with per-corpus L1/L2 counts of both videos and speakers; define the 'inconsistent presentation format' criterion and report the L1/L2 status and subject areas of the excluded material.

findings.title: EdX reference transcripts are platform captions, not independently verified as the Methodology claims; caption quality may covary with L1/L2
findings.location: p.2 'Methodology' first paragraph and 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts'; p.4 'Datasets'
findings.description: The design is introduced as pairing each recording with 'an independently verified gold-standard reference transcript', but the EdX references are 'EdX's officially published caption files' / 'platform-provided EdX SRT captions', with no evidence of human verification, no sample audit, and no error-rate estimate. Platform captions are often ASR-derived with light editing; if caption editing effort differs between L1 and L2 instructors (or between subject areas), then reference noise is correlated with the grouping variable and part of the measured 'ASR error' for L2 speakers is reference error. This matters for RQ1 and for Figure 3's per-domain comparison.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'an independently verified gold-standard reference transcript'; p.2: 'EdX's officially published caption files for EdX recordings'; p.4: 'Gold-standard transcripts are the platform-provided EdX SRT captions'.
findings.suggested_fix: Audit a stratified sample of EdX captions (by L1/L2 and subject) against the audio and report their WER; remove 'independently verified' or restrict it to M3AV.

findings.title: Open-ended grading relies on a single LLM judge (the question generator) grading against its own answer key with no human validation; reference-condition accuracy of 0.77-0.84 indicates substantial judge or item noise
findings.location: p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA' (secondary check); p.6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'; Table 4
findings.description: Open-ended answers are 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge (grounded in the reference passage ...)' under an 'adversarial' rule requiring the answer to be 'distinguishable from the multiple-choice distractors'. The judge is thus grading against a key it authored, using distractors it authored, with no inter-judge or human agreement reported. Under this judge, even the gold-reference condition scores only 0.803/0.773/0.843, so 16-23% of verified items are 'unanswerable' from the gold window by construction of the judge; the 10-14 pt drops are therefore measured against a noisy criterion, and the direction of judge bias (it knows which fact was corrupted) is uncontrolled.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge (grounded in the reference passage, and never itself an answerer)'; Table 4: ref 0.803, 0.773, 0.843; p.6: 'correct only if it clearly commits to the reference fact in a way that is distinguishable from the multiple-choice distractors'.
findings.suggested_fix: Have a second, independent judge (not Gemini) and a human sample grade the same open-ended answers blind to condition; report agreement; report open-ended results for the ASR condition using the same items where the reference condition was judged correct.

findings.title: Human intelligibility (BWER) pooled across corpora with different keyword definitions; clip-level correlations ignore speaker nesting and clip-level ASR condition is unclear
findings.location: Table 5 and Table 6 (p.6); text 'Relationship to ASR Performance'
findings.description: Table 5 pools L1 vs L2 'Int (BWER)' (0.28 vs 0.34) across EdX and M3AV clips although BWER is defined differently per corpus (slide OCR terms vs all non-function words), and 84% of clips are M3AV (168 NIH). Table 6 Spearman correlations are computed on 235 clips that are nested within speakers, so the effective N is far smaller and NIH speakers dominate. It is also unclear whether the 'ASR accuracy on the clips' was obtained by re-running the ASR systems on isolated ≤25-word clips (a different acoustic/context condition from the full-recording evaluation) or by extracting clip spans from full-recording transcripts; this determines whether RQ3's alignment result transfers to the main study. The caption says 'ASR accuracy' but the positive correlations with accentedness only make sense if the ASR variable is an error rate.
findings.evidence: Table 5 caption: 'Intelligibility (Int) is the BWER of human transcription'; Table 5: NIH n=168; Table 6 caption: 'Correlation study of human ratings and ASR accuracy'; p.6: 'Spearman correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report correlations per corpus and with speaker-level aggregation (or a mixed model); state how clip-level ASR error was computed; clarify the ASR variable's direction in Table 6.

findings.title: Reproducibility of the generated item set and API decoding is limited (temperature 0.3 generation, non-deterministic API, single run)
findings.location: p.4 'Prompt and Temperature'; p.2 'Decoding is deterministic where supported'
findings.description: Question generation used temperature 0.3 'to allow distractor diversity', so the 1,107-item set is one stochastic draw with no seed or release commitment stated; GPT4o via API is not strictly deterministic even at temperature 0 ('deterministic where supported'); all results are single runs without variance estimates. Since the main effect is a 3.7-pt pooled gap driven by 197 discordant items, run-to-run variability in generation or answering could be non-negligible relative to the effect.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'temperature 0.3 for question generation to allow distractor diversity across items'; p.2: 'Decoding is deterministic where supported'.
findings.suggested_fix: Release the item set and prompts; repeat answering runs (e.g., 3 seeds) and report variance; report the exact model versions/dates for GPT4o and Gemini.

summary: The arithmetic that can be checked mostly checks out: every McNemar p-value in Table 3 and the open-ended test reproduces exactly as a one-sided exact binomial on the reported discordant counts, Table 4's Cohen's h values reproduce, Table 1/5/7 sums and the 75/25 L2/L1 split are correct, and Figure 2's L1/L2 WERs average to Table 2's values. However, the headline QA statistics are mislabeled and partly misreported. Table 3's "N=1,107" tests are in fact pooled over three QA models (3,321 item-model pairs; the 160-37=123 net discordant pairs give an 11-pt gap per model but a 3.7-pt gap pooled, which is what h=0.140 and Figure 4 imply), so the item-level independence assumption is violated and the "for each QA model" description is wrong. The text's reference accuracies (99.3/98.3/97.9%) contradict Figure 4's own bar labels (0.954/0.940/0.935) and reconstruct instead to the GT-verified subset. Several interpretive claims are contradicted by the paper's own numbers: BWER is lower than WER for every Whisper model and every domain, the Whisper-L/L-t bars in Figure 4 outperform Whisper-S/M despite far worse WER, the relative L1/L2 gap is the same (~40%) for the best Whisper and the worst Wav2Vec2 models, and the Table 7 L2-share difference is not significant (Fisher p=0.20). No variance, CIs, or tests are reported for any human-rating comparison, and the open-ended vs multiple-choice effect-size comparison is confounded by an 15-22 pt drop in gold-context accuracy and a 7x higher "Away" rate.
strengths: All seven reported p-values (Table 3 and the open-ended test on p.6) reproduce to the stated precision as one-sided exact binomial tests on the discordant counts (e.g., 160/37 -> 9.94e-20; 14/6 -> 0.0577; 140/33 -> 3.43e-17).

Table 4's Cohen's h values reproduce from the stated accuracies (0.2395, 0.2519, 0.3379), and the open-ended accuracies are all exact multiples of 1/300 whose per-model nets (31+34+42=107) equal the reported toward-away difference 140-33=107.

Table 1 sums are internally consistent (343+1,037=1,380; 31+92=123) and the stated 75%/25% L2/L1 composition holds for both corpora (75.1% and 74.8%); 1,380-148=1,232, 1,232+123=1,355 and 457+656=1,113 all check.

Figure 2's L1/L2 WER bars, weighted 25/75, reproduce Table 2's overall WERs for every system (e.g., Whisper-S 0.058/0.081 -> 0.075; Wav2Vec2-L-s 0.135/0.174 -> 0.164), and Table 5's n's (39+196=235; topic n's sum to 235) and n-weighted means are consistent across its two groupings.
The paper reports an effect size alongside p-values and uses a paired design (same items under reference and ASR context), which is the right basic structure for the question.

findings.title: Text's reference-condition accuracies contradict Figure 4's bar labels
findings.location: Page 5, 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' first paragraph vs. Figure 4 bar labels (page 5)
findings.description: The paragraph that introduces Figure 4 states GPT4o reaches 99.3% in the reference condition, Llama3 98.3% and Qwen2.5 97.9%. The reference (grey) bars in Figure 4 are labelled 0.954, 0.940 and 0.935. These cannot both describe the same experiment. Reconstruction shows the text's numbers belong to the GT-verified subset (N=813) reported in the unavailable appendix: pooling 99.3/98.3/97.9 with the 89-12=77 net discordant pairs over 3x813 pairs gives h = 0.189 (reported 0.190), whereas pooling Figure 4's 0.954/0.940/0.935 with 160-37=123 net pairs over 3x1,107 gives h = 0.141 (reported 0.140). As written, the main text mis-describes its own figure by 4-5 percentage points.
findings.evidence: Text: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'. Figure 4 labels: ref bars 0.954 (GPT4o), 0.940 (Llama3), 0.935 (Qwen2.5). Recomputed: h(0.985, 0.985-77/2439) = 0.189; h(0.943, 0.943-123/3321) = 0.141.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the percentages with the Figure 4 values (95.4/94.0/93.5%) or explicitly state that the quoted figures are from the GT-verified subset and cite the appendix table.

findings.title: Table 3 'N=1,107'/'N=813' mislabels tests that are pooled across three QA models; independence violated
findings.location: Page 5, Table 3 and caption; page 4 'Evaluation Metrics'; page 6 open-ended test (toward=140, away=33, n=173)
findings.description: Evaluation Metrics says 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements ... and compare paired correctness', and Table 3 labels each row N=1,107 or N=813. But the discordant counts only make sense pooled over the three QA models. If 160 toward / 37 away were for one model over 1,107 items, the net 123 items would imply an 11.1-pt accuracy drop, whereas Figure 4 shows Whisper-M drops of only 2.8/4.8/3.6 pt. Summing (ref - asr) x 1,107 over the three models for the second Whisper bar gives 31.0 + 53.1 + 39.9 = 124.0, matching 123; 123/3,321 = 3.70 pt reproduces h = 0.140. The same holds for the open-ended test: Table 4 nets 31 + 34 + 42 = 107 = 140 - 33 over 3 x 300 = 900 pairs. So the tests treat the three correlated answers to one item as three independent trials, tripling the effective n and shrinking p-values (the caption's 'for all QA LLMs' is the only hint). Per-model significance would very likely survive, but the labelling and the description of the procedure are wrong.
findings.evidence: Table 3: 'Full (N=1,107) All 160 37 9.9e-20 0.140'; text p.4: 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements'. Recomputed: 160-37=123; 123/1107=11.1 pt vs Figure 4 gaps 0.954-0.926=2.8, 0.940-0.892=4.8, 0.935-0.899=3.6 pt; sum over models = 124.0 items; 123/3321 = 3.70 pt -> h = 0.141.
findings.suggested_fix: Report toward/away counts, p and h separately for each QA model (as Table 4 already does), state N as item-model pairs (3,321 / 2,439 / 900) if pooling is retained, and correct the Evaluation Metrics description.

findings.title: 'QA drop ordering closely mirrors ASR error ordering' is contradicted within the Whisper family in Figure 4
findings.location: Page 5, Figure 4 and 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' paragraph 1; Table 2 (page 4)
findings.description: In every model group of Figure 4 the two darkest Whisper bars are higher than the two lightest. If bars follow Table 2's order (S, M, L-t, L) — and the reconstruction above identifies bar 2 as Whisper-M — then Whisper-L-t and Whisper-L (WER 0.114 and 0.197 on EdX) yield higher QA accuracy than Whisper-S and Whisper-M (WER 0.075 and 0.074), and the paper's 'best working ASR' (Whisper-M) produces the largest QA drop of any Whisper system for all three LLMs. This is the opposite of the claimed mirroring. Figure 4 also never identifies which shade is which system, so the reader cannot verify the ordering at all.
findings.evidence: Figure 4 labels — GPT4o: 0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945; Llama3: 0.903, 0.892, 0.916, 0.919; Qwen2.5: 0.904, 0.899, 0.921, 0.919 (Whisper bars, left to right). Table 2 EdX WER: Whisper-S 0.075, Whisper-M 0.074, Whisper-L-t 0.114, Whisper-L 0.197. Text: 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'.
findings.suggested_fix: Label each bar with its ASR system, report a per-system table of QA accuracy, and either drop the 'mirrors' claim or restrict it to the between-family contrast; discuss why worse-WER Whisper models lose less QA accuracy (e.g., window-level vs. full-recording errors).

findings.title: BWER is lower than WER for every Whisper model and every domain, contradicting 'topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than function words'
findings.location: Page 5, 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' (Figure 3 discussion) and Table 2 (page 4)
findings.description: The text claims that keyword errors exceed general errors and that 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates'. In Table 2, BWER < WER for all four Whisper models on both corpora (differences -0.006 to -0.052), and in Figure 3 (Whisper-M by domain) BWER <= WER in all eight domains (e.g., IPP 0.039 vs 0.067; NIH 0.061 vs 0.083; MLS 0.035 vs 0.056). BWER exceeds WER only for the Wav2Vec2 models. The Figure 3 discussion also names Humanities and Social Sciences as the most robust domains although Science has the lowest BWER (0.043 vs 0.047/0.046). Note also that EdX BWER is 'approximated as all non-function words', so for EdX it is a content-word error rate rather than a technical-term rate.
findings.evidence: Table 2 Whisper-M: EdX WER 0.074 / BWER 0.064; M3AV WER 0.077 / BWER 0.053. Figure 3 Whisper-M: CS 0.081/0.072, Eng 0.093/0.074, Hum 0.047/0.047, Sci 0.044/0.043, SocSci 0.046/0.046, IPP 0.067/0.039, MLS 0.056/0.035, NIH 0.083/0.061 (WER/BWER). Text: 'topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words'.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the claim to Wav2Vec2 or remove it; report keyword-level error rates on the actual triaged keyword set for Whisper-M; mention Science as the lowest-BWER EdX domain.

findings.title: 'Gap narrowing for the strongest Whisper models' not supported: relative L1/L2 gap is ~40% for both best Whisper and worst Wav2Vec2, and largest for Whisper-L
findings.location: Page 5, Figure 2 and its discussion ('gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap')
findings.description: From Figure 2's labels the L2/L1 WER ratios are: Whisper-S 1.40, Whisper-M 1.43, Whisper-L-t 1.38, Whisper-L 1.61, Wav2Vec2-B 1.40, Wav2Vec2-L 1.39, Wav2Vec2-L-s 1.29. The relative penalty for L2 speakers is essentially identical for the best Whisper models and Wav2Vec2-B/L, is smallest for Wav2Vec2-L-s, and is largest for a Whisper model (Whisper-L). Only the absolute gap is smaller for Whisper-S/M, which is a mechanical consequence of lower overall WER. No confidence intervals or tests accompany any L1/L2 comparison, so it is also unknown whether the small absolute Whisper gaps (0.023-0.024) are distinguishable from the Wav2Vec2-L-s gap (0.039).
findings.suggested_fix: Report both absolute and relative gaps with bootstrap CIs over recordings/speakers, and revise the conclusion that recent models reduce the L1/L2 gap.

findings.title: Table 7 group differences are untested; the L2-share difference is not significant (Fisher p = 0.20)
findings.location: Page 7, Table 7 and surrounding text ('Notably, there were more L2 speakers in the clips that did not have accurate QA LLM results...')
findings.description: Table 7 compares 56 fully-correct clips with 138 partially-correct clips on percent L2 (84 vs 91), accentedness (3.8 vs 4.3), comprehensibility (3.1 vs 3.4) and human BWER (0.32 vs 0.37) with no SDs, CIs or tests. The percent-L2 contrast corresponds to 47/56 vs 126/138; a Fisher exact test gives two-sided p = 0.20 (one-sided 0.11), so the sentence 'L2 speakers are more likely to have lower QA LLM accuracy' is not supported at conventional levels. The rating differences (0.5 and 0.3 on a 9-point scale) cannot be assessed without dispersion. The 'QA Accuracy' columns (1/1/1 vs 0.9/0.84/0.85) are tautological given the grouping criterion, and the text's 'frequently 100% accurate' sits oddly with only 56/194 = 29% of clips being fully correct.
findings.evidence: Table 7: n=56, percent_L2=84; n=138, percent_L2=91. Recomputed: 0.84x56=47.0, 0.91x138=125.6 -> 47/56 vs 126/138, Fisher two-sided p=0.200. Text: 'were frequently 100% accurate'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report SDs/CIs and appropriate tests (Fisher/chi-square for L2 share, Mann-Whitney for ratings), or tone the claims down to descriptive; remove or explain the tautological QA-accuracy columns.

findings.title: Open-ended vs multiple-choice effect-size comparison is confounded by a collapse in gold-context accuracy and a 7x higher 'Away' rate
findings.location: Page 6, Table 4 and 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'
findings.description: The 300 open-ended items are drawn from the GT-verified set, on which multiple-choice reference accuracy is ~98-99%. Under the open-ended judge, reference-context accuracy falls to 80.3/77.3/84.3%, i.e., 16-23% of 'ground-truth-verified' items are not answerable from the gold passage. The 'Away' (ASR correct, reference incorrect) rate rises from 12/2,439 = 0.5% (GT multiple-choice) to 33/900 = 3.7%, and total discordance from 4.1% to 19.2%. A large part of the increased h may therefore reflect judge noise / bidirectional disagreement rather than a larger true accessibility gap, so 'the multiple-choice format was masking part of the true effect' is one of several explanations. In addition, the comparison sets pooled h values (0.14-0.19, Table 3) against per-model h values (0.24-0.34, Table 4); per-model Whisper-M multiple-choice h from Figure 4 is 0.119 / 0.175 / 0.131.
findings.suggested_fix: Report judge reliability (agreement with a second judge / human on a sample), report the discordance and Away rates under both formats, and compare like with like (per-model h in both tables).

findings.title: Inconsistent definition of the question sets: methodology says only judge-confirmed items are retained, yet 1,107 items exist with only 813 verified
findings.location: Page 4, 'Each generated item passes three checks' paragraph; page 4 'Datasets' ('1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification'); Table 3
findings.description: The methodology states 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage', which would make the full set identical to the verified set. Instead there is a Full set of 1,107 (from 1,113 keywords, so only 6 items were removed) and a GT-verified subset of 813. The 294 non-verified items (27% of items) contribute 96 of the 197 discordant pairs (49%) and 25 of the 37 'Away' pairs (68%), i.e., the Full-set statistics are disproportionately driven by items that failed verification, and the Full-set toward/away ratio (2.84 on the non-verified items vs 7.42 on the verified ones) shows these items behave differently.
findings.evidence: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords ... yielding 1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification'; Table 3: Full 160/37 vs GT-verified 89/12 -> non-verified 71/25.
findings.suggested_fix: State precisely what filtering produced 1,107 and what 'ground-truth-verified' adds; make the verified subset the headline analysis or justify including unverified items.

findings.title: Abstract/conclusion claims about topic-level QA gaps and 'substantial differences among QA LLMs' have no supporting numbers in the paper
findings.location: Page 1 Abstract ('largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material'); page 7 Conclusions ('downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'); page 4 Evaluation Metrics ('statistical tests for important differences among LLMs')
findings.description: No table or figure reports QA accuracy by topic, domain or knowledge-intensity class; Figure 3 reports only ASR error rates for Whisper-M. Likewise, no test comparing the three QA LLMs is reported, although Evaluation Metrics promises one; in Figure 4 the reference accuracies differ by at most 1.9 pt (0.954 vs 0.935), and the largest between-LLM difference is 6.3 pt under Wav2Vec2-B (0.896 vs 0.833). The abstract's and conclusion's topic-level QA claims are therefore unverifiable from the manuscript.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material'; Conclusions: 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'; no QA-by-topic table or figure exists on pages 1-9.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a QA accuracy (reference vs ASR) breakdown by topic/knowledge-intensity with per-cell n, and either add the promised between-LLM test or remove the claim.

findings.title: '2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11' refers to a table that is not in the paper; Figure 4 gives 2.8-4.8 pt
findings.location: Page 6, 'QA over Open-Ended Questions' ('10.3 to 14.0 percentage points (pt) versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11')
findings.description: The multiple-choice drop range that anchors the open-ended comparison is attributed to Table 11, which does not exist in the nine-page manuscript. From Figure 4's Whisper-M (second Whisper) bars the full-set drops are 2.8 (GPT4o), 4.8 (Llama3) and 3.6 (Qwen2.5) pt, close to but not equal to 2.7-4.7. If 2.7-4.7 refers to the GT-verified subset it cannot be checked; the mean per-model net on that subset is 77/3/813 = 3.2 pt, which is at least consistent.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite a table present in the paper (or the appendix explicitly), and state which question set the 2.7-4.7 range refers to.

findings.title: Table 6 is labelled 'ASR accuracy' but reports correlations with BWER (an error rate); sign convention inverted, stars undefined, n unstated
findings.location: Page 6, Table 6 caption and text ('Spearman correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips')
findings.description: The preceding paragraph says the correlations are 'Spearman correlations of BWER', and the positive correlations with accentedness and with human BWER only make sense for an error rate (higher accent -> higher ASR error). Yet the caption and the sentence introducing the table both say 'ASR accuracy', which would imply the opposite sign. The significance stars are not defined anywhere and the n is not stated (the star pattern is consistent with n = 235 clips and *<.05, **<.01, ***<.001: r=0.148 -> p=0.022; r=0.195 -> p=0.002; r=0.215 -> p<0.001). The text also calls 0.15-0.35 correlations 'moderate'; by usual conventions the Whisper values are weak.
findings.evidence: Table 6 caption: 'Correlation study of human ratings and ASR accuracy'; text: 'Spearman correlations of BWER'; Whisper-S Acc 0.148*, Com 0.271***, Int 0.215***.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename to 'ASR BWER', define the star thresholds and n in the caption, and describe the Whisper correlations as weak-to-moderate.

findings.title: Text misreports which models have Int-BWER correlations below .30
findings.location: Page 6, text following Table 6 ('Namely, Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t were below rs = .30')
findings.description: In Table 6's Int (BWER) column, Whisper-S (0.215) and Whisper-L-t (0.195) are the two lowest; Whisper-L (0.281) is third. Whisper-S is omitted from the sentence although it is below .30 and below Whisper-L; all Whisper models except Whisper-M (0.353) are below .30.
findings.evidence: Table 6 Int (BWER): Whisper-S 0.215, Whisper-M 0.353, Whisper-L-t 0.195, Whisper-L 0.281.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct the sentence to name Whisper-S, Whisper-L-t and Whisper-L (or 'all Whisper models except Whisper-M').

findings.title: Cohen's h benchmarks misapplied: 0.14-0.19 is below the 'small' threshold; 0.24-0.34 is within 'small', not 'small-to-medium'
findings.location: Page 6, paragraph after Table 4 and 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'
findings.description: The paper itself quotes Cohen's conventions (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) and then describes h = 0.140 and 0.190 as 'both in the conventionally small range' (they are below 0.2, i.e., smaller than small) and h = 0.24-0.34 as 'the small-to-medium range' (they are well inside 0.2-0.5 and nowhere near 0.5). The rhetorical move from 'small' to 'small-to-medium' overstates the change.
findings.evidence: 'h=0.140 on the full set and h=0.190 on the ground-truth-verified subset, both in the conventionally "small" range (h=0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large)'; 'moves from small (h=0.14-0.19) into the small-to-medium range (h=0.24-0.34)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe 0.14-0.19 as below Cohen's small threshold and 0.24-0.34 as small; let the raw percentage-point drops carry the argument.

findings.title: One-sided testing and no multiple-comparison adjustment; 'McNemar's exact test' is conventionally two-sided
findings.location: Page 4 'Evaluation Metrics'; Table 3 (page 5); page 6 open-ended test
findings.description: All p-values reproduce as one-sided exact binomials (e.g., 160/37 -> 9.94e-20; 23/8 -> 0.00534; 14/6 -> 0.0577; 140/33 -> 3.43e-17). Two-sided values would be doubled (GT-verified deletion 0.115; full-set deletion 0.0107). Seven tests are reported in the main text plus 'all the ASR systems in the Appendix', with no correction; the full-set deletion result would survive Bonferroni over seven tests only marginally (0.0053x7 = 0.037). The direction of effect is plausible a priori, but 'Away' cases are analysed as substantively meaningful, which argues for two-sided testing.
findings.evidence: 'McNemar's exact test ... (equivalently, a one-sided exact binomial test on the discordant-pair counts)'; Table 3 GT-verified Deletion 14/6 p=5.8e-2.
findings.suggested_fix: Report two-sided p-values (or justify one-sided pre-registration) and state a multiple-comparison policy.

findings.title: Items and clips are nested within recordings and speakers; no clustering adjustment
findings.location: Page 4 'Evaluation Metrics' (McNemar on items); page 6 Table 6 (Spearman on 235 clips); page 3 (27 EdX instructors)
findings.description: The 1,107 questions come from recordings by 27 EdX instructors plus M3AV speakers, and multiple questions share the same recording and transcript. The 235 human-rated clips (168 from NIH) also come from a smaller number of speakers, and ratings are averaged across listeners. Item-level McNemar tests and clip-level Spearman correlations treat these as independent observations, which overstates precision beyond the model-pooling issue already noted.
findings.evidence: 'each of the 27 unique instructors'; Table 5 NIH n=168 of 235; Table 3 tests on item counts.
findings.suggested_fix: Use speaker- or recording-level bootstrap/cluster-robust inference, or report per-speaker aggregates.

findings.title: Table 1 reports pre-exclusion counts; post-exclusion L1/L2 split absent; 'courses' vs 'instructors'
findings.location: Page 4, Table 1; page 4 'Datasets'; page 3 'L1/L2 speaker status'
findings.description: Table 1 lists 1,380 EdX videos with 343 L1 / 1,037 L2 (sums correct, 75.1% L2), but the text says 148 videos were excluded and 1,232 are used in the ASR evaluation; the L1/L2 split of the analysed 1,232 is never given, so the 75/25 claim is verified only for the pre-exclusion set. Table 1's 'Groups' column reads '27 courses' whereas the methodology refers to '27 unique instructors'.
findings.evidence: Table 1: 'EdX 1,380 27 courses 5 343 1,037'; text: 'leaving 1,232 EdX and 123 M3AV videos'; page 3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report Table 1 for the analysed set (1,232) or add a post-exclusion row; reconcile 'courses' with 'instructors'.

findings.title: Table 5 topic and group comparisons rest on tiny, highly unbalanced cells with no dispersion or tests
findings.location: Page 6, Table 5 and 'Relationship to ASR Performance'
findings.description: NIH contributes 168 of 235 clips (71%); Social Sciences has n=5, Humanities n=6, Engineering n=8. L1 vs L2 is 39 vs 196 (83% L2, versus 75% in the corpus). Means are reported with no SD/CI and no test for the L1/L2 differences (Acc 2.6 vs 4.3; Com 2.3 vs 3.4; Int 0.28 vs 0.34), and the 'Speaker Group n' column counts clips rather than speakers. Statements such as 'As expected, the ratings of accentedness were higher in the L2 speaker group' are therefore descriptive only.
findings.evidence: Table 5: Social Sciences n=5, Humanities n=6, NIH n=168; L1 39, L2 196.
findings.suggested_fix: Add SDs or CIs, appropriate tests for the L1/L2 contrast, the number of distinct speakers per cell, and caution about the small EdX cells.

findings.title: Substitution + Deletion counts equal the 'All' counts exactly, including for 'Away' pairs
findings.location: Page 5, Table 3
findings.description: 137+23 = 160 and 29+8 = 37 (Full); 75+14 = 89 and 6+6 = 12 (GT-verified). Every discordant pair — including every 'Away' pair where the ASR context produced the correct answer and the reference did not — is assigned a keyword substitution or deletion. No discordant pair exists for items whose keyword was transcribed correctly, and no insertion category appears. Either the discordant set was pre-restricted to items with a keyword error (in which case the N of the test population is not 1,107/813 and the 'losses concentrate in specific items' conclusion is partly by construction), or the error-type assignment is exhaustive by design. The paper should say which.
findings.evidence: Table 3: All 160/37; Substitution 137/29; Deletion 23/8; GT: 89/12 = 75/6 + 14/6.
findings.suggested_fix: State how discordant pairs were assigned to error types, and report how many discordant pairs occurred on items without a keyword error.

findings.title: Unclear speaker/video/clip units for M3AV: '228 candidate NIH speakers' vs 123 M3AV videos and 168 NIH clips
findings.location: Page 3 ('16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers'); Table 1 (M3AV 123 videos); Table 5 (NIH n=168)
findings.description: M3AV contributes 123 videos in total across three venues, yet 228 NIH speakers are described as candidates and the human study has 168 NIH clips. The relationship between candidate speakers, selected videos, and rated clips (and how many distinct speakers underlie the 235 rated clips) is not stated, which matters for every independence assumption in the human-study analysis.
findings.evidence: 'speakers whose background could not be resolved this way are coded as unknown and excluded from the selected set (e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers)'; Table 1 M3AV Videos 123; Table 5 NIH n=168.
findings.suggested_fix: Give a flow diagram or table of candidate speakers -> selected videos -> rated clips per venue.

findings.title: Notation and presentation: 'N' vs 'n', truncated y-axis, no error bars
findings.location: Page 5 Table 3 ('N=1,107'); page 6 ('n=173'); Figure 4 y-axis (0.75-1.00); Figures 2-4
findings.description: Table 3 uses N for the number of items while the open-ended test uses n for the number of discordant pairs, inviting confusion about what the tests are computed on. Figure 4's y-axis starts at 0.75, visually magnifying 1-6 pt differences, and none of Figures 2-4 carry confidence intervals or error bars even though the paper argues from small differences between bars.
findings.evidence: Table 3 'Full (N=1,107)'; text 'toward=140, away=33, n=173'; Figure 4 y-axis ticks 0.75, 0.80, ..., 1.00.
findings.suggested_fix: Use one consistent symbol with an explicit definition, add CIs/error bars, and either start the axis at 0 or mark the truncation.

findings.title: Small rounding discrepancy in Table 4 Cohen's h for Llama3
findings.location: Page 6, Table 4
findings.description: Recomputing h = 2 asin(sqrt(p1)) - 2 asin(sqrt(p2)) from the stated accuracies gives 0.2395 (GPT4o, reported 0.240), 0.2519 (Llama3, reported 0.253) and 0.3379 (Qwen2.5, reported 0.338). The Llama3 value is off by 0.001, presumably from unrounded inputs; harmless, but worth making consistent.
findings.evidence: Table 4: Llama3 ref 0.773, asr 0.660, h 0.253; recomputed h(0.773, 0.660) = 0.2519.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute h from the same rounded accuracies shown, or state that h uses unrounded values.

summary: The ASR component of this paper is the weakest part of an otherwise interesting downstream-QA framing. The headline ASR result -- that Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t are 'substantially worse' than Whisper-S/M (Table 2: EdX WER 0.197/0.114 vs 0.074) -- is, by the authors' own admission on p.5, a long-form decoding artifact (repetition/hallucination loops), yet it is reported as model performance and propagated into the L1/L2 gap analysis (Fig 2), the human-correlation table (Table 6), and the claim that 'recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap'. No decoding protocol (library, chunking/VAD, condition-on-previous-text, compression-ratio/log-prob fallbacks, beam size) is given, and checkpoint identities are not specified (which 'large'? what is 'L-t'? which of the three wav2vec2 models is the footnoted lv60-self checkpoint?). The wav2vec2 baselines are LibriSpeech-960h read-speech CTC fine-tunes without an LM, so the 'two families' comparison mostly measures training-data domain rather than architecture or recency. The BWER metric is defined differently for the two corpora (slide-OCR biasing words for M3AV vs 'all non-function words' for EdX) and, contrary to the text, is lower than WER for every Whisper row and every Figure 3 domain, meaning non-keyword words are misrecognized at a higher rate than keywords. Text normalization, alignment for keyword scoring and window extraction, the unit of WER computation, and the reliability of EdX SRT captions as 'gold' are all under-specified in ways that materially affect the reported numbers.
strengths: Seven systems from two families are run on identical audio with identical references, and CER, WER and a keyword-focused rate are all reported (Table 2), which is more than most accessibility studies provide.

The authors correctly identify (p.5) that the poor Whisper-L numbers stem from hallucination/repetition on long audio rather than recognition capability, rather than reporting the anomaly uncritically.
Fixing Whisper's decoding language to English (p.3) is the right call for accented English lecture audio, where language auto-detection is known to misfire and trigger translation.

The M3AV subset uses genuinely human-corrected transcripts and the corpus's own slide-derived biasing-word list, giving one clean reference condition against which the EdX results can be sanity-checked.
The L1/L2 comparison is made across all seven systems (Fig 2) and the direction is consistent, which is a useful robustness check even if the magnitude analysis needs work.
Collecting human transcriptions of the same clips and scoring them with the same BWER (Table 5) creates a direct human-vs-ASR comparison that few accented-speech studies attempt.

findings.title: Whisper-L/L-t results are an acknowledged long-form decoding artifact but are reported and reused as model performance
findings.location: Page 4 Table 2; Page 5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' and Figure 2; Page 6 Table 6
findings.description: The paper states that the 2.7x higher WER of Whisper-L (0.197 vs 0.074 for Whisper-M on EdX) is 'driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit'. This is the well-known failure mode of Whisper's sequential 30-s-window decoding with conditioning on previous text, and it is routinely mitigated (condition_on_prev_tokens=False, compression-ratio and log-prob thresholds with temperature fallback, VAD-based or chunked long-form decoding). None of these settings, nor the inference library (openai-whisper vs transformers vs faster-whisper), beam size, or chunking strategy, is reported. Rather than fixing the protocol, the artifact-laden numbers are kept in Table 2, drive the Whisper-L L1/L2 gap in Figure 2 (0.133 vs 0.214, gap 0.081 -- the largest of any Whisper model and equal to Wav2Vec2-B's 0.079), enter the human-correlation analysis in Table 6, and underpin the narrative that smaller Whisper models are 'the strongest'. Supporting signatures of loops/dropped segments are visible in the numbers themselves: Whisper-L has a CER/WER ratio of 0.75 vs 0.51 for Whisper-S/M (long inserted/deleted spans rather than near-miss substitutions), Whisper-L's EdX CER (0.148) even exceeds Wav2Vec2-B's (0.111) despite lower WER, and Whisper-L-t drops from 0.114 (EdX) to 0.081 (M3AV) while Whisper-S/M are nearly identical across corpora (0.075/0.079, 0.074/0.077), consistent with recording-length-dependent failures. Since hallucination is more frequent on low-confidence (accented) audio, the Whisper-L L2 penalty is partly a hallucination artifact, not an accent-recognition effect.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'Counter-intuitively, the larger Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t models perform substantially worse than the smaller Whisper variants. Inspection of individual transcripts shows this is driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit.' Table 2: Whisper-L EdX CER/WER/BWER 0.148/0.197/0.145 vs Whisper-M 0.038/0.074/0.064. Figure 2: Whisper-L L1 0.133, L2 0.214.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-decode Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t with standard long-form safeguards (VAD/chunked decoding with stride, condition_on_prev_tokens=False, compression_ratio_threshold, logprob_threshold, temperature fallback) and report the full decoding configuration for all systems. Report the fraction of recordings affected by repetition loops, per-system S/D/I breakdown, and median as well as mean WER. If the authors want to keep the default-setting numbers as a 'deployment as-is' condition, label them as such and do not use them for the L1/L2 gap or correlation claims.

findings.title: Whisper checkpoints are not identified; 'Whisper-L-t' is undefined and the Radford et al. 2023 citation cannot cover it
findings.location: Page 2 Methodology, footnote 1; Page 4 Table 2
findings.description: Only Whisper-M is pinned (footnote 1: openai/whisper-medium). 'Whisper-L' could be large, large-v1, large-v2 or large-v3 -- these differ substantially in hallucination propensity (v3 is widely reported to loop more than v2) and in accented-speech WER. 'Whisper-L-t' is never expanded; if it is large-v3-turbo (a 4-decoder-layer distilled model released Oct 2024), it is neither described in Radford et al. 2023 nor a plain 'larger' model, so the sentence 'the larger Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t models' is misleading. It is also unclear whether Whisper-S is the multilingual 'small' or the English-only 'small.en'. Without checkpoint identities the central ASR comparison cannot be reproduced or interpreted.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'four Whisper checkpoints: Whisper-S, Whisper-M 1, Whisper-L, and Whisper-L-t (Radford et al. 2023)' with footnote 1 = https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-medium only.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the exact Hugging Face model id (and revision) for every checkpoint, expand 'L-t', and cite the appropriate release notes for large-v3 / large-v3-turbo if those were used.

findings.title: wav2vec2 baselines are LibriSpeech-960h read-speech CTC fine-tunes; footnote identifies only one of the three
findings.location: Page 2 Methodology, footnote 2; Page 4 Table 2; Page 5 Figure 2 discussion
findings.description: Footnote 2 points to facebook/wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self, which is presumably 'Wav2Vec2-L-s' (LV-60k pretraining, LibriSpeech-960h fine-tuning with self-training); the other two are unnamed but are presumably wav2vec2-base-960h and wav2vec2-large-960h, both pretrained and fine-tuned only on LibriSpeech read audiobooks. All three are character-level CTC models with no language model, no casing, no punctuation, and numbers spelled out as words. Comparing them to Whisper (680k h of diverse weakly supervised web audio) measures training-data domain mismatch, not 'architectures and capability levels' as claimed. Consequently the conclusion 'This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap' is not supported: the L2/L1 WER ratio in Figure 2 is essentially constant at ~1.4 across Whisper-S (1.40), Whisper-M (1.43), Whisper-L-t (1.38), Wav2Vec2-B (1.40) and Wav2Vec2-L (1.39); only the absolute gap grows, which follows trivially from higher overall WER. Whether greedy or LM-rescored CTC decoding was used is also not stated; a 4-gram LM typically removes a large share of out-of-domain wav2vec2 errors.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'seven ASR systems spanning two model families and a range of parameter counts, to test whether our findings hold across both architectures and capability levels'; footnote 2 = https://huggingface.co/facebook/wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self. p.5: 'the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.' Figure 2 L1/L2 bars: 0.058/0.081, 0.056/0.080, 0.086/0.119, 0.133/0.214, 0.196/0.275, 0.171/0.238, 0.135/0.174.
findings.suggested_fix: Name all three wav2vec2 checkpoints and the decoder (greedy vs. LM beam search). Reframe the family comparison as a training-data-domain comparison, report the L2/L1 ratio (or log-WER difference) alongside the absolute gap, and consider a more comparable third family (e.g., a conformer/CTC model trained on diverse data, or a commercial captioning service actually used by platforms).

findings.title: Text normalization is under-specified and asymmetric across systems (numbers, hyphens, symbols, acronyms, disfluencies)
findings.location: Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis', first paragraph
findings.description: The only normalization described is lowercasing, 'standardizes common number forms', and removing punctuation 'that does not change lexical identity' while retaining 'content-bearing hyphens, acronyms, and symbols'. LibriSpeech-trained wav2vec2 models can only emit letters, apostrophes and spaces: they write 'twenty twenty' for '2020', cannot produce hyphens ('co-occurrence' -> 'co occurrence'), '%', '+', '=', decimal points, or unit symbols, and transcribe every disfluency verbatim. Whisper emits digits, punctuation, and drops many fillers. EdX captions use digits and edited text. Retaining hyphens/symbols therefore penalizes wav2vec2 by construction, and the direction of number standardization (digits->words or words->digits, and how years, decimals, fractions and 'x squared'/'x^2' are handled) is unstated. This matters doubly for EdX BWER, where every number token is a 'non-function word' and STEM lectures (Engineering, CS, Science) are number-dense -- exactly the domains reported as worst in Figure 3.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'Normalization lowercases text, standardizes common number forms, and removes punctuation that does not change lexical identity. We retain content-bearing hyphens, acronyms, and symbols when their distinction matters to the lesson.' p.1 Introduction stresses 'formulas spoken aloud'.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply a single published normalizer (e.g., Whisper's EnglishTextNormalizer, which handles numerals, contractions, hyphens, symbols and British/American spelling) to both hypotheses and references for all systems, state it explicitly, and report how much WER changes for each family under the normalization.

findings.title: BWER is defined differently for EdX and M3AV yet compared side by side
findings.location: Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; Page 4 Table 2; Page 5 Figure 3; Page 6 Table 5
findings.description: Chen et al. (2024) define BWER over a slide-OCR biasing word list (rare, technical terms). For EdX the authors instead use 'all non-function words in the reference', which is a content-word error rate, not a biasing-word rate. The two are not comparable, but Table 2 tabulates them in parallel columns, Figure 3 plots EdX domains next to M3AV venues on the same 'BWER' axis, and Table 5/7 pool human 'Int (BWER)' across both corpora. The numbers confirm the mismatch: on EdX BWER tracks WER almost exactly (Figure 3: Humanities 0.047/0.047, Social Sciences 0.046/0.046, Science 0.043/0.044; Table 2 EdX BWER/WER ratios 0.72-1.15), whereas on M3AV the ratio diverges sharply (wav2vec2 BWER/WER 1.45-1.53; Whisper-M 0.69). The 'stricter measure' claim therefore holds, if at all, only for M3AV. The function-word list used for EdX is also not given.
