findings.evidence: p.3: 'Biasing Word Error Rate (BWER) (Chen et al. 2024), restricted to rare/technical vocabulary: for M3AV, drawn from slide OCR text released with the corpus; for EdX, approximated as all non-function words in the reference'. Table 2: Wav2Vec2-B EdX WER 0.253 / BWER 0.290 vs M3AV WER 0.274 / BWER 0.402.
findings.suggested_fix: Either derive an EdX keyword list comparable to M3AV's (e.g., from the LLM-identified knowledge-intensive keywords already produced in Stage 1, or from course syllabi/slides), or rename the EdX metric (e.g., content-word error rate) and stop pooling it with M3AV BWER in tables, figures and the human study.

findings.title: Figure 3 and Table 2 contradict the claim that topic-specific vocabulary is harder than function words
findings.location: Page 5 Figure 3 and surrounding text; Page 4 Table 2
findings.description: The text asserts 'topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words' and that 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates'. But for Whisper-M, BWER is lower than or equal to WER in every domain in Figure 3 (CS 0.072 vs 0.081; Engineering 0.074 vs 0.093; Humanities 0.047 vs 0.047; Science 0.043 vs 0.044; Social Sciences 0.046 vs 0.046; IPP 0.039 vs 0.067; MLS 0.035 vs 0.056; NIH 0.061 vs 0.083), and in Table 2 BWER < WER for all four Whisper rows on both corpora. If the error rate on keyword tokens is below the overall rate, the error rate on the remaining (function/common) tokens must be above it -- the opposite of the stated conclusion. Only the wav2vec2 rows show BWER > WER. The high function-word error rate for Whisper is itself informative: it is the signature of a non-verbatim reference (edited captions dropping fillers, false starts, 'gonna'->'going to'), which bears on the next finding.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'We observe that topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words.' and 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates.' Figure 3 bar labels as listed; Table 2 Whisper-S EdX WER 0.075 / BWER 0.069, Whisper-M M3AV WER 0.077 / BWER 0.053.
findings.suggested_fix: Revise the claim to match the data, or report the complementary non-keyword error rate (U-WER in the Le et al./Chen et al. terminology) explicitly so the reader can see which class of words fails more. Consider reporting keyword recall/precision rather than a rate that is dominated by common words on EdX.

findings.title: EdX SRT captions are called 'independently verified gold-standard' without any verification; likely non-verbatim and possibly in Whisper's training data
findings.location: Page 2 Methodology ('paired-transcript design' and 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts'); Page 4 'Datasets'
findings.description: Platform caption files are produced by vendors or auto-captioning and then lightly edited; they are typically non-verbatim (disfluencies, repetitions and false starts removed; numbers and formulas rendered in caption style; occasional paraphrase) and their accuracy is not audited. The paper offers no spot-check WER of the captions against a human verbatim transcript, yet calls them 'independently verified'. Caption-style editing inflates WER for verbatim recognizers (wav2vec2 transcribes every 'uh'; Whisper partially suppresses fillers), inflates the EdX 'non-function-word' BWER for every caption-side edit, and depresses the Whisper function-word accuracy noted above. A speech researcher will also ask whether publicly posted EdX/YouTube captions were part of Whisper's 680k-hour web-scraped training set, which would advantage Whisper and bias it toward caption style. For M3AV, Chen et al. (2024) report WER/BWER for Whisper on the same references; the paper does not compare against those published numbers even though it would be the obvious sanity check.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'an independently verified gold-standard reference transcript'; 'Reference transcripts are not produced by the authors, but drawn from each corpus's own existing verified source: EdX's officially published caption files'. p.4: 'Gold-standard transcripts are the platform-provided EdX SRT captions'.
findings.suggested_fix: Human-transcribe a random sample of EdX segments verbatim and report the caption WER; state whether captions were professional, auto-generated, or mixed; report Whisper/wav2vec2 M3AV numbers next to those in Chen et al. 2024; and discuss training-data overlap as a threat to validity.

findings.title: Unlabeled Figure 4 bars appear to show Whisper-L/L-t giving the highest QA accuracy, contradicting the 'ordering mirrors Table 2' claim
findings.location: Page 5 Figure 4 and 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions'
findings.description: Figure 4 shows four blue (Whisper) and three orange (Wav2Vec2) bars per QA model but never labels which bar is which system. If bars follow Table 2 row order (which the wav2vec2 bars support: GPT4o 0.895/0.905/0.906 rises from B to L to L-s, matching their WER order), then the Whisper bars read S 0.933, M 0.926, L-t 0.944, L 0.945 for GPT4o; 0.903/0.892/0.916/0.919 for Llama3; 0.904/0.899/0.921/0.919 for Qwen2.5. That would make Whisper-L -- the system with 2.7x the WER of Whisper-M -- the best ASR context for every QA model, directly contradicting 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'. It would also be strong evidence that Whisper-L's Table 2 WER is inflated by insertions outside the +/-100-word keyword windows (supporting finding 1), unless items whose ASR window could not be aligned were silently dropped per system, in which case Whisper-L's QA accuracy is inflated by selection. Either way the text's interpretation cannot stand without labels and per-system item counts.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'the stronger Whisper systems produce the smallest drops. This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'. Figure 4 bar labels (read from image): GPT4o ref 0.954, Whisper 0.933/0.926/0.944/0.945, Wav2Vec2 0.895/0.905/0.906; Llama3 ref 0.940, Whisper 0.903/0.892/0.916/0.919; Qwen2.5 ref 0.935, Whisper 0.904/0.899/0.921/0.919.
findings.suggested_fix: Label every bar with its ASR system, state whether the item set is identical across the seven systems (N per system), and reconcile the discussion with the actual ordering. If Whisper-L windows really outperform Whisper-M windows, say so and connect it to the long-form decoding artifact.

findings.title: Human transcription 'BWER' of 0.28 (L1) / 0.34 (L2) on 25-word clips is implausibly high and undermines the 'models outperform humans' claim
findings.location: Page 6 Table 5 and Table 6 discussion; Page 7 Table 7
findings.description: Human listeners are reported to mistranscribe 28% of content words for L1 speakers and 34% for L2 speakers, versus ~6-7% for Whisper-S/M on the same speech. Human word error on intelligible English is typically in the low single digits; a 4-5x deficit relative to a medium Whisper model is not credible unless the human protocol was unusually hard (single playback, no replay, time pressure, non-expert or non-native raters) or the human transcripts were not normalized the same way as ASR output (typos, casing, numerals, spelling variants counted as errors). The paper does not describe the human transcription protocol or normalization, yet concludes 'these models outperform human listeners in transcription accuracy'. Clip-level BWER with roughly 10 content words per clip is also quantized in 0.1 steps and heavily zero-inflated for ASR ('numerous instances of 0 BWER'), which makes the Spearman correlations in Table 6 fragile.
findings.evidence: Table 5: L1 n=39 Int (BWER) 0.28; L2 n=196 Int (BWER) 0.34; Table 7: 0.32 / 0.37. p.6: 'the ASR models had numerous instances of 0 BWER, whereas human listeners rarely had zero when averaged across listeners. In other words, these models outperform human listeners in transcription accuracy'. p.7: 'given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the human transcription task (number of listens, time limits, rater L1 background, spelling tolerance) and apply the identical normalizer to human and ASR transcripts before scoring. Report per-clip ASR WER for all seven systems on these same clips (a hallucination-free comparison that is currently missing) and consider rank-based metrics that tolerate quantization.

findings.title: Unit of ASR evaluation is inconsistent: 'segments', 'full recordings', and 'clips' are all used without saying which WER is in which table
findings.location: Page 2 Methodology; Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; Page 6 Table 6 text
findings.description: Page 2 says 'ASR fidelity is measured both in short clips given to human raters and over full recordings'; page 3 says 'Each audio segment is transcribed independently by the seven ASR systems'; page 5 attributes failures to 'long lecture audio'; page 6 says correlations used 'ASR accuracy on the clips'. It is never stated whether Table 2 is a corpus-level WER (total errors / total reference words) or a mean of per-recording WERs, whether per-recording WER was capped at 1.0, or whether the clip-level ASR transcripts used in Table 6 came from cutting the audio or from aligning the full-recording transcript. For Whisper-L these choices change the numbers enormously: a handful of recordings with runaway repetition loops (WER >> 100%) can dominate a mean-of-recordings figure and would not appear at all in re-transcribed short clips.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'ASR fidelity is measured both in short clips given to human raters and over full recordings'; p.3: 'Each audio segment is transcribed independently'; p.3: 'We calculate WER and CER for each system, speaker, recording, and topic'; p.6: 'Spearman correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips'.
findings.suggested_fix: State precisely the audio unit fed to each recognizer, the aggregation used in every table/figure (pooled vs. macro-average, capping), and whether clip-level results come from separate decoding. Add a table of per-clip WER for all seven systems on the human-study clips.

findings.title: Alignment used for keyword scoring and ASR window extraction is undefined ('aligned ASR span', 'approved equivalent', 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic')
findings.location: Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; Page 3-4 'Question Construction' and 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'
findings.description: BWER scoring counts a keyword correct 'only when its lexical form or an approved equivalent appears in the aligned ASR span', and QA uses 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window' of +/-100 words. Neither the alignment algorithm (Levenshtein word alignment? timestamp-based? sentence-level?) nor who approves 'equivalents' is described, and the multiword 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic' is named but not defined. Mapping a reference-anchored 100-word window into an ASR transcript of different length requires word-level alignment; when the ASR output contains repetition loops or dropped segments (Whisper-L) the 'corresponding' window is ill-defined, and how such cases were handled (dropped? shifted?) determines the per-system QA results in Figure 4. A keyword substituted by a near-homophone that lands one position off in the alignment could be scored as both a deletion and an insertion depending on the aligner.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'A keyword is counted as correct only when its lexical form or an approved equivalent appears in the aligned ASR span.' p.3: 'we additionally apply a fragmentation/gluing heuristic to filter out unreliable candidate matches caused by tokenization artifacts across punctuation or line breaks.' p.4: 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window as context'.
findings.suggested_fix: Specify the aligner (e.g., jiwer/SCTK word alignment, or forced alignment with timestamps), the equivalence list and its provenance, the heuristic's rules, and the policy for unalignable windows; report how many items per ASR system were affected.

findings.title: Speaker clustering ignored: 1,232 EdX videos come from 27 instructors, but WER and L1/L2 gaps are reported per video with no CIs
findings.location: Page 3 (27 instructors); Page 4 Table 1-2; Page 5 Figure 2
findings.description: WER for the EdX corpus is aggregated over videos, yet the videos come from only 27 instructors, so recognition errors are strongly clustered by speaker (voice, microphone, accent, topic). The L1/L2 comparison in Figure 2 is therefore effectively a comparison across a small number of L1 vs. L2 instructors, not across 343 vs. 1,037 independent recordings, and a single prolific instructor can shift a group mean. No per-speaker aggregation, confidence intervals, or significance tests are given for any ASR comparison, and differences such as Whisper-S 0.075 vs Whisper-M 0.074 are described as if meaningful ('closely tied'). Standard ASR practice for speaker-group fairness analyses is to report speaker-level WER with bootstrap CIs.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors was individually researched'; Table 1: EdX 1,380 videos, L1 343, L2 1,037; Figure 2 reports single point estimates per system and group.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the number of L1 and L2 instructors, compute speaker-level WER (macro-average over instructors) with bootstrap CIs, and test the L1/L2 difference with speaker as the unit (or a mixed model with speaker random effects).

findings.title: Reference-condition QA accuracy is reported as three different numbers (text, Figure 4, Figure 1)
findings.location: Page 5 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' text vs Figure 4; Page 2 Figure 1 bottom panel
findings.description: The text says GPT4o reaches 99.3% in the reference condition, Llama3 98.3%, Qwen2.5 97.9%. Figure 4's 'ref' bars read 0.954, 0.940 and 0.935. Figure 1's evaluation panel shows 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%', 'ASR (Whisper) 90.8%', 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'. Three mutually inconsistent sets of reference accuracies make it impossible to know the actual size of the reference-to-ASR drop that the ASR results are supposed to explain (p.6 later cites '2.7 to 4.7 pt' from an unavailable Table 11).
findings.evidence: p.5: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'; Figure 4 ref bar labels 0.954 / 0.940 / 0.935; Figure 1: '94.3%', '90.8%', 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'.
findings.suggested_fix: Reconcile all three locations (possibly the text refers to the GT-verified subset and the figures to the full set -- if so, say so) and state N for each.

findings.title: language='en' handling is ambiguous ('additionally run') and interacts with code-switched speech
findings.location: Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis', first sentences
findings.description: The EdX Whisper models are 'additionally run with decoding language fixed to English' after an 'observed accuracy improvement', while M3AV 'fixes English decoding throughout'. It is unclear whether Table 2/Figure 2 report the language-fixed run, the auto-detect run, or a mix; the auto-detect results are not shown even though the observed improvement is itself a relevant accessibility finding (auto-detect misfires on accented speech). The paper also says non-English content was excluded yet mentions 'code-switched speech'; forcing English on code-switched segments makes Whisper translate or hallucinate while the caption may preserve the non-English words, producing spurious errors. Whether task='transcribe' was enforced is not stated.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'For EdX, Whisper models are additionally run with decoding language fixed to English (language="en") rather than automatic language detection, following an observed accuracy improvement on lecture audio with accented and code-switched speech; M3AV transcription fixes English decoding throughout.'
findings.suggested_fix: State which run is reported everywhere, report the auto-detect vs. fixed-English WER difference (it supports the paper's thesis), confirm task=transcribe, and quantify how much code-switched material remains after the non-English exclusion.

findings.title: wav2vec2 long-audio handling (chunking, stride) and decoding are not described
findings.location: Page 2-3 Methodology / ASR Transcription
findings.description: wav2vec2 CTC models are trained on utterances of at most ~35 s and cannot process minutes-long lecture audio in one pass (quadratic attention memory, degraded convolutional positional encoding). Running them on full recordings therefore requires chunking; unstrided fixed-length chunks split words at boundaries and add errors, whereas overlapping/strided chunking (as in the HF pipeline) does not. The chunk length, overlap, greedy vs. LM decoding, and audio resampling to 16 kHz mono are all unstated, so a nontrivial fraction of the wav2vec2 WER in Table 2 may be preprocessing-induced.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'Each audio segment is transcribed independently by the seven ASR systems.' No further inference details are given for the wav2vec2 family anywhere in the paper.
findings.suggested_fix: Report chunk length/stride, decoder, sampling-rate conversion, and any VAD for the wav2vec2 runs.

findings.title: Insertion errors are dropped from the downstream error analysis although they are the dominant Whisper-L failure mode
findings.location: Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; Page 5 Table 3
findings.description: The paper says errors are categorized into substitutions, deletions and insertions, but no S/D/I breakdown is reported for any system, and the QA-linked analysis (Table 3) only considers substitution and deletion (137 + 23 = 160 = all 'toward' cases). For Whisper-M this is defensible, but the appendix analysis 'over all the ASR systems' would then be blind to hallucinated insertions, which are precisely what corrupts Whisper-L windows and what a caption reader would experience as fabricated content. A per-system S/D/I table would also directly substantiate the hallucination explanation offered on p.5.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'Errors are categorized as substitutions, deletions, and insertions for aggregate WER/CER/BWER. The downstream question-generation stage specifically targets substitution and deletion errors on content words'. Table 3 rows: Substitution 137/29, Deletion 23/8, All 160/37.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-system S/D/I breakdown to Table 2 (or an appendix table) and include an insertion/hallucination category in the item-level error analysis.

findings.title: Whisper-M is selected as 'the best working ASR' for all downstream analyses on the basis of artifact-affected rankings
findings.location: Page 5 Figure 3 text; Page 5 Table 3; Page 6 Table 4
findings.description: All keyword-level, domain-level (Figure 3), McNemar (Table 3) and open-ended (Table 4) analyses use Whisper-M because it ranked best in Table 2. If Whisper-L were decoded with standard long-form safeguards it would very likely rank first (as it does on essentially every published long-form English benchmark), and Figure 4 already hints its keyword windows are better. The framework's headline downstream numbers thus rest on a ranking that the authors themselves say does not reflect capability. Would the topic and L1/L2 conclusions change with a properly decoded Whisper-L?
findings.evidence: p.5: 'Figure 3 further shows the performance of Whisper-M, the best working ASR'; Table 3 caption: 'over the Whisper-M ASR transcript'; Table 4 caption: 'ref vs. Whisper-M ASR transcript'.
findings.suggested_fix: Repeat the downstream analyses with the corrected Whisper-L (or report them for all systems in the main text) and discuss sensitivity of conclusions to ASR choice.

summary: The paper's numerical backbone is partly self-consistent: every p-value in Table 3 and the open-ended test reproduces exactly from the reported discordant counts, Table 4's Cohen's h values reproduce, Figure 2's L1/L2 WERs pool (25/75) to Table 2's overall WERs, and Figure 1's 94.3%/90.6%/3.7pt/p=9.9e-20 equal the 3-LLM means of Figure 4's bars and Table 3's full-set row. However, that same reconciliation exposes serious cross-reference failures: the prose reports reference QA accuracies of 99.3/98.3/97.9% that appear nowhere in Figure 1 or Figure 4 (which show ~95.4/94.0/93.5%), Table 3 is labelled N=1,107 per-item but its counts only yield the stated 3.7pt gap and h=0.14 if pooled over 3,321 item-model pairs, and the prose claims about Figure 3/Figure 4 ("BWER exposes disparities WER understates", "ordering mirrors Table 2", "gap narrows for strongest Whisper") are contradicted by the plotted values. Several headline claims (QA differences across topics/knowledge intensity, human study "confirming" QA trends) have no supporting table, and the text points to a nonexistent Table 11, a nameless "Section", and an Appendix that is not in the submission. The seven-ASR/three-LLM/two-dataset framing is consistent throughout, but the methodology's "retain only verified items" rule conflicts with the primary use of the unverified 1,107-item set.
strengths: Table 3 and open-ended McNemar/exact-binomial p-values reproduce exactly from the reported toward/away counts (e.g., 160 vs 37 -> 9.94e-20; 140 vs 33 -> 3.43e-17; 14 vs 6 -> 0.0577), and substitution+deletion counts sum exactly to the 'All' rows (137+23=160, 29+8=37; 75+14=89, 6+6=12).

Table 4 arithmetic is internally consistent: drops 10.3/11.3/14.0 pt match ref-asr, Cohen's h recomputes to 0.240/0.252/0.338, and the pooled open-ended net drop (140-33)/900 = 11.9 pt matches the mean of the three drops (11.87).
Figure 2's L1/L2 WERs, weighted 25/75 as stated for the corpus, reproduce Table 2's overall WERs to within 0.001 for all seven systems (e.g., Whisper-S 0.25*0.058+0.75*0.081=0.075).

Count bookkeeping is consistent: Table 1 L1+L2 = video totals (343+1,037=1,380; 31+92=123), 1,380-148=1,232, 1,232+123=1,355, keywords 457+656=1,113, Table 5 topic n's sum to the speaker-group n (235), and Table 7 rows sum to the stated 194 clips.

Figure 1's summary numbers (94.3% vs 90.6%, 3.7 pt, p=9.9e-20) are exactly the 3-LLM mean of Figure 4's reference bars (0.943) and second-Whisper bars (0.906) and Table 3's full-set row, so the figure, Table 3 and Figure 4 agree with one another.

The seven ASR systems / three QA LLMs / two datasets framing is used consistently in the contributions, Methodology, Table 2, Figure 2, Figure 4 and Table 6 (all list the same seven systems in the same order).

findings.title: Text reference-QA accuracies (99.3/98.3/97.9%) contradict Figure 4 and Figure 1
findings.location: Page 5, 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' paragraph vs Figure 4 (page 5) and Figure 1 (page 2)
findings.description: The prose states GPT4o reaches 99.3% in the reference condition, Llama3 98.3% and Qwen2.5 97.9%. Figure 4's y-axis runs 0.75-1.00 and the grey 'ref' bars top out near 0.95: the bar labels read approximately 0.954 (GPT4o), 0.940 (Llama3), 0.935 (Qwen2.5). Their mean is 0.943, which is exactly Figure 1's 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%'. Thus Figure 1 and Figure 4 agree with each other and both disagree with the text by 4-5 points. No table reports the 99.3/98.3/97.9 values, and if they were true the Whisper-M drops quoted as '2.7 to 4.7 pt' would put ASR-condition accuracies at ~96.6/93.6/94.3, which also do not appear in Figure 4.
findings.evidence: Text: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'. Figure 4 ref bar labels ~0.954 / 0.940 / 0.935 (all below the 0.95-1.00 gridline region); Figure 1: 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%'.
findings.suggested_fix: Reconcile the prose with the figures; if 99.3/98.3/97.9 refer to a different subset (e.g., GT-verified) or a different denominator, state it explicitly and add a table giving reference and per-ASR accuracies for every model so the numbers can be cross-checked.

findings.title: Table 3 'N=1,107' is inconsistent with its own counts, the 3.7 pt gap, and the per-model test described in Methods
findings.location: Page 5, Table 3 and caption; page 4 'Evaluation Metrics'; page 2 Figure 1; page 6 text 'h = 0.140'
findings.description: Methods say 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements ... via McNemar's exact test', yet Table 3 gives one row per question set 'for all QA LLMs' with N labelled 1,107 (and 813). With 160 toward / 37 away on 1,107 items the net accuracy drop would be (160-37)/1107 = 11.1 pt, which contradicts Figure 1's 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points' and the '2.7 to 4.7 pt' drops quoted on page 6. The counts only yield 3.7 pt if pooled over 3 LLMs x 1,107 = 3,321 item-model pairs ((160-37)/3321 = 3.70 pt), and Cohen's h(0.943, 0.906) = 0.141 matches the reported 0.140 only under that pooled reading. So the N label is wrong (or the counts are), per-model results promised in Methods are never reported, and the pooling of paired tests across three dependent answerers is undisclosed.
findings.evidence: Table 3 rows 'Full (N=1,107) All 160 37 9.9x10^-20 0.140'; Methods: 'For each QA model, we identify disagreements between the reference-context and ASR-context answer on identical items'; Figure 1: 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'; computed 123/1107 = 11.1 pt vs 123/3321 = 3.7 pt.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel N as the number of item-model pairs actually tested (or report three per-model rows as the Methods describe), and state explicitly whether counts are pooled across LLMs.

findings.title: Claim that QA ordering 'mirrors' Table 2 is contradicted by Figure 4 within the Whisper family
findings.location: Page 5, 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' vs Figure 4 (page 5) and Table 2 (page 4)
findings.description: The text says the QA-accuracy ordering 'closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'. In Figure 4, within every LLM group the two dark-blue bars (positions 4-5) are the tallest Whisper bars (~0.944/0.945 GPT4o, 0.916/0.919 Llama3, 0.921/0.918 Qwen2.5) while the second bar is the lowest (~0.926/0.892/0.899). The second bar must be Whisper-M: its 3-LLM mean (0.906) equals Figure 1's 'ASR (Whisper) 90.6%' and its drops (2.8/4.8/3.6 pt) match the '2.7 to 4.7 pt' quoted on page 6. Under the paper's consistent ordering (Table 2, Figure 2, Table 6: S, M, L-t, L) the tallest Whisper bars are Whisper-L-t and Whisper-L, which have the worst Whisper WER in Table 2 (EdX 0.114 and 0.197 vs 0.074 for Whisper-M). Hence the best-WER model yields the lowest QA accuracy among Whisper systems and the worst-WER model the highest, the reverse of the claimed mirroring. The figure legend labels only families, so individual bars cannot be identified by the reader.
findings.evidence: Text: 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'; Table 2 WER EdX: Whisper-M 0.074, Whisper-L-t 0.114, Whisper-L 0.197; Figure 4 Whisper bars (GPT4o) ~0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945; Figure 1 'ASR (Whisper) 90.6%' = mean(0.926, 0.892, 0.899).
findings.suggested_fix: Label each bar in Figure 4 with its ASR system (or provide the table), and revise the claim to reflect the actual within-family ordering, or explain why Whisper-L/L-t hallucination failures on long audio do not affect the +/-100-word QA windows.

findings.title: 'Technical vocabulary is a greater challenge than function words' / 'BWER exposes disparities WER understates' contradicted by Figure 3 and Table 2
findings.location: Page 5, 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' vs Figure 3 (page 5) and Table 2 (page 4)
findings.description: The text asserts, citing Figure 3 (Whisper-M by domain), that topic-specific vocabulary is harder than surrounding function words, and earlier that BWER exposes disparities that WER understates. In Figure 3, BWER is at or below WER in all eight domains (EdX CS 0.072 vs 0.081; Engineering 0.074 vs 0.093; Humanities 0.047 vs 0.047; Science 0.043 vs 0.044; Social Sciences 0.046 vs 0.046; M3AV IPP 0.039 vs 0.067; MLS 0.035 vs 0.056; NIH 0.061 vs 0.083). In Table 2, BWER < WER for all four Whisper models on both datasets (Whisper-M: 0.064 vs 0.074 EdX, 0.053 vs 0.077 M3AV); BWER exceeds WER only for the three Wav2Vec2 rows. For the 'best working ASR' the paper's own figure shows the opposite of the stated claim.
findings.evidence: Text: 'We observe that topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words' and 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates'; Figure 3 M3AV IPP WER 0.067 vs BWER 0.039; Table 2 Whisper-M M3AV WER 0.077 vs BWER 0.053.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the claim to the Wav2Vec2 family where Table 2 supports it, or explain how the EdX BWER approximation ('all non-function words') and the M3AV OCR keyword set produce BWER below WER for Whisper while still supporting the claim.

findings.title: 'Gap narrows for strongest Whisper, widens for weaker Wav2Vec2' not supported by Figure 2's labels
findings.location: Page 5, Figure 2 discussion vs Figure 2 bar labels (page 5)
findings.description: The text says the L1/L2 gap widens for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrows for the strongest Whisper models, concluding 'recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap'. Figure 2's labels give absolute gaps of 0.023 (Whisper-S), 0.024 (Whisper-M), 0.033 (Whisper-L-t), 0.081 (Whisper-L), 0.079 (Wav2Vec-B), 0.067 (Wav2Vec-L), 0.039 (Wav2Vec-L-s): the largest gap belongs to a Whisper model. Relative gaps (L2/L1 - 1) are 40%, 43%, 38%, 61%, 40%, 39%, 29%: the strongest Whisper models (S, M) have the same relative disparity as Wav2Vec-B/L, and the smallest relative gap is Wav2Vec2-L-s. The narrative sentence is therefore inconsistent with the plotted numbers under either an absolute or relative reading.
findings.evidence: Text: 'with the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.' Figure 2: Whisper-L 0.133 vs 0.214 (gap 0.081, +61%); Wav2Vec-L-s 0.135 vs 0.174 (gap 0.039, +29%); Whisper-S 0.058 vs 0.081 (+40%).
findings.suggested_fix: State whether the gap is measured absolutely or relatively, report it explicitly per system, and soften or remove the 'recent models reduce the gap' inference given Whisper-L.

findings.title: Abstract/Conclusion claim QA differences 'across topics' and 'knowledge-intensive material' that no table or figure reports
findings.location: Page 1 Abstract; page 7 Conclusions; page 2 Methodology (knowledge-intensity classification); Results pages 5-7
findings.description: The Abstract states results 'show substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material', and the Conclusion says 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'. The Results contain no QA-by-topic or QA-by-knowledge-intensity breakdown: Figure 4 is LLM x ASR system, Table 3 is by error type, Table 4 is open-ended, Table 7 is by QA-correctness group. The lower/higher knowledge-intensity segment classification described on page 2 is never used anywhere in Results. Moreover, page 5 describes the LLMs' reference performance as 'very similar' and Figure 4 shows <=2 pt spread among the three reference bars, contradicting 'substantial differences among QA LLMs'.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material'; page 5: 'Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%) show very similar performance'; page 2: 'segments are classified as lower or higher in knowledge intensity' (never referenced again).
findings.suggested_fix: Either add the QA-by-topic and QA-by-knowledge-intensity results to the main text or remove these claims from the Abstract and Conclusion.

findings.title: Methodology says only judge-verified items are retained, but primary analyses use the 1,107 unverified 'Full' set
findings.location: Page 4 first column (answerability check) vs page 4 'Datasets' paragraph, Table 3, Figure 4, Figure 1
findings.description: The answerability check states 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage'. The Datasets paragraph then reports '1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification', and the headline results (Table 3 'Full (N=1,107)', Figure 4, Figure 1's p=9.9e-20) are computed on all 1,107, i.e., including 294 items that were not confirmed. The phrase 'after ... answerability verification' for the 1,107 set is also self-contradictory if only 813 passed. Separately, page 3 says each selected keyword yields 'one four-option multiple-choice question', yet 1,113 keywords produce 1,107 questions with no explanation of the 6 missing items.
findings.evidence: 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct' vs 'yielding 1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-veriﬁed) after leak-ﬁltering and answerability veriﬁcation'; Table 3 'Full (N=1,107)'; '1,113 knowledge-error keywords (457 EdX, 656 M3AV)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the retention rule and the analysed set agree: either designate the 813-item set as primary or describe the Full set as pre-verification and justify its use; account for the 1,113 -> 1,107 difference.

findings.title: References to nonexistent Table 11, an unnamed 'Section', and an Appendix that is not in the submission
findings.location: Page 6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions' ('Table 11', 'see Section for details'); page 5 and page 6 Appendix references (x5)
findings.description: The paper has Tables 1-7 only, but the open-ended section compares to '2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11'; those multiple-choice drops appear nowhere in the manuscript (they can only be approximated by subtracting Figure 4 bar labels: ~2.8/4.8/3.6 pt). The same paragraph cites '(see Section for details)' with the section name missing. Five results are deferred to an Appendix that does not exist in the 9-page file: verified-subset QA accuracies (p.5), McNemar tests over all ASR systems (p.6), human-study design and quality control (p.6), and 'other correlations' (p.6). Consequently, the per-ASR statistical claims and the human-study protocol cannot be checked.
findings.evidence: '(10.3 to 14.0 percentage points (pt) versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11)'; 'distractors (see Section for details)'; 'We further report the accuracies from the veriﬁed question subset in the Appendix'; 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix'; 'other correlations are available in the appendix'.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the table and section references, include the appendix (or move the essential deferred numbers into the main text), and report the 2.7-4.7 pt multiple-choice drops in a table.

findings.title: Table 6 caption and text say 'ASR accuracy' while the correlated quantity is BWER (an error rate)
findings.location: Page 6, Table 6 caption and 'Relationship to ASR Performance' paragraphs
findings.description: The paragraph introducing the analysis says correlations are of 'BWER', but Table 6's caption reads 'Correlation study of human ratings and ASR accuracy' and the text says 'Spearman correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips'. All 21 coefficients are positive (0.148-0.522). Positive correlation of accentedness with ASR accuracy would mean more-accented speech is transcribed more accurately, contradicting the paper's narrative; the signs only make sense if the ASR variable is BWER. Table 5's caption similarly defines 'Int' as 'the BWER of human transcription' while the column is labelled 'Intelligibility', so higher values mean lower intelligibility; the text then says 'lower intelligibility (i.e., more words mistranscribed)', requiring the reader to invert the label.
findings.evidence: 'Spearman correlations of BWER' vs Table 6 caption 'human ratings and ASR accu-racy' and 'correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips'; Table 6 Wav2Vec2-L Acc 0.453***, Com 0.522***, Int 0.430*** (all positive).
findings.suggested_fix: Rename the caption and text to 'ASR BWER' (or report accuracy with sign flipped) and label Table 5/6 columns so that direction is unambiguous.

findings.title: Human study 'confirms' QA trends, but Table 7 gives no test or correlation and contradicts 'frequently 100% accurate'
findings.location: Page 1 Abstract; page 2 contribution bullet 3; page 7 Conclusions vs Table 7 and its paragraph (page 7)
findings.description: The Abstract says the human study 'shows consistent observations with ASR and QA LLMs' performance', contribution 3 says it 'confirms the observed performance trends', and the Conclusion says 'perceived accentedness correlates with ASR errors and downstream QA loss'. For QA, the only evidence is Table 7: two-group descriptive means (Acc 3.8 vs 4.3, Com 3.1 vs 3.4, BWER 0.32 vs 0.37, %L2 84 vs 91) with no significance test, no correlation coefficient, and no statement of which ASR transcript was used for the clip QA. The word 'correlates' is thus not backed by any correlation statistic. The same paragraph says the QA LLMs 'were frequently 100% accurate', but Table 7 shows only 56 of 194 clips (29%) at 100% and 138 (71%) below 100%.
findings.evidence: Conclusion: 'perceived accentedness correlates with ASR errors and downstream QA loss'; Table 7: 'QA 100%Correct n=56 ... QA < 100%Correct n=138'; text: 'were frequently 100% accurate'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report a test or correlation for the Table 7 comparison, name the ASR system used, and tone down 'confirms/correlates' and 'frequently 100% accurate' to match the descriptive evidence.

findings.title: Text lists Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t as the sub-.30 correlations but Table 6 also has Whisper-S below .30
findings.location: Page 6, 'Relationship to ASR Performance' vs Table 6 Int (BWER) column
findings.description: The text says 'several models had significant but very low correlations with human transcription error rates. Namely, Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t were below rs = .30.' Table 6's Int (BWER) column reads Whisper-S 0.215, Whisper-M 0.353, Whisper-L-t 0.195, Whisper-L 0.281. findings.title: The 148 excluded EdX recordings are attributed to different criteria on page 2 and page 4

findings.title: Human-study paragraph says the QA LLMs generated the questions, contradicting the Gemini-only generation design

findings.title: Footnote URLs do not line up with the model names they should identify

findings.title: Contribution bullet promises closed- and open-ended questions, but Abstract and Conclusion describe closed-form only
findings.location: Page 2 contribution bullet 2 vs page 1 Abstract and page 7 Conclusions; page 6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'

findings.title: 'Humanities and Social Sciences are more robust' omits Science, which has the lowest error in Figure 3

findings.evidence: 'EdX Humanities and Social Sciences recordings are more robust'; Figure 3: EdX Science WER 0.044, BWER 0.043 (lowest).

findings.title: Which ASR system's errors define the 'knowledge-error keywords' used for all seven systems?
findings.location: Page 3 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation'; page 4 'Datasets' ('1,113 knowledge-error keywords'); Table 3; Figure 4
findings.description: Keywords are selected as reference/ASR pairs ('keeping only pairs where the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept') and are called 'knowledge-error keywords'. In Table 3 the substitution and deletion counts sum exactly to the 'All' counts (137+23=160, 29+8=37), implying every discordant item involves a keyword mis-transcribed by Whisper-M. Yet Figure 4 evaluates all seven ASR systems on the same 1,107 questions, and Table 3 is reported 'over the Whisper-M ASR transcript' only. The paper never states which system's error set defined the keywords, which matters for interpreting the cross-system comparison in Figure 4.
findings.evidence: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords (457 EdX, 656 M3AV) surviving keyword triage'; Table 3 caption 'over the Whisper-M ASR transcript'; Figure 4 shows seven ASR bars per LLM.
findings.suggested_fix: State explicitly which ASR output(s) were used to select keyword pairs and how items were defined for the other six systems.

findings.title: Table 7: which ASR transcript and which grouping rule were used?
findings.location: Page 7, Table 7 and accompanying paragraph
findings.description: Table 7 reports QA accuracy for the human-study clips split into 'QA 100% Correct' (n=56) and 'QA < 100% Correct' (n=138), with per-model accuracies 1/1/1 vs 0.9/0.84/0.85. It does not say which ASR system's transcript was used for these clip-level questions, whether '100% correct' means all three LLMs correct on all questions for a clip, or how many questions each clip had. Table 7's implied L2 share (0.84*56+0.91*138)/194 = 89% also differs from Table 5's 196/235 = 83%, suggesting the 194 clips are a non-random subset of the 235; the selection rule should be stated.
findings.suggested_fix: Specify the ASR system, the per-clip question counts, the grouping definition, and how the 194 clips relate to the 235 rated clips.

summary: The human study (pp. 6-7, Tables 5-7) adopts the Munro & Derwing tripartite construct (accentedness, comprehensibility, intelligibility) without citing it and without reporting the most basic design facts an applied-linguistics reviewer needs: number of raters, rater L1/dialect and accent familiarity, training, listening conditions, replays, blinding, inter-rater reliability, and IRB/consent are all absent from the main text and deferred to an appendix that is not in the submission. The L1/L2 comparison in Table 5 is severely confounded with venue/topic: 168 of 235 clips are NIH biomedical talks, the L2 row (4.3/3.4/0.34) is essentially the NIH row (4.2/3.4/0.36), and between-topic ranges (accentedness 2.3-4.6; human BWER 0.07-0.36) exceed the L1/L2 gaps (1.7 and 0.06), yet no cross-tabulation, stratification, or regression is presented. "Intelligibility" is operationalized as human-transcription BWER restricted to rare/technical vocabulary (and defined differently for EdX vs M3AV clips), so it measures listener domain knowledge and spelling of jargon rather than speaker intelligibility; a human BWER of 0.28 for L1 speakers is not credible as an intelligibility score. Table 6 does not state n or unit (the star pattern implies ~235 rater-averaged clips, ignoring nesting within speakers and zero-inflated clip-level ASR BWER), and Table 7 dichotomizes the outcome post hoc and reports no test (my Fisher test on the 84% vs 91% L2 proportion gives p~0.20). The headline human-study finding, that perceived accentedness correlates with ASR error, is already well documented in the very literature the paper cites, and the study never tests the paper's central construct (whether humans can recover knowledge from ASR transcripts). Finally, assigning L1/L2 status from author-name origin and affiliation for the M3AV speakers, with verification only for an unreported subset, raises both validity and ethics concerns that the paper does not address.
strengths: Uses the standard three-construct design (accentedness scale, comprehensibility scale, transcription-based intelligibility) rather than a single accent judgment, which is the right framework for L2 speech perception.
Applies the same BWER metric to human transcriptions and ASR outputs (Table 5 caption, p. 6), enabling a like-for-like human-vs-machine comparison in principle.
Spearman correlation is an appropriate choice for ordinal 9-point rating data (Table 6).
The clip sample (n=235) is larger than many L2 perception studies, and the EdX L1/L2 labels were assigned per instructor by individual biographical research (p. 3) rather than by name alone.
The Limitations section (p. 7) correctly acknowledges that ratings depend on the listener sample and reference variety and that correlation cannot establish causation.

findings.title: L1/L2 human-study comparison is confounded with venue/topic; L2 row is essentially the NIH row
findings.location: Page 6, Table 5 and accompanying text ('As expected, the ratings of accentedness were higher in the L2 speaker group')
findings.description: Table 5 shows 168 of 235 clips (71.5%) come from a single venue (M3AV NIH), and 196 of 235 (83.4%) are L2; at least 168+196-235 = 129 NIH clips must be L2. The L2 row (Acc 4.3, Com 3.4, Int 0.34) is nearly identical to the NIH row (4.2, 3.4, 0.36), so the 'L2' result is largely an 'NIH biomedical talk' result. Between-topic differences are larger than the L1/L2 differences: accentedness ranges 2.3 (Humanities) to 4.6 (Engineering), a 2.3-point spread vs the 1.7-point L1/L2 gap; human BWER ranges 0.07 to 0.36 (0.29 spread) vs a 0.06 L1/L2 gap. Since 'Topic labels describe the content rather than the speaker' (p. 2), topic differences in accentedness can only arise from unequal speaker composition across topics, i.e., confounding. No L1/L2-by-topic cross-tabulation, stratified comparison, or regression with topic as covariate is provided, so the paper cannot attribute any of Table 5 to L1/L2 status rather than to content domain, recording conditions, or individual speakers.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the L1/L2 x topic cross-tab and number of unique speakers per cell; fit a mixed-effects model (rating ~ L1/L2 + topic + (1|speaker) + (1|rater)) or at minimum compare L1 vs L2 within NIH only; balance the clip sample across topics or match L1 and L2 clips on venue.

findings.title: Human-transcription BWER on rare/technical vocabulary is not a valid intelligibility measure and is defined differently for the two corpora
findings.location: Page 6, Table 5 caption ('Intelligibility (Int) is the BWER of human transcription') and text ('Their transcriptions were subjected to the same BWER metric as in the ASR study'); page 3, ASR Transcription and Error Analysis (BWER definition)
findings.description: In the L2 speech perception literature, intelligibility is measured by orthographic transcription of utterances whose lexical content is familiar to listeners, precisely so that the score reflects the speaker's speech and not the listener's vocabulary. Here BWER is 'restricted to rare/technical vocabulary' (p. 3): a lay listener who has never encountered a biomedical enzyme name cannot transcribe it correctly (or spell it to match 'its lexical form or an approved equivalent') regardless of the speaker's accent, so the measure indexes listener domain knowledge and spelling, not speaker intelligibility. The resulting numbers are implausible as intelligibility: L1 speakers are 'unintelligible' on 28% of keywords, and Humanities clips (0.07) vs NIH clips (0.36) differ fivefold, tracking jargon density rather than accent. Worse, the keyword set differs by corpus: for M3AV, keywords come from slide OCR; for EdX, they are 'all non-function words in the reference'. Thus the Int column is not comparable between the EdX and M3AV rows of Table 5, and the L1 and L2 rows pool two different metrics.
findings.evidence: p. 3: 'BWER ... restricted to rare/technical vocabulary: for M3AV, drawn from slide OCR text ... for EdX, approximated as all non-function words'. Table 5: L1 Int 0.28; Humanities 0.07; NIH 0.36. p. 6: 'human listeners rarely had zero when averaged across listeners'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report conventional whole-utterance intelligibility (word-level transcription accuracy on all words) alongside BWER; use a single keyword definition across corpora; report per-corpus Int separately and do not pool; consider a rater familiarity check on the technical terms.

findings.title: Rater sample and procedure are entirely unreported in the submission
findings.location: Page 6, 'Human Study of Perceived Accented Speech' ('More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix'); page 7, Limitations ('shaped by the listener sample and the selected reference variety')
findings.description: The main text never states how many raters participated, how many rated each clip, their L1 and regional variety, whether any were L2 speakers themselves, their familiarity with the accents in the corpus, training or anchoring, hearing screening, listening environment, number of allowed replays, presentation order/randomization, whether they saw topic context or slides, whether they were blind to speaker identity/L1 status, or any inter-rater reliability statistic (ICC, Cronbach's alpha, Krippendorff's alpha). A grep of the full text finds no occurrence of 'inter-rater', 'reliab', 'ICC', 'Prolific', 'crowd', 'participant', or a rater count. The Limitations section refers to 'the selected reference variety' but never says what it is. A reviewer in applied linguistics cannot evaluate a single number in Tables 5-7 without this information, and the appendix it is deferred to is not in the file.
findings.evidence: p. 6: 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.' No rater n, L1, or reliability anywhere in pp. 1-9.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the main text: rater n, raters per clip, rater L1/variety and accent familiarity, recruitment/compensation, instructions and scale anchors, replays, blinding, randomization, and inter-rater reliability for each of the three measures.

findings.title: No IRB/ethics approval, consent, or compensation statement for the human-subjects study
findings.location: Page 7, 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' section; page 6, human study section
findings.description: The paper reports a human listening experiment but nowhere mentions ethics-board approval, informed consent, or participant compensation; the section titled 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' discusses only QA-model proxies, topic distribution, and listener-sample generalization. A grep for 'IRB', 'consent', 'compensat' returns nothing. Human-subjects research reported at a top venue requires this statement in the main text.
findings.evidence: The 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' section (p. 7) contains no reference to approval, consent, or compensation; the words 'IRB' and 'consent' do not appear in the paper.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an ethics statement covering approval body, consent procedure, compensation, and data handling for rater responses.

findings.title: L1/L2 status inferred from author name origin and affiliation for M3AV speakers: invalid and ethically problematic
findings.location: Page 2-3, 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' (L1/L2 speaker status paragraph); page 2 contributions ('enriched with speakers' demographics')
findings.description: The paper claims 'L1/L2 speaker status is established through biographical research rather than assumed from name or accent alone' but then states that for M3AV 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers'. For the unverified remainder, the label rests on name-origin inference, which the paper's own sentence disavows. Name origin does not indicate native language (US-born speakers with non-Anglo names, heritage speakers, adoptees, married names), affiliation does not indicate origin, and 'L1' is never defined (does it include Indian, Nigerian, Scottish English L1 speakers?). The verified-subset size is not reported. Ethically, the study compiles national origin, native language, PhD country, year of arrival, and years of US residence for identifiable public individuals (named EdX instructors and NIH presenters) without consent and lists 'speakers' demographics' as a released contribution. Collected covariates (years of residence, arrival year) are never analyzed, and the L2 group's L1 backgrounds are never reported, collapsing enormous heterogeneity into one binary.
findings.evidence: p. 3: 'For M3AV, an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup against academic metadata (OpenAlex ...), recording PhD institution and country, year of arrival in the US, and total years of US residence'. p. 2 contribution bullet: 'enriched with speakers' demographics'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the fraction of M3AV speakers whose status was actually verified and analyze verified speakers only (or report sensitivity); define L1 precisely and report L1 backgrounds of the L2 group; discuss consent/privacy for the demographic labels and whether they will be released; use residence/arrival variables as continuous predictors or drop them.

findings.title: Table 5 reports no dispersion, confidence intervals, tests, or effect sizes for L1 vs L2 differences
findings.location: Page 6, Table 5 and text ('As expected, the ratings of accentedness were higher in the L2 speaker group ... The results indicate lower intelligibility ... for the L2 speech')
findings.description: The L1 (n=39) vs L2 (n=196) comparison is reported as means only, with no SD, CI, test statistic, or effect size, and the topic rows rest on cells as small as n=5 and n=6. The claimed L2 disadvantage in Int is 0.06 (0.28 vs 0.34), a difference whose reliability cannot be assessed without variance. The unusually high L1 accentedness mean of 2.6 on a 9-point scale also needs interpretation (non-US L1 varieties? rater L1?), which the paper does not provide.
findings.evidence: Table 5: L1 Int 0.28 vs L2 0.34; Acc 2.6 vs 4.3; Humanities n=6, Social Sciences n=5.
findings.suggested_fix: Report SDs/CIs, a rater-aware mixed model or Mann-Whitney with effect size (Cliff's delta or r), and per-clip distributions.

findings.title: Table 7 dichotomizes the outcome post hoc, reports no test, and the reported differences are small (L2 proportion not significant)
findings.location: Page 7, Table 7 and text ('Notably, there were more L2 speakers in the clips that did not have accurate QA LLM results ... L2 speakers are more likely to have lower QA LLM accuracy, particularly when their accent is more marked')
findings.description: Clips are split by whether all three QA LLMs were 100% correct (n=56) or not (n=138) and mean ratings are compared without any test or dispersion. The differences are small: percent_L2 84 vs 91, Acc 3.8 vs 4.3, Com 3.1 vs 3.4, Int 0.32 vs 0.37. Reconstructing counts (47/56 vs ~126/138 L2), a Fisher exact test gives p~0.20 for the L2 proportion, so the headline claim 'more L2 speakers in the clips that did not have accurate QA' is not statistically supported. Dichotomizing a continuous outcome and then comparing predictor means is the reverse of the appropriate analysis (predict QA correctness from accentedness with topic controlled). It is also unclear which ASR system's transcript was used, how many questions each <=25-word clip yielded, and whether the reference-condition QA was also run (so that <100% could be item difficulty rather than ASR-induced loss). The sentence 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria' suggests questions were generated from ASR output, contradicting the methodology (generation from reference transcripts), and 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions' misattributes generation (Gemini) to the answering models.
findings.evidence: Table 7: n=56 percent_L2=84 Acc 3.8 Com 3.1 Int 0.32 QA 1/1/1; n=138 percent_L2=91 Acc 4.3 Com 3.4 Int 0.37 QA 0.90/0.84/0.85. p. 7: 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples and were frequently 100% accurate'.
findings.suggested_fix: Model per-question or per-clip QA correctness (ASR minus reference) as a function of accentedness/comprehensibility with topic and speaker random effects; report tests and effect sizes; specify the ASR system, question counts per clip, and whether reference-condition QA was run on the same clips.

findings.title: Table 6 does not state n, unit of analysis, or star thresholds; implied clip-level analysis ignores rater variance and speaker nesting
findings.location: Page 6, Table 6 and text ('Spearman correlations were conducted with ASR accuracy on the clips')
findings.description: Neither the caption nor the text gives n, the unit (clip vs rater-by-clip), or what *, **, *** mean. The star pattern (Whisper-S Acc 0.148 = *, Whisper-L-t Acc 0.202 = **, Whisper-S Int 0.215 = ***) is consistent with n~235 clips at two-tailed .05/.01/.001 thresholds (critical r = 0.128/0.168/0.215 at n=235) and inconsistent with n=194, so the analysis appears to correlate rater-averaged ratings with clip-level ASR BWER. That discards rater variability entirely and treats 235 clips as independent although 168 NIH clips must come from far fewer speakers (M3AV has only 123 videos in total), producing pseudo-replication. Twenty-one correlations are reported without multiple-comparison correction. The caption says 'ASR accuracy' while the text says 'correlations of BWER'; the positive sign with accentedness shows these must be error rates, so the caption is wrong. Clip-level ASR BWER on <=25-word clips takes few values and is zero-inflated (the paper notes 'numerous instances of 0 BWER'), so Spearman is computed on heavily tied data, and the inference that lower Whisper correlations mean less accent sensitivity is confounded with floor effects, which the paper acknowledges only for the Int column, not for Acc/Com. The text also states 'Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t were below rs = .30' for Int, but Whisper-S (0.215) is also below .30 and Whisper-L (0.281) is higher than Whisper-S.
findings.evidence: Table 6 caption: 'Correlation study of human ratings and ASR accuracy'; values e.g. Whisper-S Acc 0.148*, Com 0.271***, Int 0.215***; Wav2Vec2-L Com 0.522***. p. 6: 'the ASR models had numerous instances of 0 BWER'.
findings.suggested_fix: State n, unit, and thresholds; correct the caption to error rate; report clip-level ASR BWER distributions; use a mixed model or speaker-level aggregation; apply a multiplicity correction; discuss floor effects for all three columns.

findings.title: The accentedness-ASR error correlation is not novel and the human study does not test the paper's central construct
findings.location: Page 7, Conclusions ('perceived accentedness correlates with ASR errors and downstream QA loss'); page 2 contributions ('An augmentation study of human listeners that confirms the observed performance trends'); page 7 Related Work
findings.description: That listener-rated accentedness/comprehensibility correlates moderately with ASR error for L2 speech is established in the papers the authors themselves cite (Inceoglu, Chen & Lim 2023; Chanethom & Henderson 2022; Issa, Ali & Hirschi 2026; McCrocklin et al. 2026; Hirschi & Kang 2024). The Related Work even asserts that ASR penalizes L2 speakers 'in ways that do not align with human perception', yet Table 6 reports significant alignment (rs 0.15-0.52) and the discrepancy is never discussed. More fundamentally, the paper's thesis is that transcripts fail to convey the lesson to human learners, but no human ever read an ASR transcript or answered a comprehension question in this study; raters only judged audio. The study therefore cannot 'confirm' the QA-based accessibility findings; it addresses only RQ3.
findings.evidence: p. 7: 'speakers whose first language is other than English are penalized in unpredictable ways that do not align with human perception (Hirschi and Kang 2024; Inceoglu, Chen, and Lim 2023; McCrocklin ...)'. Table 6: Wav2Vec2-L Com 0.522***; Whisper-M Acc 0.270***.
findings.suggested_fix: Position the human study explicitly as a replication and reconcile with prior findings; add a human reading study in which listeners/readers answer the generated questions from reference vs ASR transcripts (the paper's own future-work item), which is the only direct test of the accessibility claim.

findings.title: Scale anchors unstated and construct labels inverted; foundational speech-perception literature uncited
findings.location: Page 6, Table 5 caption and text ('the comprehensibility was also higher (i.e., raters identified L2 speech as more challenging to understand)')
findings.description: The 9-point accentedness and comprehensibility scales are given without endpoint labels. A higher 'comprehensibility' score meaning harder to understand follows Munro & Derwing (1995) (1 = extremely easy, 9 = extremely difficult), but the paper does not say so or cite it, and the column header 'Com' invites the opposite reading; likewise 'Intelligibility' is reported as an error rate, so higher = less intelligible. All three headers therefore point in the direction opposite to their construct names. None of the foundational work on these constructs (Munro & Derwing 1995; Derwing & Munro 1997; Derwing & Munro 2009) is cited, despite the design being taken directly from it, and rater accent-familiarity effects (Gass & Varonis 1984) are not considered.
findings.evidence: Table 5 caption: 'Accentedness (Acc) and Comprehensibility (Com) are on a 9-point scale, Intelligibility (Int) is the BWER of human transcription.' Reference list contains no Munro or Derwing entries.
findings.suggested_fix: State anchors for both scales; relabel columns as 'Comprehensibility difficulty' and 'Human keyword error (1-intelligibility)' or reverse the coding; cite and situate the design in the Munro & Derwing framework.

findings.title: Clip sampling procedure, speaker counts, and clip length limit what can be inferred
findings.location: Page 2 ('ASR fidelity is measured both in short clips given to human raters and over full recordings'); page 7 ('given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less')
findings.description: The paper does not say how the 235 clips were selected (random? stratified by speaker/topic? from which portions of recordings?), how many unique speakers they represent, or how many clips per speaker. The composition (83% L2, 71.5% NIH) departs from the stated 75/25 L2/L1 design target and from EdX's share of the corpus (EdX supplies 1,232 of 1,355 videos but only 38 of 235 clips), so the human sample is not representative of the ASR evaluation it is meant to corroborate. Topic cells of n=5-6 cannot support topic-level claims. Accentedness can be judged from a 10-second clip, but comprehensibility of a decontextualized <=25-word excerpt of dense biomedical content is largely a content-difficulty judgment, and generating knowledge questions from 25 words produced a degenerate QA task (41 clips yielded no question; results 'frequently 100% accurate'), unlike the +/-100-word windows used in the main pipeline.
findings.evidence: Table 5: EdX 38 clips vs M3AV 197; Humanities n=6, Social Sciences n=5. p. 4: 'targeting the same overall 75%/25% L2/L1 composition'. p. 7: '25 words or less ... only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples and were frequently 100% accurate'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe clip selection; report unique speakers and clips per speaker; stratify or reweight to match corpus composition; use longer clips (or full QA windows) for the QA-linked analysis.

findings.title: 'ASR outperforms human listeners' claim is not supported by reported numbers and is not a fair comparison
findings.location: Page 6-7 ('In other words, these models outperform human listeners in transcription accuracy, but are also significantly correlated to speaker accentedness')
findings.description: Clip-level ASR BWER means are never reported; Table 2 gives full-recording BWER (e.g., Whisper-M 0.053-0.064) while human BWER is clip-level (0.28-0.36) on technical keywords. Human raters presumably transcribed on one or a few listens, without slides, without domain expertise, under unspecified conditions, and with strict lexical matching of jargon spellings; ASR gets full audio with a learned lexicon. The comparison as stated conflates listener knowledge with perception.
findings.evidence: Table 2 (recording-level BWER) vs Table 5 (clip-level human BWER 0.28/0.34); no clip-level ASR BWER table.
findings.suggested_fix: Report clip-level ASR BWER for the same 235 clips next to human BWER, and describe listening conditions; temper the claim.

findings.title: Relative L1/L2 WER disparity is constant (~1.4x) across systems, contradicting 'recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap'
findings.location: Page 5, Figure 2 and text ('the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap')
findings.description: Reading the bar labels in Figure 2, the L2/L1 WER ratios are Whisper-S 0.081/0.058 = 1.40, Whisper-M 0.080/0.056 = 1.43, Whisper-L-t 1.38, Whisper-L 1.61, Wav2Vec2-B 0.275/0.196 = 1.40, Wav2Vec2-L 1.39, Wav2Vec2-L-s 1.31. The relative penalty for L2 speakers is essentially unchanged between the best Whisper and worst Wav2Vec2 models; only the absolute gap shrinks because everything shrinks. From a fairness standpoint, the proportional disparity is the relevant quantity, and the claim of a narrowing gap is not supported. No error bars, tests, or speaker-level aggregation are given; with 27 EdX instructors each teaching one course, L1/L2 is fully nested within instructor and topic, so the video-level comparison is heavily pseudo-replicated.
findings.evidence: Figure 2 bar labels: Whisper-S 0.058/0.081; Whisper-M 0.056/0.080; Wav2Vec2-B 0.196/0.275; Wav2Vec2-L 0.171/0.238. Table 1: 27 courses / 27 unique instructors.
findings.suggested_fix: Report relative disparity (ratio or log-ratio) with speaker-level CIs; state the number of L1 and L2 speakers per corpus.

findings.title: Inconsistent speaker/video counts around L1/L2 assignment for M3AV
findings.location: Page 3 ('16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers'); page 2 ('all M3AV recordings retained'); Table 1 (M3AV 123 videos)
findings.description: The paper says 228 candidate NIH speakers were screened (16 excluded as unknown), yet Table 1 lists only 123 M3AV videos across three venues and the Methodology says all M3AV recordings were retained. The selection from ~212 resolved NIH speakers down to the NIH portion of 123 videos, done while 'targeting ... 75%/25% L2/L1 composition', is not described; L1 status was evidently a sampling criterion, which affects how the L1/L2 comparison (and the 168 NIH clips in Table 5) should be interpreted.
findings.evidence: p. 3: 'speakers whose background could not be resolved this way are coded as unknown and excluded from the selected set (e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers)'; Table 1: M3AV Videos 123, L1 31, L2 92.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the selection from candidate speakers to the final 123 videos and report speaker counts per venue and L1/L2 status.

findings.title: How many raters rated each clip, what were their L1s and accent familiarity, and what was the inter-rater reliability for each measure?
findings.location: Page 6, human study section
findings.description: The text implies multiple listeners per clip ('averaged across listeners') but gives no count, background, or reliability. Ratings of accentedness are strongly rater-dependent (L1 variety, exposure to specific L2 accents), and the paper's own Limitations acknowledges this without describing the sample.
findings.evidence: p. 6: 'human listeners rarely had zero when averaged across listeners'; p. 7: 'Perceived-accentedness ratings are shaped by the listener sample and the selected reference variety.'

findings.title: Which ASR system's transcripts underlie Table 7, how many questions per clip, and was reference-condition QA run on the same clips?
findings.location: Page 7, Table 7 and text
findings.description: Table 7 reports QA accuracy per LLM without naming the ASR condition; the main-text tests used Whisper-M but this is not stated for the clips. If reference-condition QA was not run, <100% accuracy cannot be attributed to ASR error rather than to question difficulty on 25-word clips.
findings.evidence: p. 7: 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria'; Table 7 columns gpt4o/llama/qwen with no ASR label.

findings.title: What was the 'selected reference variety' and how is 'L1' defined (does it include non-US L1 English varieties)?
findings.location: Page 7, Limitations; page 3, L1/L2 assignment
findings.description: An L1 mean accentedness of 2.6/9 suggests either that L1 includes speakers of non-reference varieties or that raters' own varieties differ from the speakers'. The paper never defines the reference variety or the L1 category.
findings.evidence: Table 5: L1 Acc 2.6; p. 7: 'the selected reference variety'.

findings.title: Were raters allowed to replay clips, did they see topic/slide context, and were they blind to speaker identity and L1 status?
findings.location: Page 6, human study section
findings.description: Transcription-based intelligibility scores depend heavily on number of listens and available context; accentedness ratings can be biased by visible speaker names or affiliations. None of these procedural details are given.
findings.evidence: p. 6: 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix' (appendix absent).

summary: The QA pipeline (Gemini generates and grades, GPT4o+Llama3 verify and answer, Qwen2.5 answers) is described at the level of intent rather than procedure, and several of its load-bearing measurements are circular or confounded. The two verifier models are also two of the three answerers, so their reference-condition accuracy on the 813-item verified set (99.3%, 98.3%) is close to guaranteed by construction, and the McNemar 'Toward' asymmetry on that subset is partly built in. The headline open-ended result (10-14pt drop vs 2.7-4.7pt under multiple choice) is presented as 'unmasking' a hidden effect, but the reference/ASR odds ratios are essentially identical across formats (1.72 vs 1.75/1.75/2.27); the larger absolute gap is mostly a baseline shift caused by an unvalidated, strict, generator-as-judge grader that marks 16-23% of gold-context answers wrong. The question set is conditioned on ASR keyword errors (every item has a substitution/deletion type), so QA accuracy is not an estimate of 'how much knowledge remains accessible' as the abstract claims, and models still answer 90.6% of these corrupted-keyword items correctly, which questions the probe's sensitivity and the learner-proxy framing. Finally, the text's reference accuracies (99.3/98.3/97.9%) do not match Figure 4's bar labels (0.954/0.940/0.935), Table 3's N=1,107 is really 3,321 pooled model-item pairs, and no prompt text, model versions, window-alignment procedure, or option-ordering control is given, so the pipeline is not reproducible from the paper.
strengths: Paired reference-vs-ASR design on identical items with McNemar's exact test and Cohen's h; I recomputed all seven p-values in Table 3 (e.g., 160 vs 37 -> 9.94e-20; 14 vs 6 -> 5.77e-02) and all three h values in Table 4 (0.240, 0.252, 0.338) and they are correct.

The paper explicitly discloses the partial role overlap between verifiers and answerers (p.4 Methodology and p.4 Experiment Settings) rather than hiding it, and keeps the generator out of the answerer pool.
Substitution vs deletion breakdown of discordant pairs (Table 3) links each QA failure to a specific ASR error mechanism, which is the right granularity for an accessibility argument.
The superficial-cue filter (rejecting stems/options containing the keyword or its mishearing) and the narrow-window restriction are sensible design choices to prevent trivial lexical matching.
Deterministic decoding, matched prompts/max-tokens across QA models, cleared conversation history, and inclusion of both commercial (GPT4o) and open-weight (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) answerers.
The open-ended re-test of the same 300 stems with the same windows is a well-motivated format-ablation design in principle (only the format changes).

findings.title: Verifier models are also answerers, making the GT-verified reference accuracy and McNemar direction partly circular
findings.location: p.4 Methodology (Answerability check paragraph), p.4 Experiment Settings 'ASR and QA LLMs', p.5 Table 3 GT-verified rows, p.5 text '99.3% / 98.3%'
findings.description: GPT4o and Llama3 are the two post-hoc answerability judges ('an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage') and are then asked, at temperature 0, to answer the same items given the same reference passage. Confirming that the marked option is correct given the passage is nearly the same computation as selecting that option given the passage, so on the 813-item verified subset the reference-condition correctness of these two models is essentially pre-selected. This inflates reference accuracy for 2 of 3 models (99.3%, 98.3% vs 97.9% for the non-verifier Qwen2.5) and biases the 'Toward' (reference correct, ASR incorrect) vs 'Away' counts in Table 3's GT-verified rows (89 vs 12), since 'Away' requires a reference-condition error that verification has largely filtered out. The paper notes the check 'certifies that the answer is well-supported ... rather than establishing full three-way independence' but does not recognize that it also contaminates the dependent variable.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'shown to two LLM judges (GPT4o and Llama3) ... drawn from the same pool of models used for downstream answering'; p.4: 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage'; p.5: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'; Table 3 GT-verified All: Toward 89, Away 12. Recomputing h with mean ref = (0.993+0.983+0.979)/3 = 0.985 and pooled net drop 77/2439 gives h = 0.189, matching the stated 0.190, confirming these percentages are the verified-subset values.
findings.suggested_fix: Use verifier models disjoint from the answerer set (or a human audit), or report reference accuracy and McNemar results for Qwen2.5 (the only non-verifier) separately and treat GPT4o/Llama3 reference accuracy on the verified subset as a selection artifact. Report the verified-subset results per model, not pooled.

findings.title: Open-ended 'unmasking' claim is confounded by a stricter, unvalidated judge; odds ratios are unchanged across formats
findings.location: p.6 Table 4 and 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'; p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA' scoring paragraph
findings.description: The paper concludes that multiple choice 'was masking part of the true effect' because the absolute drop grows from 2.7-4.7pt to 10.3-14.0pt. But the reference-condition accuracy also collapses from 94-99% to 77-84%, i.e., 16-23% of answers produced with the GOLD window are marked wrong by the judge. When the baseline shifts this much, absolute gaps and Cohen's h grow mechanically. The reference/ASR odds ratio is 1.72 under MC (pooled, 0.943 vs 0.906) and 1.75 (GPT4o), 1.75 (Llama3), 2.27 (Qwen) under open-ended; relative error increase is 1.55-1.80x (MC) vs 1.50-1.89x (OE). The formats therefore show the same effect, not a larger one. The judge is the question-generation model (Gemini), grading 'adversarially' against 'the multiple-choice distractors' that the open-ended answerer never saw, with no human validation, no inter-judge agreement, and no reported examples of rejected gold-context answers. Whether the 77-84% ceiling reflects judge strictness, stems that are ambiguous without options ('What does the speaker call...' has many valid free-text renderings), or real model failure is unknowable from the paper.
findings.evidence: Table 4: GPT4o ref 0.803 asr 0.700; Llama3 0.773/0.660; Qwen2.5 0.843/0.703. p.6: 'grade each answer adversarially, i.e., correct only if it clearly commits to the reference fact in a way that is distinguishable from the multiple-choice distractors'; p.4: 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge'; p.6: 'This confirms that the multiple-choice format was masking part of the true effect'. Computed: MC OR 1.72 vs OE OR 1.75/1.75/2.27.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the open-ended judge against human grading on a stratified sample (report agreement/kappa); use a judge model distinct from the generator; grade against the reference fact rather than unseen distractors; report the open-ended result as odds ratios or relative risk alongside absolute drops; report how many gold-context answers were rejected and why.

findings.title: Text reports reference accuracies (99.3/98.3/97.9%) that contradict Figure 4's bar labels (0.954/0.940/0.935)
findings.location: p.5 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' first paragraph vs Figure 4 (p.5) and Figure 1 bottom panel (p.2)
findings.description: The text explicitly attributes 99.3%/98.3%/97.9% reference accuracies to Figure 4, but the reference (grey) bars in Figure 4 are labeled 0.954 (GPT4o), 0.940 (Llama3), 0.935 (Qwen2.5). The mean of the Figure 4 reference bars is 94.3% and the mean of the second Whisper bar is 90.6%, which exactly matches Figure 1's 'Reference (Correct) 94.3% / ASR (Whisper) 90.6% / Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points' and Table 3's pooled full-set gap ((160-37)/3321 = 3.7pt). The 99.3/98.3/97.9 numbers instead reproduce the GT-verified h=0.190. The paper therefore mixes full-set and verified-subset numbers under a single figure reference, and the ceiling-effect discussion depends on which is meant (94% leaves ~63 items per model wrong even with the gold window; 99% leaves ~6).
findings.evidence: p.5: 'Figure 4 shows the accuracies ... GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'. Figure 4 bar labels read from the rendered image: GPT4o ref 0.954, Whisper 0.933/0.926/0.944/0.945, Wav2Vec 0.896/0.905/0.906; Llama3 ref 0.940; Qwen2.5 ref 0.935. Figure 1: '94.3%', '90.6%', 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'.
findings.suggested_fix: State which item set each number comes from; correct the text to match Figure 4 (full set) or relabel; add a table with per-model, per-ASR accuracies for both full and verified sets in the main paper rather than deferring to an appendix that is not included.

findings.title: Question set is conditioned on ASR keyword errors, so QA accuracy does not estimate 'how much knowledge remains accessible' and cross-ASR comparison is biased
findings.location: p.3 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation' filtering paragraph; p.4 Experiment Settings 'Datasets'; p.5 Table 3 error-type rows; Abstract
findings.description: Keywords are selected as (reference term, ASR output) pairs where 'the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept', and the paper calls them 'knowledge-error keywords'. Every one of the 1,107 items in Table 3 has an error type (137+29 substitution + 23+8 deletion = 197 = 160+37 discordant), confirming that every item targets a keyword the ASR corrupted. Two consequences: (a) the abstract's claim that QA performance 'estimates how much of the recording's knowledge remains accessible after transcription' is not what is measured; it measures accuracy conditional on a keyword error, on a window chosen around that error. (b) Figure 4 compares seven ASR systems on a keyword set defined by one system's failures (Figure 1 says 'ASR Transcript (Whisper)'; the paper never states which system's errors define the set), so systems whose errors fall elsewhere are evaluated on someone else's failure points. Additionally, since the keyword is corrupted in 100% of items yet models still answer 90.6% correctly, the probe is largely insensitive to the very errors it was built to detect, implying the answers are recoverable from surrounding context or parametric knowledge rather than the keyword.
