findings.evidence: p.3: 'keeping only pairs where the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept'; p.4: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords (457 EdX, 656 M3AV) surviving keyword triage'; Table 3: Substitution 137/29 + Deletion 23/8 = All 160/37; Abstract: 'The performance of QA tasks estimates how much of the recording's knowledge remains accessible after transcription'; Figure 1 header 'ASR Transcript (Whisper)'.
findings.suggested_fix: State which ASR system's errors define the keyword set; add a control set of knowledge-intensive keywords that the ASR transcribed correctly so that the reported gap is an unconditional estimate; when comparing ASR systems, either define keywords per system or use an ASR-independent keyword set.

findings.title: 'Dependency check built into generation' is an unverifiable prompt instruction; no closed-book baseline; Figure 1's own example is answerable from general knowledge
findings.location: p.3-4 'Each generated item passes three checks' (First check); Figure 1 p.2 Question Construction panel; p.7 Limitations
findings.description: The first of the three checks is described as a property of the generator's instructions ('distractors must be indistinguishable ... to a reader without access to the local window'), not as a measurement. Nothing in the pipeline tests whether an item is answerable without the window. The standard control, a no-context (closed-book) run of the same QA models on the same items, is absent, even though the Limitations section concedes 'QA models may rely on pretrained knowledge even when instructed to use only the transcript.' The showcase item in Figure 1 illustrates the problem: asked which mechanism recognizes a damaged base displaced from the stack, option B 'Removal of damaged segments via specialized enzymatic pathways' is the textbook definition of base excision repair; any biology-literate model picks it without the transcript. Without a closed-book baseline, the 94-99% reference accuracy cannot be attributed to reading the window, and the small MC gap cannot be separated from parametric recall.
findings.evidence: p.3-4: 'First, a dependency check is built into generation itself: distractors must be indistinguishable from the correct answer to a reader without access to the local window'; Figure 1 Q: 'When a damaged base is displaced from the stack due to structural instability, which specific cellular mechanism is identified as the primary pathway for its recognition?' correct option B 'Removal of damaged segments via specialized enzymatic pathways'; p.7: 'QA models may rely on pretrained knowledge even when instructed to use only the transcript.'
findings.suggested_fix: Run all three QA models with no context (and with a shuffled/unrelated window) on every item and report accuracy; drop or flag items answerable closed-book; report the reference-vs-ASR gap on the remaining window-dependent items.

findings.title: Full set (N=1,107) includes 294 items that failed answerability verification, contradicting the stated retention rule; headline numbers are on unverified items
findings.location: p.4 Methodology (retention rule) vs p.4 Experiment Settings 'Datasets', Table 3 'Full (N=1,107)' rows, Figure 4, Figure 1 '3.7 percentage points'
findings.description: The Methodology says an item is retained only if both verifier judges confirm it, yet the reported question set is 1,107 items of which only 813 (73.4%) are 'ground-truth-verified'. The 26.6% rejection rate is high and unexplained (verifier disagreement? Llama-3.1-8B failures? genuinely bad items?), and no analysis or examples of rejected items are given. Despite this, the paper's primary results (Figure 4, Table 3 first block, the 3.7pt gap in Figure 1) are computed on the full set including the 294 unverified items, whose 'marked-correct' answer is by definition not confirmed. The ~5.7% reference-condition error on the full set (about 63 items per model) is consistent with the full set containing flawed items, which adds noise to both conditions and the discordant-pair test.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage'; p.4: 'yielding 1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification'; Table 3 rows 'Full (N=1,107)' and 'GT-verified (N=813)'; Figure 4 reference bars 0.954/0.940/0.935.
findings.suggested_fix: Either report only on the verified set or explicitly justify including unverified items; characterize the 294 rejected items (which judge rejected, why, per-corpus breakdown); reconcile the Methodology retention rule with the reported counts.

findings.title: Table 3's 'N=1,107' is actually 3,321 pooled model-item pairs; pooling three answerers into one McNemar test treats clustered answers as independent
findings.location: p.5 Table 3 caption and rows; p.6 open-ended test 'toward=140, away=33, n=173'
findings.description: Table 3 is captioned 'for all QA LLMs' and lists N=1,107 (full) and N=813 (verified), but the Toward/Away counts only make sense if the three models' answers are pooled: (160-37)/(1,107x3) = 3.7pt matches Figure 1's stated gap and reproduces h = 0.142 (stated 0.140) from the Figure 4 means, whereas (160-37)/1,107 would be 11.1pt. Likewise the open-ended test (140 vs 33, n=173 discordant) pools 300x3 = 900 pairs. Pooling three models' responses to the same item as independent Bernoulli trials in a one-sided binomial test ignores item-level clustering (the same corrupted keyword drives all three models), so the extremely small p-values (9.9e-20, 3.4e-17) overstate evidence. No per-model McNemar results are given anywhere in the main text.
findings.evidence: Table 3: 'Full (N=1,107) All 160 37 9.9e-20 0.140'; Figure 1: 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'; computed (160-37)/3321 = 0.0370; p.6: 'toward=140, away=33, n=173' with 300 sampled items x 3 models = 900 pairs.
findings.suggested_fix: Label N as model-item pairs or, better, report McNemar per model (each model's own paired items are independent across items); if pooling, use a clustered/permutation test at the item level or a mixed-effects logistic model with item random effects.

findings.title: Pipeline is not reproducible: no prompt text, unspecified Gemini/GPT4o versions, no ASR-window alignment method, no option-order control, unspecified sampling
findings.location: p.4 'Prompt and Temperature'; p.4 'ASR and QA LLMs'; p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'; p.6 'randomly sample 300 questions'; footnote 3 p.2; references (Gemini Team 2024)
findings.description: The generator, verifier, QA and open-ended judge prompts are each described in one clause ('answer using only the provided transcript context and return a single option letter') with no verbatim text, system prompt, or few-shot examples. The generator is 'Gemini (Gemini Team 2024)' citing arXiv:2312.11805 (the Gemini 1.0 report) with no model name or version; GPT4o has no snapshot date. 'Maximum tokens are matched' without saying to what. Multiple-choice evaluation with 7-8B models is sensitive to option position, but option shuffling/balancing is never mentioned (the only shown item, Figure 1, has the correct answer at B). The ASR-condition context is 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window', but locating a +/-100-word window in an ASR transcript where the anchor keyword was substituted or deleted requires an alignment procedure that is not described. The superficial-cue filter rejects 'its ASR-mishearing' without saying which of the seven systems' mishearing is used. The 300 open-ended items are 'randomly sampled' with no seed, stratification, or list. No code or data release is mentioned.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'All QA systems receive the same minimal instruction: answer using only the provided transcript context and return a single option letter, with no explanation'; p.4: 'Question generation uses Gemini (Gemini Team 2024)'; p.4: 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window as context'; p.4: 'any question whose stem or options contain the literal target keyword, its ASR-mishearing, or an obvious variant'; p.6: 'we randomly sample 300 questions'.
findings.suggested_fix: Release all prompts verbatim (generator, keyword triage, verifier, QA, open-ended judge), exact model identifiers and dates, max-token settings, the window alignment algorithm (and how deletions are handled), option-shuffling procedure, the 300-item sample list, and the full item set with answers.

findings.title: Superficial-cue/leak filter removed at most 6 of 1,113 items, an implausibly small effect for a keyword-anchored generator
findings.location: p.4 Experiment Settings 'Datasets' counts; p.4 Methodology second check
findings.description: The generator is given the keyword and asked to write a question about it, so one would expect many stems or options to contain the keyword or a variant. Yet 1,113 keywords yield 1,107 questions 'after leak-filtering and answerability verification', so leak-filtering (plus any generation failures) removed at most 6 items (0.5%), while answerability verification removed 294. Either the filter was applied inside the generator prompt (in which case it is not the 'programmatic' post-hoc check described) or the filter is too narrow to catch paraphrastic leakage (e.g., the correct option restating the keyword's definition, as in Figure 1's option B). Either way, the paper gives no leak-rate statistics, no examples of rejected items, and no test of whether stems/options still cue the answer.
findings.evidence: p.4: '1,113 knowledge-error keywords ... yielding 1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified) after leak-filtering and answerability verification'; p.4: 'a specificity/superficial-cue check is applied programmatically: any question whose stem or options contain the literal target keyword, its ASR-mishearing, or an obvious variant of either is rejected'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the number of items rejected at each stage separately (generation failures, leak filter, verifier disagreement); include an answer-only or question-only baseline (models choose among options without any transcript) to quantify residual cueing.

findings.title: Generator also acts as keyword triager and open-ended judge, contradicting 'never judges its own output'; judge's validity is untested
findings.location: p.3 keyword triage sentence; p.4 'the question generator itself never judges its own output'; p.4 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge'; p.6
findings.description: Gemini performs three roles: it triages surviving keyword candidates ('Surviving candidates are triaged by an LLM judge, and the same commercial model used for question generation'), generates the items, and grades all open-ended answers. The Methodology asserts the generator 'never judges its own output', but grading free-text answers to its own questions against its own reference facts and its own distractors is a judging role with known self-preference and intended-answer bias. The claim that the generator 'never itself an answerer' does not address this. No human or second-model agreement is reported for either the keyword triage or the open-ended grading, and the triage sentence itself is garbled, so the role assignment is not even clearly stated.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'Surviving candidates are triaged by an LLM judge, and the same commercial model used for question generation to keep separate from the three QA answering models for alignment quality and topic centrality.'; p.4: 'the question generator itself never judges its own output'; p.4: 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge (grounded in the reference passage, and never itself an answerer)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a distinct judge model (or two, with agreement reported) for open-ended grading; have humans grade a stratified sample of at least 100 open-ended answers per condition and report agreement; rewrite the triage sentence and clarify all roles in a table.

findings.title: QA-LLM-as-learner proxy is undermined by the paper's own numbers: with the keyword corrupted in every item, models still answer 90.6% correctly
findings.location: Abstract; p.5 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions'; p.7 Related Work 'QA LLMs' and Limitations; Figure 4
findings.description: The paper frames the QA LLMs as 'standardized readers' that 'estimate how much knowledge survives transcription for a human learner'. But every item is built around a keyword the ASR corrupted (Table 3 error types cover all discordant pairs), the keyword is excluded from stem and options, and the models nevertheless get ~90.6% (Whisper-M, full set) right. The paper interprets this as 'the great majority of questions are answered identically' and a 'modest' effect, but for the proxy argument it means LLMs recover the fact from surrounding context or parametric knowledge in ways a Deaf or L2 learner encountering 'basic session repair' cannot. The Limitations section concedes LLMs are 'proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners', yet the Abstract and Conclusions still present QA accuracy as measuring learner accessibility. No human-learner QA comparison is run on the same items (the human study measures accentedness ratings and transcription, not comprehension).
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'The performance of QA tasks estimates how much of the recording's knowledge remains accessible after transcription'; p.7: 'using multiple LLMs as standardized readers ... to estimate how much knowledge survives transcription for a human learner'; Figure 1: 'ASR (Whisper) 90.6%'; Table 3: all 197 discordant pairs classified as substitution or deletion; p.7 Limitations: 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners'.
findings.suggested_fix: Run a small human comprehension study on a matched sample of items (reference vs ASR windows) to calibrate the LLM proxy; or reframe claims to 'LLM-recoverable content' rather than learner accessibility; report the closed-book baseline to separate parametric recall from context use.

findings.title: Abstract/Conclusion claims of 'substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics' are not supported by any reported QA result
findings.location: Abstract; p.7 Conclusions; Figure 4 p.5; Figure 3 p.5
findings.description: The abstract states 'substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material', and the Conclusions say 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'. The main text contains no per-topic QA result at all (Figure 3 is per-topic ASR error for Whisper-M, not QA), and the between-model QA differences in Figure 4 are 0.954 vs 0.940 vs 0.935 in the reference condition and 2.8/4.8/3.6pt Whisper-M drops, i.e., within about 2 points of each other. No statistical comparison among QA LLMs is reported despite 'statistical tests for important differences among LLMs' being promised in Evaluation Metrics.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'The results show substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics'; p.4: 'We assess the QA LLMs with accuracy and statistical tests for important differences among LLMs'; Figure 4 reference bars 0.954/0.940/0.935; p.7: 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a per-topic QA table (reference vs ASR accuracy by EdX subject and M3AV venue, per model) or remove the claim; add the promised between-model tests or drop 'substantial differences among QA LLMs'.

findings.title: Figure 4 Whisper bars are unlabeled, and in Table 2 order the worst-WER Whisper-L yields the highest QA accuracy, contradicting the 'mirrors ASR error ordering' claim
findings.location: Figure 4 p.5 and accompanying text p.5
findings.description: Figure 4 distinguishes the seven ASR systems only by color shade with a family-level legend, so individual systems cannot be identified. The consistency check (mean of the second Whisper bar = 90.6% = Figure 1's Whisper-M figure) implies the bars follow Table 2 order (S, M, L-t, L). Under that order, GPT4o accuracy is 0.933 (Whisper-S), 0.926 (Whisper-M), 0.944 (Whisper-L-t), 0.945 (Whisper-L): the two large Whisper models with WER 0.114-0.197 give HIGHER QA accuracy than the best-WER models (0.074-0.075). The same pattern holds for Llama3 (0.916/0.919 vs 0.903/0.892) and Qwen (0.921/0.919 vs 0.904/0.899). This directly contradicts the text's claim that the QA ordering 'closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'. A likely reason is that the +/-100-word window makes the QA probe blind to Whisper-L's hallucination/repetition failures elsewhere in the transcript, which is itself a limitation of the window-based accessibility measure that the paper does not discuss.
findings.evidence: Figure 4 bar labels (GPT4o): 0.954, 0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945, 0.896, 0.905, 0.906; Table 2 EdX WER: Whisper-S 0.075, Whisper-M 0.074, Whisper-L-t 0.114, Whisper-L 0.197; p.5: 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'; p.5: 'driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio'.
findings.suggested_fix: Label each bar by ASR system (or replace with a table); revise the 'mirrors' claim to describe the within-Whisper reversal; discuss that window-local QA cannot detect transcript-level failures such as hallucination loops.

findings.title: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct used as a ground-truth verifier; 26.6% rejection rate unexplained and unaudited
findings.location: p.4 answerability check; footnote 3 p.2; p.4 'Datasets' counts
findings.description: One of the two gatekeeping verifiers is an 8B-parameter open model, and an item survives only if both verifiers agree. With 294 of 1,107 items (26.6%) rejected, the paper gives no breakdown of which verifier rejected, whether rejections correlate with corpus/topic, or whether a human audit found the rejected items actually flawed. A weak verifier at temperature 0 could systematically reject long or technically dense items (exactly the 'knowledge-intensive' items the paper says matter most), biasing the verified subset toward easier items and inflating its reference accuracy to 98-99%.
findings.evidence: Footnote 3: 'https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct'; p.4: 'two LLM judges (GPT4o and Llama3) ... an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm'; p.4: '1,107 generated questions (813 ground-truth-verified)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report per-verifier acceptance rates and agreement (kappa); human-audit a random sample of accepted and rejected items; check whether rejected items are concentrated in knowledge-intensive topics.

findings.title: Human-study QA (Table 7) deviates from the described pipeline: questions generated from ASR output on 25-word clips, roles conflated, condition unspecified
findings.location: p.7 Table 7 and preceding paragraph
findings.description: The Methodology insists 'Generation uses the reference transcript rather than an ASR output' with a +/-100-word window, but for the human-study clips the paper says 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria' on content of '25 words or less', and that 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples'. This (a) generates items from ASR transcripts, contaminating the answer key with recognition errors the paper elsewhere warns about; (b) cannot use the +/-100-word window; (c) attributes generation to the QA LLMs rather than Gemini. Table 7 then reports 'QA 100% Correct' vs '< 100% Correct' clips without stating which transcript condition (reference or which ASR) or how many items per clip were answered, so the 0.9/0.84/0.85 figures cannot be interpreted.
findings.evidence: p.3-4: 'Generation uses the reference transcript rather than an ASR output. This prevents recognition errors from contaminating the answer key'; p.7: 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria, but given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less, the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples and were frequently 100% accurate'; Table 7 columns gpt4o/llama/qwen 1/1/1 and 0.9/0.84/0.85.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the clip-level pipeline separately (generator, source transcript, window, number of items per clip, answer condition); if items were generated from ASR output, either regenerate from reference or explain why the contamination concern does not apply.

findings.title: Multiple-choice ceiling plus a window pre-selected to contain the keyword makes the closed-form task near-trivial for LLMs
findings.location: p.3 'Question Construction' window paragraph; p.5 Figure 4; p.6 'the multiple-choice format may understate the true accessibility gap'
findings.description: The QA model receives a ~200-word window centered on the keyword plus four options, with the correct option written from that same window. Full-set reference accuracy is 94-95% and verified-subset accuracy 98-99%, so the reference condition is at ceiling and the ASR condition (90.6% for Whisper-M) has little room to differ; the paper itself concedes the MC format 'may understate the true accessibility gap'. The ceiling is not merely a format issue but a consequence of handing the model the exact passage the item was written from. Deletion-type errors in particular (23 vs 8, 14 vs 6 discordant) barely register, which is implausible if deleted keywords truly 'leave no trace at all' and the item depended on them; it indicates the window still contains enough paraphrase to answer, i.e., the item does not depend on the keyword.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'The keyword and a +/-100-word window of surrounding context are provided to the generator'; p.4: 'the reference (gold) window and the corresponding ASR-transcribed window as context'; Figure 4 ref bars 0.954/0.940/0.935; Table 3 Deletion rows 23/8 and 14/6; p.6: 'the multiple-choice format may understate the true accessibility gap'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report item-level discrimination (fraction of items where any model changes answer); use larger or full-transcript contexts to simulate a real learner's search task; add harder distractor generation validated by closed-book failure; consider item-response analysis rather than raw accuracy.

findings.title: 300-item open-ended sample: per-model CIs of +/-4.5-5.2pt, no per-model tests, single ASR system, sampling not described
findings.location: p.6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions' and Table 4
findings.description: With n=300 per model, the 95% CI half-width on an accuracy of 0.80 is +/-4.5pt and on 0.70 is +/-5.2pt, so the per-model drops (10.3, 11.3, 14.0pt) are not distinguishable from one another and the implied model ordering is unsupported. Only the pooled McNemar (900 pairs) is reported. Open-ended results exist only for Whisper-M, so the format effect for the Wav2Vec2 systems (where the MC gap is largest) is unknown. The sampling procedure (seed, stratification by corpus/topic/error type) is not given. The sample is adequate for detecting the pooled effect but not for the per-model comparisons Table 4 invites.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'we randomly sample 300 questions from the ground-truth-verified set'; Table 4 drops 10.3pt/11.3pt/14.0pt; p.6: 'toward=140, away=33, n=173'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report per-model McNemar and bootstrap CIs on the drops; either run all 813 verified items open-ended or state the sample as pooled-only evidence; specify sampling.

findings.title: Cohen's h of 0.24-0.34 described as 'small-to-medium' despite the paper's own stated convention
findings.location: p.6 second paragraph after Table 4
findings.description: The paper cites Cohen's thresholds (0.2 small, 0.5 medium) and then labels h = 0.24-0.34 as moving 'into the small-to-medium range'. All three values are below the midpoint between small and medium and are conventionally 'small'. The wording overstates the format effect.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'both in the conventionally "small" range (h=0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large)' followed by 'The effect size moves from small (h=0.14-0.19) into the small-to-medium range (h=0.24-0.34)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe both as small effects; rely on odds ratios or item-level analyses for the format comparison.

findings.title: Determinism claim for GPT4o at temperature 0 is not guaranteed; single run, no variance reported
findings.location: p.4 'Prompt and Temperature'; p.2 'Decoding is deterministic where supported'
findings.description: The paper states decoding is deterministic (temperature 0) for QA and verification, but the GPT4o API is not bit-deterministic at temperature 0, and Gemini generation at temperature 0.3 is stochastic by design. No repeat runs, seeds, or variance across runs are reported for any stage, so the stability of the 1,107-item set, the 813 verified items, and the discordant-pair counts is unknown.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'Decoding is deterministic where supported'; p.4: 'decoding is deterministic (temperature 0) for QA and ground-truth verification, and temperature 0.3 for question generation'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report repeat-run agreement for QA answers and verification decisions (e.g., three runs), and seeds where supported.

findings.title: Broken cross-references to appendix material that is not in the submission ('Table 11', 'see Section for details')
findings.location: p.6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'; p.5 'We further report the accuracies from the verified question subset in the Appendix'; p.6 'test results over all the ASR systems in the Appendix'
findings.description: The multiple-choice comparison figures '2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11' are central to the open-ended argument but Table 11 does not exist in the 9-page submission; 'see Section for details' has an empty section reference. The per-ASR McNemar results and verified-subset accuracies that would let a reader check the QA claims are all deferred to an appendix that is not provided.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11'; p.6: '(see Section for details)'; p.5: 'We further report the accuracies from the verified question subset in the Appendix.'
findings.suggested_fix: Include a per-model, per-ASR accuracy table for full and verified sets in the main paper; fix the cross-references.

findings.title: How is the +/-100-word ASR window located when the anchor keyword is substituted or deleted?
findings.location: p.3 'Question Construction'; p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'
findings.description: The reference window is defined around the keyword, but in the ASR condition the keyword may be replaced ('basic session') or absent. The paper says only 'the corresponding ASR-transcribed window'. Is a word-level alignment (e.g., Levenshtein alignment used for WER) applied to map reference word indices to ASR indices? For deletions, is the window centered on the aligned gap? Are ASR windows the same length as reference windows? This determines whether deletion items receive comparable context and whether the 23/8 deletion result is meaningful.
findings.evidence: p.4: 'the reference (gold) window and the corresponding ASR-transcribed window as context for QA LLMs'; p.3: 'a deletion leaves no trace at all'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the alignment algorithm and window construction for both error types; report mean window length in each condition.

findings.title: Are multiple-choice options shuffled, and is answer-position balanced?
findings.location: p.3-4 'Question Construction' and 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'; Figure 1 example
findings.description: Position bias in 7-8B instruction-tuned models can shift accuracy by several points on 4-option MC. The only displayed item (Figure 1) has the correct answer at B. The paper does not say whether Gemini's option order was randomized post-generation or whether the correct-answer position distribution was checked. Given that the reported reference-vs-ASR gaps are 2.7-4.7pt, an unbalanced key could rival the effect size.
findings.evidence: Figure 1 Question Construction panel: correct option marked 'B. Removal of damaged segments via specialized enzymatic pathways'; p.4: 'return a single option letter'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the correct-answer position distribution and randomize/balance option order (or evaluate with all four permutations).

findings.title: Which ASR system's errors define the 'knowledge-error keywords' and the 'ASR-mishearing' used by the cue filter?
findings.location: p.3 filtering paragraph; p.4 'Datasets'; Figure 1
findings.description: Keywords are chosen as reference/ASR pairs denoting different concepts, and the cue filter rejects stems containing 'its ASR-mishearing'. With seven ASR systems, the mishearing differs per system. Figure 1 shows Whisper. If Whisper-M's errors define the set, Figure 4's comparisons across the other six systems are on a Whisper-M-selected set; if the union of all systems' errors is used, the per-item error-type labels in Table 3 (computed for Whisper-M) would not apply to all items. The paper must state this.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'keeping only pairs where the ASR output denotes a genuinely different concept'; p.4: 'its ASR-mishearing, or an obvious variant of either is rejected'; Table 3 caption: 'over the Whisper-M ASR transcript'.
findings.suggested_fix: State the keyword-selection ASR system explicitly and report how many items have a keyword error under each of the seven systems.

summary: The paper correctly diagnoses a real problem (WER does not tell an institution whether a transcript conveys a lesson) and builds a defensible ASR-to-LLM robustness benchmark on real educational recordings. However, what it measures is how well three LLMs answer keyword-anchored multiple-choice questions from a ±100-word transcript window, and it never connects that measurement to any Deaf/hard-of-hearing, multilingual, or other human learner; the abstract explicitly redefines accessibility as a transcript's "potential for use in LLM-driven downstream tasks." The central equity claim in the title and conclusion (that accented instructors' lessons become less usable) is never tested: QA accuracy is reported pooled across speakers, with no L1/L2 split anywhere in Figure 4 or Tables 3-4, and the only speaker-group-to-QA link (Table 7, 84% vs 91% L2) is untested and non-significant on reconstructed counts. The "human study" is of hearing listeners rating accent from audio, the inverse of the population the paper claims to serve, and cannot validate the proxy. Effect sizes are small by the paper's own reporting (2.7-4.7pt multiple-choice drop with the best ASR, Cohen's h 0.14-0.19), the reference accuracy is reported as three different numbers, and the paper offers institutions no actionable guidance despite the unsourced "99% accuracy" policy hook and the fact that every system tested fails that bar. The limitations section is candid, but the title, abstract, and conclusion do not carry that candor.
strengths: Correctly argues (p.1 Introduction; p.7 Related Work 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy') that WER is insufficient for educational content because it weights a mis-recognized enzyme name the same as a function word, and operationalizes this with a keyword-level BWER and a task-based QA stage rather than stopping at the critique.

Uses a large corpus of genuine educational recordings (1,232 EdX + 123 M3AV videos, 1,107 questions, Table 1 and p.4 'Datasets') with existing human-verified transcripts rather than read speech, which is the right setting for an accessibility argument.

Reports Cohen's h alongside p-values and explicitly states (p.6) that the multiple-choice gap is 'highly statistically robust but modest in absolute size', then probes whether format masks the effect with an open-ended variant (Table 4). This is more honest than most ASR-bias papers.

The Limitations section (p.7) candidly states that 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners, multilingual students, or people with different levels of prior knowledge' and calls for human learner studies.

The finding that Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t are substantially worse than Whisper-S/M on long lecture audio due to hallucination and repetition (p.5, Table 2) is practically important for any institution choosing a captioning backend.

The human accent-rating study (Tables 5-6) shows ASR error correlates with perceived accentedness even where human transcription BWER does not, which is a relevant signal that ASR is sensitive to speaker features beyond intelligibility.
Figure 1's worked example ('base excision repair' -> 'basic session repair') is a clear illustration of the fluent-but-wrong failure mode the paper is concerned with.

findings.title: The core equity claim is never tested: QA accuracy is not disaggregated by L1/L2 speaker status
findings.location: p.5 Figure 4 and Table 3; p.6 Table 4; p.7 Conclusions; title
findings.description: The title ('Accented Educational Speech'), abstract, and conclusion frame the contribution as showing that accented instructors' lessons become less accessible. But the knowledge-access measure (QA accuracy) is reported only pooled across all speakers: Figure 4 is model x ASR system, Table 3 is McNemar over the full 1,107 items, Table 4 is over a 300-item sample. Nowhere in the main text is QA accuracy, the reference-vs-ASR drop, or Cohen's h broken down by L1 vs L2 instructor, even though every video carries an L1/L2 label (Table 1: 343 L1 / 1,037 L2 EdX videos). Figure 2 shows only WER by group; ASR BWER (the knowledge-term metric) is also never split by L1/L2. The only speaker-group-to-QA link is Table 7 (p.7), a 194-clip subset from the human study where the L2 share is 84% vs 91% between fully-correct and not-fully-correct clips, with no test reported; on reconstructed counts (47/56 vs 126/138) a two-sided Fisher test gives p ~ 0.20. The conclusion's 'they can make some instructors' knowledge less searchable, reviewable, and usable than others'' is therefore not demonstrated by the paper's own data. Without this split, the paper shows that ASR errors reduce LLM QA accuracy, and separately that L2 speech has higher WER, but not that the lesson is disproportionately missing for accented instructors.
findings.evidence: Conclusion (p.7): 'These findings recast ASR bias as an educational access problem: errors do not merely alter text; they can make some instructors' knowledge less searchable, reviewable, and usable than others'.' Abstract: 'errors from transcribing accented speech affect knowledge terms that carry a lesson's disciplinary meaning.' Table 7: percent_L2 = 84 (QA 100% correct, n=56) vs 91 (QA < 100% correct, n=138), no test reported.
findings.suggested_fix: Report QA accuracy, reference-vs-ASR drop, McNemar toward/away counts and Cohen's h separately for L1 and L2 instructors (and by accentedness tertile from the human ratings) on the full 1,107-item set, plus ASR BWER by L1/L2. If the L2 drop is not larger than the L1 drop, revise the title, abstract, and conclusion accordingly.

findings.title: 'Accessibility' is operationalized as LLM QA accuracy on transcript windows; no disabled or multilingual learner is involved, and the abstract redefines accessibility as LLM-downstream utility
findings.location: Abstract (p.1, final sentence); Methodology p.3 'Question Construction'; p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'; Limitations p.7
findings.description: The paper's measure of whether 'a learner can recover the knowledge' is whether GPT4o/Llama3/Qwen2.5 select the correct option letter given the question and a ±100-word transcript window. This differs from a Deaf/hard-of-hearing or multilingual learner's situation in ways that push in both directions: the LLM has vast pretrained domain knowledge (the paper admits on p.7 that 'QA models may rely on pretrained knowledge even when instructed to use only the transcript'), receives a targeted question that tells it which fact matters, and reads a pre-selected window; a human learner has slides, lip-reading, prior lecture context, and the ability to re-read the whole transcript, but no question pointing to the corrupted term and, in live captioning, no window to review at all. No validation of the proxy against any human reader is offered. The Limitations section concedes that 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners, multilingual students', yet the abstract concludes that 'the accessibility of transcription should be evaluated through a comprehensive assessment of its potential for use in LLM-driven downstream tasks', which is a definition of pipeline robustness, not of accessibility. Accessibility in the disability-studies and HCI sense is a relation between a person with a disability and an artifact; the paper measures a property of text for a machine reader. 'Deaf and hard-of-hearing' appears exactly once (p.1); 'accessib*' appears 16 times. As written, the paper is an ASR-to-LLM robustness benchmark carrying an accessibility label it has not earned.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'These findings suggest that, alongside utility measurements, the accessibility of transcription should be evaluated through a comprehensive assessment of its potential for use in LLM-driven downstream tasks.' p.4: 'The prompt instructs the model to use only the provided context and return a single option letter, with no explanation.' p.7 Limitations: 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners, multilingual students, or people with different levels of prior knowledge.' p.7 Related Work: 'using multiple LLMs as standardized readers ... to estimate how much knowledge survives transcription for a human learner.'
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) reframe the paper honestly as a downstream-robustness benchmark for ASR in educational content and remove 'accessibility' from the title and abstract's definitional sentence, or (b) add a small validation study in which human readers (ideally including DHH and L2 participants) answer a subset of the same items from reference vs ASR windows, and report agreement between human and LLM item-level outcomes. At minimum, the abstract should carry the same caveat as the Limitations.

findings.title: The human study does not validate the proxy and samples the inverse of the target population (hearing listeners rating audio)
findings.location: Abstract (p.1); Contributions bullet 3 (p.2); p.6 'Human Study of Perceived Accented Speech'; Tables 5-7
findings.description: The abstract says the framework is complemented 'with a human study that shows consistent observations with ASR and QA LLMs' performance', and the contributions list 'An augmentation study of human listeners that confirms the observed performance trends of ASR and QA LLMs.' A reader will take this as evidence that the LLM proxy tracks human knowledge recovery. It does not: the human study asks hearing listeners to rate accentedness/comprehensibility and transcribe 25-word audio clips. It measures perception of accent from audio, not recovery of a lesson from a transcript. The paper's motivating population is 'learners who cannot access the audio' (p.1); the participants are people who can. No information about the raters (number, hearing status, L1, domain expertise, ratings per clip, compensation, ethics approval) appears in the main text; all of it is deferred to an appendix that is not in the submission. The conclusion's 'perceived accentedness correlates with ASR errors' is already well established in the paper's own related work (Hirschi and Kang 2024; Inceoglu et al. 2023), so the study adds little to the accessibility argument.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'We further complement this evaluation with a human study that shows consistent observations with ASR and QA LLMs' performance.' p.6: 'The human study measures how listeners perceive accented speakers in the recording corpus ... More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.' p.1: 'fall hardest on learners who cannot access the audio.' Table 5 caption: 'Intelligibility (Int) is the BWER of human transcription.'
findings.suggested_fix: Move rater demographics, hearing status, number of raters per clip, and ethics approval into the main text. Reword abstract and contributions so the human study is described as an accent-perception study, not as confirmation of the QA proxy. Ideally add transcript-reading participants.

findings.title: The '99% accuracy' institutional policy claim is unsourced, and the paper never relates its results to it even though every system tested fails the bar
findings.location: p.1 Introduction, paragraph 3; Table 2 (p.4); Figure 2 (p.5)
findings.description: The introduction states that 'many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech' with no citation, no example institution, and no definition of what 'accuracy' means (word accuracy? caption accuracy per DCMP/FCC-style guidelines?). This is the paper's only concrete institutional hook and it is never returned to. Yet the results speak directly to it: from Figure 2's bar labels, the best system (Whisper-M) reaches word accuracy of about 94.4% for L1 and 92.0% for L2 speech; Table 2 gives 92.5-92.6% overall. Every one of the seven systems, on both speaker groups, falls short of 99%, and the L2 shortfall is roughly 1.4x the L1 shortfall. Connecting the numbers to the policy would be the single most useful thing the paper could tell an institution, and it is absent.
findings.evidence: p.1: 'In response to this threat of inaccessible content, many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech.' (no citation). Figure 2 labels: Whisper-M WER 0.056 (L1) vs 0.080 (L2); Table 2: Whisper-M WER 0.074 (EdX), 0.077 (M3AV).
findings.suggested_fix: Cite the policies (e.g., specific university captioning standards or the guidelines they derive from), define 'accuracy', and add a short analysis of which systems/speaker groups meet or miss the threshold and by how much.

findings.title: Abstract and conclusion claim QA gaps are largest in knowledge-intensive material and differ 'substantially across topics', but no QA-by-topic result exists in the paper
findings.location: Abstract (p.1); Conclusions (p.7); Figure 3 (p.5)
findings.description: The abstract states that results 'show substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material', and the conclusion says 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics.' The only topic-level data in the paper is Figure 3, which shows Whisper-M CER/WER/BWER by domain (an ASR metric, not QA). Figure 4, Table 3, and Table 4 contain no topic breakdown, and the text never points to an appendix table for one. Similarly, 'substantial differences among QA LLMs' is contradicted by the paper's own text ('Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%) show very similar performance') and by Figure 4's reference bars (0.954/0.940/0.935). The 'lower vs higher knowledge intensity' segment classification described on p.2 is never used in any reported result.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'The results show substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material.' Conclusion: 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics.' Figure 3 caption: 'Performance of Whisper-M by domain/topics' (error rate, not QA). p.2: 'segments are classified as lower or higher in knowledge intensity' (never reported on).
findings.suggested_fix: Add QA accuracy and reference-vs-ASR drop by topic family and by the lower/higher knowledge-intensity label to the main text, or remove these claims from the abstract and conclusion.

findings.title: Title and framing ('The Lesson Is Missing') overstate effect sizes the paper itself calls small
findings.location: Title; Abstract; p.6 paragraph after Table 4; Table 4
findings.description: By the paper's own numbers, using the best ASR (Whisper-M) the multiple-choice drop is 2.7-4.7pt with Cohen's h = 0.14-0.19, which the text labels 'conventionally small' and 'modest in absolute size'. The open-ended variant on a 300-item sample yields 10.3-14.0pt drops with h = 0.24-0.34; the paper describes this as moving 'into the small-to-medium range', but all three values are below Cohen's 0.5 threshold for medium, so they remain small. Under the adversarial open-ended grading the reference (gold-transcript) condition itself scores only 77-84%, meaning the proxy fails 16-23% of items even with a perfect transcript, which bounds how much of the ASR-condition drop can be attributed to lost knowledge rather than grader strictness. A title asserting that 'the lesson is missing' is not a responsible summary of 85-97% of items surviving; nor are 'the words there' when 1 in 13 words is wrong (WER 7.4%). The measured phenomenon is 'a small but consistent fraction of knowledge-bearing items becomes unrecoverable', which is a legitimate and publishable finding when stated plainly.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'h = 0.140 on the full set and h = 0.190 on the ground-truth-verified subset, both in the conventionally "small" range'; 'the reference-vs-ASR accuracy gap is highly statistically robust but modest in absolute size'; 'The effect size moves from small (h=0.14-0.19) into the small-to-medium range (h=0.24-0.34)'. Table 4: ref 0.803/0.773/0.843, asr 0.700/0.660/0.703.
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle to reflect the finding (e.g., that knowledge-term errors produce a consistent, concentrated loss), describe h = 0.24-0.34 as small, and report the gold-condition ceiling explicitly as a limit on the proxy's sensitivity.

findings.title: Reference QA accuracy is reported as three different values (99.3% vs 95.4% vs 94.3%), and Figure 4's unlabeled bars appear to contradict the 'mirrors ASR error ordering' claim
findings.location: p.5 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' text; Figure 4 (p.5) bar labels; Figure 1 (p.2) 'Accuracy Comparison' box
findings.description: The p.5 text says GPT4o reaches 99.3% in the reference condition, Llama3 98.3%, Qwen2.5 97.9%. Figure 4's bar labels read 0.954, 0.940, 0.935 for the same condition. Figure 1's 'Accessibility Evaluation' box shows 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%, ASR (Whisper) 90.6%, Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points', a third set. Since the size of the reference-to-ASR gap is the paper's accessibility claim, this must be reconciled. Separately, Figure 4 labels only families (Whisper vs Wav2Vec) and not individual systems; if the four Whisper bars follow Table 2 order (S, M, L-t, L), then for GPT4o the ASR-condition accuracies are 0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945, i.e., Whisper-L (WER 0.197) gives the smallest QA drop (0.9pt) and Whisper-M (WER 0.074, the 'best working ASR') gives the largest within-family drop (2.8pt); the same pattern holds for Llama3 (0.903/0.892/0.916/0.919) and Qwen2.5 (0.904/0.899/0.921/0.919). That contradicts 'the stronger Whisper systems produce the smallest drops' and 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'. It also matters for the accessibility argument: it would show that hallucination/repetition errors that inflate WER barely affect knowledge recoverability, while low-WER systems can still corrupt the terms that matter, which is exactly why WER should not be used to validate the QA measure.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%)'. Figure 4 reference bars: 0.954 / 0.940 / 0.935. Figure 1: 'Reference (Correct) 94.3% ... ASR (Whisper) 90.6% ... Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'. p.5: 'the stronger Whisper systems produce the smallest drops. This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'.
findings.suggested_fix: State which question set each number refers to and make text, Figure 1, and Figure 4 agree. Label each bar in Figure 4 with its ASR system and revise the ordering claim to match the data.

findings.title: 'Recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap' holds only in absolute WER; the relative disparity is unchanged
findings.location: p.5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains', Figure 2
findings.description: The text says the L1/L2 gap is 'narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.' From Figure 2's labels, the L2/L1 WER ratio is 1.40 (Whisper-S), 1.43 (Whisper-M), 1.38 (Whisper-L-t), 1.61 (Whisper-L), 1.40 (Wav2Vec2-B), 1.39 (Wav2Vec2-L), 1.29 (Wav2Vec2-L-s). The best Whisper models have the same or a larger relative penalty for L2 speakers than the Wav2Vec2 models; only the absolute gap shrinks because all errors shrink. For an equity argument, the relative burden is the relevant quantity: an L2 instructor's students face roughly 40% more errors per word regardless of which family is used. The sentence as written could lead a platform to conclude that adopting Whisper resolves the disparity.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'with the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.' Figure 2 labels: Whisper-M 0.056 vs 0.080 (ratio 1.43); Wav2Vec2-B 0.196 vs 0.275 (ratio 1.40); Wav2Vec2-L-s 0.135 vs 0.174 (ratio 1.29).
findings.suggested_fix: Report both absolute and relative L1/L2 gaps and revise the claim; note that the relative disparity persists in the strongest models.

findings.title: No engagement with the accessible-computing literature on caption quality for Deaf/hard-of-hearing viewers, which already established the WER-is-insufficient argument and word-importance metrics
findings.location: p.7 Related Work, 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy' paragraph; p.1 Introduction
findings.description: The paper's central methodological premise (that WER treats all words equally while DHH consumers need the important words right) has a decade of prior work in ASSETS/TACCESS/CHI, including word-importance-weighted caption quality metrics validated against DHH users' comprehension (the ACE metric line by Kafle and Huenerfauth), studies of DHH students' use of automatic captions in STEM lectures (e.g., Kushalnagar and colleagues), and DHH users' genre-specific caption accuracy needs (Berke et al.). None of this is cited. The 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy' paragraph instead cites a psychiatry-research paper (Just et al. 2025), a master's thesis on air-traffic control (Maaz 2023), and a 2008 keyword-error-rate paper (Park et al. 2008). The only DHH-specific citations in the entire paper are Wald and Bain 2008 and Zárate 2021, both in the first sentence of the introduction. For a paper whose title claims to evaluate 'ASR Accessibility', the absence of the accessibility research community's own metrics and user studies is a serious gap, and it means the paper cannot position its BWER/keyword approach relative to already-validated importance-weighted metrics.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'Research in medical and aviation contexts indicates that these costs are significant and could result in grave consequences (Just et al. 2025; Maaz 2023). Keyword-focused metrics narrow this gap but still assess textual correspondence rather than whether a learner can recover the underlying knowledge (Park et al. 2008).' Introduction p.1 is the only place DHH learners are mentioned.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a related-work paragraph on caption evaluation for DHH users (word-importance/ACE metrics, DHH lecture-caption studies) and explain how the proposed knowledge-keyword approach differs from or extends importance-weighted metrics validated with DHH participants.

findings.title: Ethics: biographical profiling of identifiable instructors and name-based origin inference are not discussed in the 'Ethical Concerns' section; internal contradiction on name-based inference
findings.location: p.2-3 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' (L1/L2 labeling); p.7 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns'
findings.description: L1/L2 labels were assigned by researching real, publicly identifiable instructors: 'each of the 27 unique instructors was individually researched for country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US, and accent/background'. For M3AV, 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation', then verified for only 'a subset of speakers' via OpenAlex lookup of PhD institution and 'year of arrival in the US'. Inferring national origin or native language from a person's name is a practice the fairness literature treats as ethically fraught and error-prone, and compiling immigration-related biographical dossiers on named individuals without consent raises privacy concerns regardless of public availability. The sentence 'L1/L2 speaker status is established through biographical research rather than assumed from name or accent alone' is contradicted by the M3AV procedure two sentences later. The section titled 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' contains no ethical concerns: it does not mention this profiling, whether the human-rater study received ethics approval, rater consent, or whether instructors' labels will be released with the dataset (the contributions list a dataset 'enriched with speakers' demographics').
findings.evidence: p.2-3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors was individually researched for country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US, and accent/background'; 'For M3AV, an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup'. p.2 Contributions: 'enriched with speakers' demographics'. p.7 section 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' has no sentence addressing data-subject privacy, consent, or ethics review.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an ethics statement covering IRB/ethics approval for the human study, the basis for compiling instructor biographical data, how (or whether) per-instructor demographic labels will be released, and the error rate/validation of name-based inference. Correct the 'not assumed from name' sentence.

findings.title: No actionable implications for institutions or platforms, despite several practically important findings buried in the results
findings.location: p.7 Conclusions and Future Work; p.5 Table 2 discussion; p.3 BWER description
findings.description: The conclusion ends with 'Future work will investigate the mitigation strategies of such ASR biases' and offers nothing an accessibility office, LMS vendor, or instructor could act on. Yet the paper contains directly usable findings that are never surfaced as recommendations: (1) the larger Whisper-L/L-t checkpoints are worse than Whisper-S/M on lecture audio because of hallucination/repetition, so 'use the biggest model' is the wrong default; (2) no system meets a 99% standard for either speaker group, so automatic captions alone cannot satisfy the policies the paper invokes; (3) substitution errors on technical terms (Table 3: 137 toward vs 29 away) dominate deletions, which suggests where human post-editing effort should go; (4) BWER for M3AV is computed from slide OCR text, which implies slide-text contextual biasing or glossary injection as a mitigation, never discussed; (5) EdX Engineering/CS and NIH biomedical content carry the highest technical-term error (Figure 3), which points to where institutions should prioritize human review, especially for L2 instructors. An accessibility paper at a top venue should translate its measurements into at least a short set of evidence-based recommendations.
findings.evidence: p.7 Conclusions: 'Future work will investigate the mitigation strategies of such ASR biases.' p.5: 'Inspection of individual transcripts shows this is driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit.' p.3: 'for M3AV, drawn from slide OCR text released with the corpus'. Table 3: Substitution toward 137 / away 29 vs Deletion 23 / 8.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Implications for practice' paragraph: model selection guidance, where to target human review (topic x speaker group), the gap to policy thresholds, and slide/glossary-based biasing as a concrete mitigation to test.

findings.title: Table 7 inference is untested, rests on a NIH-dominated subset, and the '<100% correct' group size contradicts 'frequently 100% accurate'
findings.location: p.7 Table 7 and surrounding text; Table 5 (p.6)
findings.description: The paper concludes 'L2 speakers are more likely to have lower QA LLM accuracy, particularly when their accent is more marked' from Table 7, which compares 56 fully-correct clips (84% L2) with 138 not-fully-correct clips (91% L2). No statistical test is given; on reconstructed counts (47/56 vs 126/138) a two-sided Fisher exact test gives p of about 0.20, and the accentedness difference (3.8 vs 4.3 on a 9-point scale) is likewise untested. The sample is 71.5% NIH biomedical clips (168/235 in Table 5), so speaker group is confounded with domain; EdX domain rows have n = 5-10 clips each, making the Table 5 topic comparisons (e.g., Humanities Com 1.3 on n = 6) anecdotal. The text also says QA LLMs on the clips 'were frequently 100% accurate', but 138 of 194 clips (71%) are in the '<100% correct' row. Finally, the per-model accuracies in Table 7 (gpt4o 0.90, llama 0.84, qwen 0.85 in the imperfect group) are of a different scale from Figure 4, and the number of questions per clip is not given.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples and were frequently 100% accurate.' Table 7: n = 56 (100% correct) vs 138 (<100% correct); percent_L2 84 vs 91; Acc 3.8 vs 4.3. Table 5: NIH n = 168 of 235; Humanities n = 6. Conclusion of section: 'L2 speakers are more likely to have lower QA LLM accuracy, particularly when their accent is more marked.'
findings.suggested_fix: Report tests (or CIs) for the Table 7 comparisons, control for venue/domain, state questions per clip, and soften or remove the causal-sounding conclusion if not supported.

findings.title: Human listeners miss 28-34% of technical keywords from audio while Whisper-M misses 5-7%; the paper does not reckon with what this means for its accessibility framing
findings.location: p.6 Table 5 'Int (BWER)' column; p.6-7 text 'these models outperform human listeners in transcription accuracy'
findings.description: Table 5 reports human transcription BWER of 0.28 (L1) and 0.34 (L2) on 25-word clips, versus ASR BWER of roughly 0.05-0.07 for Whisper-M (Table 2). The paper notes ASR 'outperform[s] human listeners in transcription accuracy' but does not consider the implication for its own argument: if hearing listeners recover far fewer technical terms from the audio than the transcript contains, then for many learners (including hearing multilingual learners) the ASR transcript may be more accessible than the audio, and the relevant comparison for a DHH learner is not transcript vs gold transcript but transcript vs no access. The authors should clarify how the human transcription task was run (single listen? domain-naive raters?) and discuss how this bears on the claim that ASR transcripts leave 'the lesson missing'.
findings.evidence: Table 5: L1 Int (BWER) 0.28, L2 0.34. Table 2: Whisper-M BWER 0.064 (EdX), 0.053 (M3AV). p.6-7: 'these models outperform human listeners in transcription accuracy, but are also significantly correlated to speaker accentedness.'
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the human transcription protocol and add a paragraph discussing the audio-vs-transcript baseline for different learner groups.

findings.title: Table 7's QA accuracy: which transcript condition and which ASR system?
findings.location: p.7 Table 7 and preceding paragraph
findings.description: Table 7 reports QA accuracy per model for the human-study clips, but the text says only that 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria'. It is not stated whether the accuracies are from the ASR-transcript condition (and if so, which of the seven systems), the reference condition, or a difference between them. If the accuracy is on the reference transcript, Table 7 says nothing about ASR bias; if on ASR, the system matters greatly given Figure 4. This must be stated for the section's conclusion about L2 speakers to be interpretable.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria, but given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less, the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples'. Table 7 header: 'QA Accuracy: gpt4o llama qwen' with no condition specified.
findings.suggested_fix: Specify the transcript condition and ASR system for Table 7 and, ideally, report both reference and ASR conditions.

findings.title: Binary L1/L2 label stands in for 'accent'; collected residence data and within-L2 accentedness variation are never used; live vs offline captioning is not distinguished
findings.location: p.2-3 L1/L2 labeling; Table 5 (L2 Acc mean 4.3/9); p.2 'unit of analysis'
findings.description: The title refers to accented speech, but the main analyses use a binary native/non-native label. The paper collected 'years of residence in the US' and per-clip 9-point accentedness ratings (L2 mean 4.3, implying wide within-group variation) but never uses either as a continuous predictor of ASR or QA outcomes, which would be a far more direct test of the accent claim than an L1/L2 dummy. Separately, the paper's learner scenarios include DHH students who typically rely on live captions during a lecture; the evaluation is entirely offline (full-recording ASR, ±100-word review windows), and the difference is not acknowledged. The 'multilingual learners' listed as beneficiaries (p.1) are learner-side; the study's L2 construct is instructor-side, and the paper does not consider that learners sharing an instructor's L1 may repair errors differently.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'researched for country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US'. Table 5: L2 Acc 4.3, L1 2.6 on 9-point scale. p.1: 'support Deaf and hard-of-hearing learners, people studying in noisy or quiet environments, multilingual learners'. p.2: 'ASR fidelity is measured both in short clips given to human raters and over full recordings, while the question-answering stage uses bounded local windows'.
findings.suggested_fix: Use accentedness rating and years of residence as continuous predictors of WER/BWER/QA drop; add a sentence distinguishing live-caption from offline-transcript use cases and scoping the claims to the latter.

summary: The paper's actual novelty is the intersection: applying an LLM-QA probe to real ASR output on accented (L1/L2-labelled) educational recordings, with BWER-style keyword error analysis and a human accentedness study alongside. Each component, however, has a substantial prior literature that the one-column Related Work (p.7) does not engage: task-/QA-based evaluation of lecture transcripts (Munteanu et al. 2006; Favre et al. 2013), spoken-QA-under-ASR-noise benchmarks (Spoken SQuAD, ODSQA, SLUE, ASR-GLUE), question-generation-based consistency evaluation (QAGS/FEQA/QuestEval and especially MQAG, which is essentially the same MCQ generate-then-answer design), semantic alternatives to WER (SemDist), DHH caption-usability metrics (Kafle & Huenerfauth), Whisper hallucination and accent-bias studies (Koenecke et al. 2024; Sanabria et al. 2023), and the Munro & Derwing paradigm that the human study reproduces without attribution. Consequently the two central gap statements ("the quality of transcripts as inputs to the downstream LLMs is underexplored", p.1; "A task-based evaluation is needed", p.7) and the framing of the first contribution bullet are overstated, and several findings presented as new or "counter-intuitive" (MCQ format understating the gap; Whisper-L hallucination) are known phenomena. There are also concrete citation problems (BWER attributed to the M3AV paper rather than the contextual-biasing literature; intro cites for "LLMs producing transcripts" that do not support the claim). The empirical study remains a useful, well-motivated data point, but the paper needs a substantially rewritten Related Work and a more modest, precise statement of what is new.
strengths: The specific intersection studied (L1/L2 accent disparity x downstream LLM QA x educational/knowledge-intensive speech x human ratings) is not, to my knowledge, covered by any single prior paper; the combination is a reasonable contribution even though each component is established.

The paper correctly identifies and cites the core sociolinguistic ASR-bias literature (Koenecke et al. 2020; Martin & Wright 2023; Wassink et al. 2022; Tatman 2017; Dubois et al. 2024) and several recent L2-focused ASR-vs-human studies (Inceoglu et al. 2023; Hirschi & Kang 2024; McCrocklin et al. 2026; Issa et al. 2026; Kuhn et al. 2023).

Using a keyword-restricted error rate (BWER) alongside WER/CER, and separating substitution from deletion errors on knowledge terms (p.3, 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'), is well motivated and more informative than WER-only reporting.

The MCQ vs. open-ended comparison (Table 4, p.6) is a useful methodological observation that a QA-based probe's sensitivity depends on answer format, and the McNemar/Cohen's h reporting is more careful than most ASR-downstream papers.
Curating L1/L2 labels for two educational corpora (EdX, M3AV; Table 1) is a nontrivial data effort that, if released, would be valuable to the accent-bias community.

findings.title: Core gap claim and Contribution 1 are pre-empted by existing task-/QA-based evaluation of ASR transcripts
findings.location: p.1 Introduction (end of para 1); p.2 contribution bullet 1; p.7 Related Work 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy' and 'QA LLMs'
findings.description: The paper positions QA-based/task-based evaluation of transcripts as a gap it fills, but this is a long-standing line of work that the Related Work omits entirely. (a) Munteanu, Baecker, Penn, Toms & James (Interspeech 2006, 'Measuring the acceptable word error rate of machine-generated webcast transcripts') had participants answer comprehension quiz questions about lecture webcasts using transcripts at controlled WER levels, in exactly this educational-lecture setting, and concluded WER alone is an inadequate usability measure. (b) Favre et al. (Interspeech 2013, 'Automatic human utility evaluation of ASR systems: Does WER really predict performance?') is an explicit task-based evaluation of ASR output. (c) Spoken SQuAD (Lee et al., Interspeech 2018) and ODSQA (Lee et al., SLT 2018) are the canonical benchmarks measuring QA accuracy as a function of ASR errors in the passage; SLUE / SLUE Phase-2 (Shon et al. 2022, 2023) and ASR-GLUE (Feng et al. 2021) benchmark downstream NLU/QA under ASR noise. (d) Generating questions from a reference text and answering them against a degraded text to measure information preservation is the QA-based evaluation paradigm from summarization (APES, Eyal et al. 2019; QAGS, Wang et al. 2020; FEQA, Durmus et al. 2020; QuestEval, Scialom et al. 2021), and MQAG (Manakul, Liusie & Gales, AACL 2023) does it specifically with LLM-generated multiple-choice questions answered under two conditions, which is the paper's Stage 1 + Stage 2 design. Given the paper cites Sidiropoulos et al. 2022 (which builds on the spoken-QA literature), omitting Spoken SQuAD is especially conspicuous. The framework is a recombination of these ideas applied to accented educational speech; that application is legitimate, but the 'underexplored' / 'is needed' framing and the description of the framework as the first contribution are not defensible as written.
findings.evidence: p.1: 'the quality of transcripts as inputs to the downstream LLMs is underexplored.' p.7: 'A task-based evaluation is needed to determine whether transcription errors interrupt the specific use learners make of a transcript.' p.7 'QA LLMs' paragraph cites only Sidiropoulos et al. 2022 and Shapira et al. 2025 as prior downstream-task work.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the Related Work with a subsection on task-based and QA-based evaluation of ASR output (Munteanu et al. 2006; Favre et al. 2013; Spoken SQuAD/ODSQA; SLUE; ASR-GLUE) and on question-generation-based consistency evaluation (QAGS/FEQA/QuestEval/MQAG). Restate the contribution as 'applying and adapting QA-based evaluation to L2 accented educational speech with knowledge-term-centred items', and explicitly say what differs from MQAG and Spoken SQuAD (real ASR systems, accent labels, keyword targeting).

findings.title: Accessibility framing ignores the DHH caption-evaluation literature that already argues WER does not predict caption usability
findings.location: p.7 Related Work 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy'; title and Abstract
findings.description: The paper's argument that WER is 'insensitive to the communicative value of individual words' and therefore insufficient for accessibility is supported only by a psychiatry paper (Just et al. 2025) and a master's thesis on air-traffic control (Maaz 2023). The directly relevant accessibility literature is missing: Kafle & Huenerfauth (ASSETS 2017, 'Evaluating the usability of automatically generated captions for people who are deaf or hard of hearing') showed WER correlates poorly with DHH users' judgments and proposed a word-importance-weighted metric (ACE); Kafle & Huenerfauth (ACM TACCESS 2019, 'Predicting the understandability of imperfect English captions for people who are deaf or hard of hearing') extended it; Berke, Caulfield & Huenerfauth (ASSETS 2017) studied DHH perspectives on imperfect ASR captions; Kafle & Huenerfauth (LREC 2018) released a word-importance corpus for transcripts. There is also follow-up work comparing ACE and WER on live captions. This body of work makes the same 'important words matter more than WER' argument the paper presents as motivation and provides metrics the paper should compare against. Because the title claims to evaluate 'ASR Accessibility' while the Limitations admit 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners' (p.7), the paper must at least position itself relative to studies that measured accessibility with the intended users.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'WER treats every substitution, deletion, and insertion as equally costly, but it is insensitive to the communicative value of individual words ... Research in medical and aviation contexts indicates that these costs are significant (Just et al. 2025; Maaz 2023). Keyword-focused metrics narrow this gap ... (Park et al. 2008).'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a paragraph on caption-usability research with DHH users (Kafle & Huenerfauth 2017, 2019; Berke et al. 2017) and word-importance metrics (ACE); state explicitly that the proposed QA probe is a complement, and ideally report ACE or a word-importance-weighted error alongside BWER.

findings.title: Semantic alternatives to WER are not discussed, so the case for an LLM-QA probe over cheaper metrics is not made
findings.location: p.7 Related Work 'Accessibility and ASR Accuracy'; p.3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'
findings.description: There is an established line of 'beyond WER' metrics that the paper neither cites nor compares against: Semantic Distance / SemDist (Kim et al., Interspeech 2021, 'Semantic Distance: A New Metric for ASR Performance Analysis Towards Spoken Language Understanding'; Kim et al., Interspeech 2022 on user perception), Szymański et al. (Findings of EMNLP 2020, 'WER we are and WER we think we are'), and several embedding/semantic WER variants proposed 2019-2024. These metrics were designed precisely to weight semantically consequential errors more heavily and have been validated against downstream SLU and human judgments. Without positioning against them, it is unclear what a costly LLM-QA pipeline adds over a semantic-distance score computed directly on the transcript pair, and the Related Work reads as if WER and keyword error rate (Park et al. 2008) were the only prior options.
findings.evidence: p.7 lists only WER and 'Keyword-focused metrics ... (Park et al. 2008)' as prior metric options; no embedding- or semantics-based ASR metric is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite SemDist and related semantic ASR metrics; report at least one such metric on the same recordings and show whether the QA-accuracy gap adds information beyond it (e.g., correlation with QA loss per recording).

findings.title: The 'counter-intuitive' Whisper-Large result is a known long-form hallucination artifact; relevant literature (including Koenecke et al. 2024) is not cited
findings.location: p.4 Table 2; p.5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' para 1
findings.description: Table 2 reports Whisper-L at WER 0.197 (EdX) / 0.168 (M3AV) versus Whisper-M at 0.074 / 0.077, and the text attributes this to 'hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio'. Whisper repetition/hallucination in long-form decoding is well documented: Radford et al. 2023 (which the paper cites) devotes a section to long-form decoding heuristics (temperature fallback, compression-ratio and log-prob thresholds, previous-text conditioning) that mitigate exactly this; Koenecke et al. (FAccT 2024, 'Careless Whisper: Speech-to-Text Hallucination Harms') characterise Whisper hallucinations and their disproportionate harm; chunked/VAD-based pipelines (WhisperX, Bain et al. 2023; Distil-Whisper, Gandhi et al. 2023) exist specifically to avoid it. Presenting this as a novel counter-intuitive observation, rather than positioning it against this literature and reporting which decoding settings were used, leaves the most striking ASR result unexplained and likely an artifact. It also bears on novelty: Koenecke et al. 2024 is the closest prior work on Whisper errors that corrupt content for vulnerable groups and is absent.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'Counter-intuitively, the larger Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t models perform substantially worse than the smaller Whisper variants. Inspection of individual transcripts shows this is driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio rather than a genuine capability deficit.'
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Radford et al.'s long-form decoding section, Koenecke et al. 2024, and WhisperX/Distil-Whisper; report the decoding configuration; either re-run Whisper-L with standard long-form safeguards or clearly label the result as pipeline-dependent.

findings.title: BWER is misattributed to the M3AV paper, and the EdX variant is not BWER; M3AV's own baselines and slide-context mitigation are not positioned against
findings.location: p.3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; p.4 Table 2; p.7 Related Work
findings.description: The paper writes 'Biasing Word Error Rate (BWER) (Chen et al. 2024)'. B-WER (with U-WER) originates in the contextual-biasing ASR literature, most commonly credited to Le et al. (Interspeech 2021, 'Contextualized Streaming End-to-End Speech Recognition with Trie-Based Deep Biasing and Shallow Fusion') and related Meta work; M3AV adopted it. Moreover, for EdX the metric is 'approximated as all non-function words in the reference', which is a content-word WER, not a biasing-word error rate, yet Table 2 labels both columns BWER and the text compares them. Separately, the paper takes both the M3AV corpus and its slide-OCR keyword lists from Chen et al. 2024 but never compares its Whisper WER/BWER numbers with the ASR baselines M3AV itself reports, nor discusses that M3AV's contextual-ASR benchmark (using slide text as biasing context) directly addresses the knowledge-term errors this paper documents, which is a highly relevant mitigation for the 'Future work' on mitigation (p.7).
findings.evidence: p.3: 'We additionally calculate the Biasing Word Error Rate (BWER) (Chen et al. 2024), restricted to rare/technical vocabulary: for M3AV, drawn from slide OCR text released with the corpus; for EdX, approximated as all non-function words in the reference'. Table 2 column headers 'BWER' for both corpora.
findings.suggested_fix: Attribute B-WER to the contextual-biasing literature (Le et al. 2021) and cite Chen et al. 2024 as the source of the M3AV keyword lists; rename the EdX measure (e.g., content-word WER); add a comparison to M3AV's reported ASR/BWER results and discuss slide-informed contextual biasing as prior mitigation work.

findings.title: Whisper/L2 accent-bias literature is under-cited; the RQ1 result replicates known findings without acknowledgement
findings.location: p.5 Figure 2 and para 2 of 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains'; p.7 Related Work 'ASR Performance Disparities'
findings.description: The finding that L2 speakers have higher WER across all systems and that the gap narrows for Whisper (Figure 2: e.g., Whisper-M 0.056 vs 0.080; Wav2Vec2-B 0.196 vs 0.275) is presented without reference to prior accent-bias evaluations of the same model families: Sanabria et al. (ICASSP 2023, Edinburgh International Accents of English Corpus, EdAcc) benchmark Whisper and wav2vec2 across L1/L2 English accents; Graham & Roll (JASA Express Letters 2024) evaluate Whisper across accents and speaker traits; Chan et al. (Interspeech 2022, 'Training and typological bias in ASR performance for world Englishes'); DiChristofano et al. (2022, global accent disparities in commercial ASR); Meyer et al. (LREC 2020, Artie Bias Corpus); Liu et al. (ICASSP 2022, Casual Conversations fairness); Feng et al. (2021, 'Quantifying bias in ASR'). Aksënova et al. 2022 and Issa et al. 2026 are cited but only in the Introduction, not used to interpret results. The paper's own RQ1 is therefore largely confirmatory and should be framed as such, with novelty resting on the educational domain and downstream QA.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'L2 speakers show consistently higher error rates than L1 speakers across every ASR system, with the gap widening for the weaker Wav2Vec2 models and narrowing for the strongest Whisper models. This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add the accent-bias benchmarks above to Related Work; state that RQ1 replicates prior L1/L2 gap findings on a new domain and quantify agreement (e.g., compare relative L2/L1 WER ratios to EdAcc).

findings.title: Human study reproduces the Munro & Derwing paradigm without citation, and its novelty claim conflicts with the paper's own account of prior ASR-vs-human work
findings.location: p.2 contribution bullet 3; p.6 'Human Study of Perceived Accented Speech', Tables 5-6; p.7 Related Work 'ASR Performance Disparities'
findings.description: Table 5 measures accentedness and comprehensibility on 9-point scales and intelligibility via listener transcription accuracy. This is the standard Munro & Derwing (1995, Language Learning, 'Foreign accent, comprehensibility, and intelligibility in the speech of second language learners'; also Derwing & Munro 1997) operationalisation and the source of the three-construct distinction, yet neither is cited.
