In addition, the contribution bullet describes the human study as 'an augmentation study of human listeners that confirms the observed performance trends', but the Related Work itself lists several prior studies that already compared ASR errors with human L2 perception (Hirschi & Kang 2024; Inceoglu et al. 2023; McCrocklin et al. 2026; Issa et al. 2026) and summarises them as finding that L2 speakers 'are penalized in unpredictable ways that do not align with human perception'. Table 6 instead reports significant correlations between accentedness ratings and every ASR model (e.g., Wav2Vec2-L r=0.453***). The paper neither positions its human study as a replication/extension of those works nor reconciles the apparent contradiction; as a result the third contribution's novelty is unclear.
findings.evidence: p.6 Table 5 caption: 'Accentedness (Acc) and Comprehensibility (Com) are on a 9-point scale, Intelligibility (Int) is the BWER of human transcription.' p.7: 'speakers whose first language is other than English are penalized in unpredictable ways that do not align with human perception (Hirschi and Kang 2024; Inceoglu, Chen, and Lim 2023; McCrocklin ... 2026).' p.6: 'accentedness ratings correlated significantly with all models'.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Munro & Derwing (1995) and Derwing & Munro (1997) for the constructs and scales; in Related Work and Discussion, state what the human study adds beyond Inceoglu 2023 / Hirschi & Kang 2024 / Issa 2026 and explain why the correlation pattern differs from the 'do not align' characterisation.

findings.title: MCQ-artifact and LLM-generated-question validity literature is missing; the 'MCQ masks the gap' finding is a known phenomenon
findings.location: p.3-4 'Question Construction' and 'Each generated item passes three checks'; p.6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions'
findings.description: The paper's headline methodological insight is that multiple-choice items understate the reference-vs-ASR gap because 'a QA LLM can sometimes eliminate distractors using its internal comprehensive capability without needing the gold reference' (p.6). That reading-comprehension items can be answered without the passage, and that LLMs answer MCQs from options alone, is well established: Kaushik & Lipton (EMNLP 2018, 'How much reading does reading comprehension require?'), Sugawara et al. (2018, 2020) on RC question difficulty, and Balepur, Ravichander & Rudinger (ACL 2024, 'Artifacts or Abduction: How do LLMs answer multiple-choice questions without the question?'). None is cited, and the paper's 'dependency check' (p.4) is exactly the passage-ablation test from that literature. Likewise, the pipeline's reliance on LLM-only validation of LLM-generated MCQs is not positioned against the educational question-generation validity literature: Kurdi et al. (IJAIED 2020 systematic review), Elkins et al. (AIED 2023, 'How useful are educational questions generated by LLMs?'), Doughty et al. (ACE 2024, GPT-4 vs human MCQs), and the paper's own intro cites Ahmed et al. 2025 and Ling & Afzaal 2024 on AI-generated question validity but never uses them to justify or bound the item-validation design, which involves no human item review.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'the multiple-choice format may understate the true accessibility gap, since a QA LLM can sometimes eliminate distractors using its internal comprehensive capability without needing the gold reference.' p.4: 'an item is retained only if both judges independently confirm the answer is correct given the passage.' (both judges are LLMs; no human validation reported).
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Kaushik & Lipton 2018 and Balepur et al. 2024 when motivating the dependency check and the open-ended variant; cite the AQG validity literature and either add a human validation sample of items or explicitly scope the contribution as LLM-validated only.

findings.title: Educational/lecture ASR and MOOC captioning prior work is absent, and the EdX corpus is uncited and undescribed as a dataset contribution
findings.location: p.2 contribution bullet 2; p.2 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts'; p.4 'Datasets'; p.7 Related Work
findings.description: Contribution bullet 2 claims 'two datasets with real-world educational recordings that have been cleaned and enriched with speakers' demographics and knowledge-centered questions'. Positioning of this claim is weak on two counts. (a) A long line of lecture-ASR and classroom-captioning work is not cited: the Liberated Learning Project (Bain, Basson & Wald, ASSETS 2002; Wald's subsequent work beyond the single 2008 cite), the MIT Spoken Lecture Processing project (Glass et al., Interspeech 2007), TED-LIUM (Rousseau et al. 2012; Hernandez et al. 2018), How2 instructional videos (Sanabria et al. 2018), Ranchal et al. (IEEE TLT 2013, real-time captioning and lecture transcription in the classroom), and DHH-focused caption accuracy studies in classrooms. Only Wald & Bain 2008 and Kuhn et al. 2023 are cited. (b) The 'EdX' corpus (1,380 videos, 27 courses, Table 1) has no citation, no description of how the videos were obtained or under what license, and no statement that the videos, L1/L2 labels, keywords, or questions will be released. Without release, 'cleaned and enriched' datasets are not a community contribution, and without provenance the corpus cannot be positioned against existing lecture corpora.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'An empirical evaluation over two datasets with real-world educational recordings that have been cleaned and enriched with speakers' demographics and knowledge-centered questions'. p.2: 'Inclusion requires ... permission for research use or availability under applicable terms'. Table 1 lists 'EdX 1,380 27 courses 5 343 1,037' with no citation for EdX.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite the lecture-ASR and classroom-captioning literature; describe the EdX source and licensing; state a release plan for labels, keywords and questions (or drop 'datasets' from the contribution list).

findings.title: The ASR systems evaluated (2020-2022 checkpoints) do not represent deployed captioning or current models, undermining the 'extensible framework' and 'recent models narrow the gap' positioning
findings.location: p.2 'We evaluate seven ASR systems...' and contribution bullet 1; p.5 'This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.'
findings.description: The motivation is captioning on platforms (p.1: 'online lectures, tutorials'), and the paper cites Dubois et al. 2024 on transcription bias in social-media and videoconferencing platforms, yet no deployed captioning system (YouTube, Zoom, commercial APIs) or any post-2022 open model (Whisper large-v3, NVIDIA Canary/Parakeet, OWSM, SeamlessM4T) is evaluated. The two families compared differ mainly in training data (wav2vec2 fine-tuned only on LibriSpeech read speech vs. Whisper's 680k-hour weak supervision), so the inference that 'recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap' conflates recency with training-distribution breadth, a point the paper's own cited Aksënova et al. 2022 makes. Contribution bullet 1 rests on 'seven ASR systems and three QA LLMs that can be easily extended', but a benchmark of off-the-shelf 2020-2022 checkpoints is not itself a research contribution, and without current systems the paper cannot speak to the state of practice it motivates against.
findings.evidence: p.2 contribution 1: 'An assessment framework with seven ASR systems and three QA LLMs that can be easily extended with recent model advancements.' p.2 footnote 2: 'facebook/wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self'. p.5: 'This suggests recent models reduce the L1/L2 accessibility gap.'
findings.suggested_fix: Include at least one current open model (e.g., Whisper large-v3 or Canary) and one deployed captioning API, or explicitly restrict claims to the two families tested and remove the recency inference; reframe contribution 1 around the evaluation methodology rather than the set of models.

findings.title: Introduction citations do not support the claims they are attached to
findings.location: p.1 Introduction paras 1 and 3
findings.description: The sentence 'Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous for producing transcripts (Shapira, Chazan, and Cohen 2025; Zheng et al. 2023; Sidiropoulos, Vakulenko, and Kanoulas 2022)' cites an LLM-as-a-judge paper (Zheng et al. 2023, MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena), a passage-retrieval-under-ASR-noise paper (Sidiropoulos et al. 2022), and a transcription-noise-on-SLU paper (Shapira et al. 2025); none concerns LLMs producing transcripts. Similarly, 'If an ASR system substitutes a function word ... a reader may recover the intended meaning from context (Baese-Berk et al. 2019)' cites a psychoacoustics study of distal speech rate and perception of function words by listeners, not reader recovery from transcript errors. The LLM-based ASR error-correction literature (e.g., HyPoradise, Chen et al. NeurIPS 2023; Whispering LLaMA, Radhakrishnan et al. EMNLP 2023; Ma et al. 2023) would be the appropriate support for LLMs' role in producing transcripts.
findings.evidence: p.1: 'While Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous for producing transcripts (Shapira, Chazan, and Cohen 2025; Zheng et al. 2023; Sidiropoulos, Vakulenko, and Kanoulas 2022)'. p.1: 'a reader may recover the intended meaning from context (Baese-Berk et al. 2019)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with citations that support each claim (LLM-based ASR/generative error correction for the first; reading-comprehension or caption-comprehension work for the second) or reword the claims.

findings.title: Uncited policy claim about 99% accuracy requirements
findings.location: p.1 Introduction para 3
findings.description: The statement that 'many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech' is a load-bearing motivational claim with no citation. The relevant sources exist (the DCMP Captioning Key's accuracy guideline, the FCC's 2014 Closed Captioning Quality Report and Order, WCAG 2.x caption success criteria, and university captioning policies), and the accessibility literature (e.g., Kafle & Huenerfauth 2017) discusses why a flat accuracy threshold is a poor proxy, which would strengthen the paper's own argument.
findings.evidence: p.1: 'In response to this threat of inaccessible content, many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech.' (no citation)
findings.suggested_fix: Cite the DCMP/FCC/WCAG sources or a specific institutional policy, and connect the threshold critique to prior caption-usability work.

findings.title: 'Recast ASR bias as an educational access problem' overstates novelty relative to work the paper itself cites
findings.location: p.7 Conclusions and Future Work
findings.description: The conclusion claims the findings 'recast ASR bias as an educational access problem'. That framing already exists in the cited literature: Kuhn et al. 2023 is published in ACM Transactions on Accessible Computing and specifically reports L2 lecture WER increases; Wald & Bain 2008 frames ASR as universal-access infrastructure for learning; Bandodkar et al. 2024 (AAAI) frames accent robustness as 'Accessible Communication'; and the Liberated Learning / classroom-captioning literature (uncited) has treated it this way for two decades.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'These findings recast ASR bias as an educational access problem: errors do not merely alter text; they can make some instructors' knowledge less searchable, reviewable, and usable than others'.' Compare p.7 Related Work: 'This is particularly problematic in educational contexts where Kuhn et al. 2023 found a 45% increase in WER in university lectures by second language speakers of English.'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'recast' with language that acknowledges the existing framing and states the incremental finding (downstream QA loss concentrated on knowledge terms for L2 speakers).

findings.title: Internal inconsistency in positioning the cause of L1/L2 disparities
findings.location: p.1 Introduction para 2 vs. p.5 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' para 2
findings.description: The Introduction attributes disparities to 'imbalances in training data and modeling choices' citing Aksënova et al. 2022, but the Results claim that because no system reverses the L1/L2 ordering, 'the L1/L2 disparity is a property of the recordings and speakers rather than an artifact of any one ASR system's training distribution.' All seven systems are trained predominantly on L1 English (wav2vec2 on LibriSpeech; Whisper on web-scraped, majority-L1 English), so a consistent ordering is exactly what a shared training-distribution bias predicts; the inference contradicts the paper's own cited framing and the accent-bias literature (Chan et al. 2022; Aksënova et al. 2022).
findings.evidence: p.1: 'These disparities reflect imbalances in training data and modeling choices ... (Aksënova et al. 2022).' p.5: 'indicating the L1/L2 disparity is a property of the recordings and speakers rather than an artifact of any one ASR system's training distribution.'
findings.suggested_fix: Revise the p.5 inference to 'shared across systems' rather than 'not a training-distribution artifact', and connect it to Aksënova et al. 2022 / Chan et al. 2022.

findings.title: LLM-based ASR error correction and contextual biasing are unmentioned though directly relevant to interpretation and stated future work
findings.location: p.7 Conclusions ('Future work will investigate the mitigation strategies'); p.4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'
findings.description: Two mitigation lines bear directly on the paper: (a) LLM-based generative ASR error correction (HyPoradise, Chen et al. NeurIPS 2023; Whispering LLaMA, Radhakrishnan et al. EMNLP 2023; Ma et al. 2023 'Can generative LLMs perform ASR error correction?'), which also implies that a QA LLM reading a noisy transcript may implicitly repair errors, an effect the paper should discuss when interpreting small MCQ gaps; (b) contextual biasing for rare/technical words (Pundak et al. SLT 2018 'Deep context'; Le et al. 2021; M3AV's slide-text contextual ASR), which targets precisely the knowledge-term substitutions the paper identifies. Neither is cited, so the 'Future work' statement reads as if mitigation were open ground.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'Future work will investigate the mitigation strategies of such ASR biases.' p.5: 'Some transcripts achieve comparatively low overall error while substituting several central terms with frequent everyday words.'
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short paragraph on generative error correction and contextual biasing as existing mitigations and discuss implicit correction by the QA LLM as a confound.

findings.title: Cascaded ASR-to-LLM design is not positioned against end-to-end speech LLMs and their spoken-QA benchmarks
findings.location: p.2 Methodology (framework design); Figure 1
findings.description: The framework assumes a cascade (ASR transcript -> text LLM). Since 2023-2024, speech-capable LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o audio, Qwen2-Audio, SALMONN) can answer questions from audio directly, and benchmarks such as VoiceBench and AudioBench (2024) evaluate exactly this. For a paper about whether 'the lesson' survives transcription, the obvious question is whether end-to-end models preserve knowledge terms better for accented speakers, or whether they inherit the same biases. The paper does not mention this alternative or explain why the cascaded framing is the right unit of accessibility evaluation (e.g., because captions/transcripts are the artifact learners actually receive).
findings.evidence: p.2: 'We present a two-stage framework ... which includes ASR transcription and LLM-driven question-answering (QA) stages' (Abstract); Figure 1 shows only the cascaded path.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence justifying the cascade (transcripts are the accessibility artifact) and cite speech-LLM evaluation work as an alternative/future comparison.

findings.title: Accent labelling by biographical inference is not positioned against self-report practice in prior accent-bias corpora
findings.location: p.2-3 'L1/L2 speaker status is established through biographical research'
findings.description: For M3AV, 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation', then partially verified via OpenAlex metadata. Prior accent-bias datasets (EdAcc, Sanabria et al. 2023; Artie Bias Corpus, Meyer et al. 2020; Casual Conversations, Liu et al. 2022) and Koenecke et al. 2020 use self-reported speaker metadata, and recent critical work (e.g., Prinos et al., FAccT 2024, on accent misconceptions in ASR research) specifically warns against inferring accent/L1 from names or nationality. The paper does not discuss how its labelling compares, what error rate it may have, or how misclassification would bias the L1/L2 gap.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'For M3AV, an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup against academic metadata (OpenAlex ...)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Position the labelling method against self-report-based corpora, report the fraction of M3AV speakers actually verified, and cite critical work on accent-proxy labelling.

findings.title: Keyword identification from lecture transcripts presented as new without reference to lecture keyphrase-extraction work
findings.location: p.3 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation'
findings.description: The 'LLM-driven knowledge-intensive keyword identification' with criteria such as centrality, definition, discipline-specificity and recurrence is presented without any citation, although keyphrase/concept extraction from lecture transcripts for indexing, segmentation and navigation is an established line (e.g., work on automatic keyphrase extraction and segmentation of video lectures, MOOC concept extraction, and the broader keyphrase-extraction literature). Positioning would clarify what the LLM-based criteria add over these.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'We first design LLM-driven knowledge-intensive keyword identification. Candidate keywords are extracted from noun phrases, named entities, definitions, repeated domain terms, quantities, and relations expressed in the reference transcript.' (no citations in the subsection)
findings.suggested_fix: Cite representative lecture keyphrase/concept extraction work and state the delta.

findings.title: Related Work is short, placed after Results, and uses an LLM-as-judge citation to justify LLMs as reader proxies
findings.location: p.7 Related Work 'QA LLMs'
findings.description: The Related Work occupies roughly one column at the end of the paper and its third paragraph ('QA LLMs') cites only two downstream-task papers. It supports the claim of 'using multiple LLMs as standardized readers' with Zheng et al. 2023, which is about LLMs as judges of chatbot responses, not about LLMs as proxies for human readers/learners. The Limitations section itself concedes 'QA LLMs are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners', so the Related Work should engage prior work that has used LLMs or QA models as reader proxies (QA-based summarization evaluation, MQAG) rather than a judge paper.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'We extend this task-based framing to accessibility specifically, using multiple LLMs as standardized readers (Zheng et al. 2023) to estimate how much knowledge survives transcription for a human learner.'
findings.suggested_fix: Expand Related Work into the four areas the paper spans (accent bias, accessibility/caption usability, ASR metrics beyond WER, QA-based evaluation) and replace the Zheng et al. cite with QA-based-evaluation literature.

summary: From an ethics and reproducibility standpoint the paper is substantially under-documented for a study whose central independent variable is an inferred, sensitive personal attribute (L1/L2 status) of identifiable people. The L1/L2 labels are produced by per-person "biographical research" on 27 named EdX instructors and by name-origin/affiliation guessing (verified only "for a subset") for M3AV academics, with no operational definition of L2, no consent, no IRB/ethics statement, and a stated intent to ship the datasets "enriched with speakers' demographics". The human-listener study (one of three claimed contributions) is reported with no rater count, recruitment, compensation, consent, scale anchors, or ethics approval; everything is deferred to an appendix that is not in the submission, along with "Table 11" and the prompts. Reproducibility is further weakened by unspecified checkpoints (Whisper-L v1/v2/v3? "L-t"?), unspecified long-form decoding settings that directly determine the headline Whisper-L "hallucination" result, undated GPT-4o and unnamed Gemini versions, no seeds or repeats, no hardware, no code/data/question-set release, and several internal inconsistencies about which M3AV recordings were retained. The Limitations section covers proxy validity and correlation-vs-causation reasonably, but omits privacy, consent, licensing, dual-use, label noise, and compute.
strengths: The paper is candid about role overlap in its LLM pipeline: p.4 explicitly states that the two ground-truth verifiers (GPT4o, Llama3) 'are drawn from the same pool of models used for downstream answering, so role separation is guaranteed against the generator but not fully among verifier and answerer roles'.

Unresolvable M3AV speakers are coded as unknown and excluded rather than guessed (p.3: '16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers'), and the authors state they tried to go beyond name/accent for EdX instructors.

Reference transcripts are drawn from the corpora's own released sources rather than authored by the paper's team (p.2), and the paper explicitly disclaims that one orthography 'exhausts the speaker's linguistic intent'.

Hugging Face URLs are given for three checkpoints (footnotes 1-3: whisper-medium, wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), temperatures are stated (0 for QA/verification, 0.3 for generation), the QA prompt's intent is described, and the statistical test is fully specified (McNemar exact / one-sided binomial on discordant pairs, plus Cohen's h).

The Limitations section (p.7) correctly acknowledges that QA LLMs 'are proxies for text use, not models of disabled learners', that ratings depend on 'the listener sample and the selected reference variety', that correlation cannot establish causation, and that QA models may leak pretrained knowledge.

The framing in the Conclusion ('recast ASR bias as an educational access problem') keeps the focus on system-induced inequity rather than on speaker deficiency, which is the ethically appropriate framing for this problem.

findings.title: L1/L2 label, the key independent variable, is undefined and partly name-inferred, contradicting the paper's own claim
findings.location: Page 2-3, Methodology, 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' (lines 189-209); Table 1 (p.4); Figure 2 (p.5)
findings.description: RQ1 and Figure 2 hinge entirely on the L1/L2 split, yet the paper never states what criterion makes a speaker 'L2' (which languages? bilingual from birth? L1 English speakers of Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean or British varieties? US-born children of immigrants?). For M3AV, the text says the label starts from 'author name origin and affiliation' and is verified only 'for a subset of speakers', so an undisclosed fraction of the 92 L2 / 31 L1 M3AV labels rests on name-origin inference alone, which the preceding sentence claims the paper does not do. No coverage of verification, no inter-annotator agreement, and no label-noise acknowledgment is given. For EdX the label is assigned per instructor and propagated to all of that instructor's videos, so the 343/1,037 video counts in Table 1 correspond to only 27 individuals. Because the labels are inferred sensitive attributes with unknown error, the main disparity claim ('L2 speakers show consistently higher error rates than L1 speakers across every ASR system', p.5) cannot be evaluated or reproduced.
findings.evidence: p.2-3: 'L1/L2 speaker status is established through biographical research rather than assumed from name or accent alone.' ... 'For M3AV, an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation, then verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup against academic metadata (OpenAlex ...)'. No definition of L1/L2 appears anywhere; Table 1 reports only 'L1 343 / L2 1,037' and 'L1 31 / L2 92'.
findings.suggested_fix: State the operational definition of L1/L2 (and how non-US L1 English varieties are coded); report how many M3AV speakers were actually verified vs. name-inferred; report agreement between two independent annotators; add a sensitivity analysis restricted to verified speakers; report the number of unique speakers per group alongside video counts; acknowledge label noise in Limitations.

findings.title: Biographical profiling of identifiable instructors and academics without consent, ethics review, or a data-protection statement; release of these 'demographics' is implied
findings.location: Page 2 contributions bullet 2 (lines 108-112); Page 3 lines 198-209; Page 7 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns'
findings.description: The authors compiled, for each of 27 named EdX instructors, country of origin, native language, years of US residence and 'accent/background', and for M3AV academics PhD institution/country, 'year of arrival in the US' and total US residence, via OpenAlex and other lookups. These are real, easily identifiable public figures; national origin and native language are sensitive personal attributes in most data-protection regimes, and 'accent/background' is a subjective characterization. No IRB/ethics-board review, consent, opt-out, data-minimization, retention policy, or lawful basis is mentioned anywhere. Worse, the second contribution advertises datasets 'enriched with speakers' demographics', implying that per-speaker inferred labels linked to identifiable instructors will be released. The Limitations section does not mention this at all.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors was individually researched for country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US, and accent/background, yielding a directly assigned L1/L2 label per instructor.' p.2: 'real-world educational recordings that have been cleaned and enriched with speakers' demographics'. The Limitations section (p.7) contains no sentence about consent, privacy, or the biographical research.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an ethics statement (IRB/ethics-board determination or exemption, including for the biographical research); describe the sources consulted and how the dossiers are stored/retained; label these attributes as inferred rather than 'demographics'; release only aggregate or de-identified per-speaker labels (no course/instructor identifiers), or obtain consent; discuss the privacy trade-off in Limitations.

findings.title: Human-listener study reported with no IRB, consent, compensation, rater count, rater background, scale anchors, or clip-selection procedure
findings.location: Page 6, 'Human Study of Perceived Accented Speech' (lines 561-573) and Table 5; Page 7 Table 7 and lines 640-657; Page 7 Limitations line 732-734
findings.description: The human study is one of the three stated contributions and supports RQ3, yet the main text gives none of the information needed to assess or reproduce it: how many raters, how they were recruited and compensated, whether they consented and under what ethics approval, their own L1/dialect background (which the Limitations concede shapes the ratings), how many raters judged each clip, the anchors/direction of the 9-point scales, how the 235 clips were sampled, and how the '25 words or less' clips were cut. All of this is deferred to an appendix that is not in the submission. The clip sample is also compositionally different from the corpus (83.4% L2 clips vs the 75% corpus target; 168/235 = 71.5% of clips are NIH), without explanation.
findings.evidence: p.6: 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.' Table 5 gives only n=39 (L1) and n=196 (L2) with no rater count. p.7 Limitations: 'Perceived-accentedness ratings are shaped by the listener sample' but the listener sample is never described. Table 5: NIH n=168 of 235 clips.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the essential protocol into the main text: rater N, recruitment platform, payment, consent/IRB approval number or exemption, rater L1 profile, ratings per clip, exact scale wording, clip sampling rule, and inter-rater reliability. Explain why the clip sample over-represents L2 and NIH speakers relative to the corpus.

findings.title: No data, code, prompt, or question-set availability statement despite claiming a dataset and an extensible framework as contributions
findings.location: Page 2 contributions (lines 105-114); Page 4 'Prompt and Temperature' (lines 394-402); Page 3 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation'; entire paper (no URL, footnote, or availability sentence)
findings.description: The paper claims 'an assessment framework ... that can be easily extended' and two 'cleaned and enriched' datasets, but nowhere states whether the code, the 1,107 generated questions (813 verified), the 1,113 keyword list, the per-speaker labels, the normalization rules, or the human-rating data will be released. Prompts are only paraphrased ('answer using only the provided transcript context and return a single option letter'); the keyword-extraction prompt, the priority criteria prompt, the LLM-judge triage prompt, the question-generation prompt, the two answerability-verification prompts, and the adversarial open-ended grading prompt are all absent. The only footnotes are Hugging Face model URLs.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'An assessment framework with seven ASR systems and three QA LLMs that can be easily extended'; 'two datasets ... cleaned and enriched with speakers' demographics and knowledge-centered questions'. p.4: 'All QA systems receive the same minimal instruction: answer using only the provided transcript context and return a single option letter, with no explanation.' No verbatim prompt appears anywhere in pages 1-9.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Data and Code Availability statement; release code, verbatim prompts, the question set with answer keys, keyword lists, normalization/equivalence lists, and de-identified human ratings under a stated license; if EdX terms prevent redistribution of audio/captions, release video IDs and derived annotations.

findings.title: ASR checkpoints and long-form decoding configuration are underspecified, although a headline result depends on them
findings.location: Page 2 lines 130-138 and footnotes 1-2; Page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis' (lines 210-223); Page 5 lines 435-439; Table 2 (p.4)
findings.description: Only 2 of the 7 ASR systems have identified checkpoints (footnote 1: whisper-medium; footnote 2: wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self). 'Whisper-S', 'Whisper-L', 'Whisper-L-t', 'Wav2Vec2-B' and 'Wav2Vec2-L' are never resolved: Whisper-L could be large-v1/v2/v3 (which differ markedly on accented speech and hallucination), and 'L-t' is never expanded (turbo? tiny?). Parameter counts are never listed despite the claim of 'a range of parameter counts'. Long-form decoding settings that govern the very failure mode the paper reports for Whisper-L ('hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio') are absent: chunking vs sequential decoding, chunk length, beam size, temperature fallback, compression-ratio/no-speech thresholds, condition_on_previous_text. Whether Wav2Vec2 used an n-gram LM is not stated. It is also ambiguous whether the EdX numbers in Table 2 use language='en' or auto-detection, because Whisper is described as 'additionally run' with the fixed language. No hardware is reported.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'four Whisper checkpoints: Whisper-S, Whisper-M [fn1], Whisper-L, and Whisper-L-t'; p.5: 'the larger Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t models perform substantially worse ... driven by hallucination and repetition failures on long lecture audio'; p.3: 'For EdX, Whisper models are additionally run with decoding language fixed to English (language="en")'. Table 2 reports Whisper-L WER 0.197 vs Whisper-M 0.074 on EdX without saying which configuration produced these numbers.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the exact Hugging Face IDs and parameter counts of all seven models; specify the long-form inference pipeline and all decoding hyperparameters; state whether Wav2Vec2 used an LM; clarify which Whisper language setting Table 2 reports (or report both); list GPU type and total compute.

findings.title: Commercial LLM versions unspecified and the same unnamed Gemini model plays three roles; no seeds, repeats, or variance
findings.location: Page 2 line 142; Page 3 lines 272-275; Page 4 'ASR and QA LLMs' and 'Prompt and Temperature' (lines 386-402), 'Transcript-Conditioned QA' (lines 348-357); Page 6 lines 536-542
findings.description: GPT-4o is used 'via API' with no model snapshot date (the 2024-05, 2024-08 and 2024-11 snapshots behave differently), and the citation is the system card. Gemini is cited via arXiv:2312.11805 (the Gemini 1.0 report) with no model name (1.5 Flash/Pro? 2.x?). This unnamed Gemini model is the keyword-triage judge (p.3), the question generator (p.4), and the adversarial grader of open-ended answers (p.4, p.6), so Table 4 cannot be reproduced without knowing which model and prompt did the grading. Question generation runs at temperature 0.3 with no seed, GPT-4o at temperature 0 is not deterministic, and the 300 open-ended items are 'randomly sample[d]' without a seed; every result is a single run with no variance estimate. The maximum-token value that is 'matched across all three QA models' is not given, nor how the 'at most fifteen words' constraint was enforced.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'GPT4o (OpenAI 2024) (via API)'; p.4: 'Question generation uses Gemini (Gemini Team 2024) for cost-efficiency'; p.4: 'scored by the question-generation model acting as judge'; p.4: 'temperature 0.3 for question generation to allow distractor diversity'; p.6: 'we randomly sample 300 questions'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report exact API model identifiers and access dates for GPT-4o and Gemini; report seeds where supported and repeat stochastic stages (generation, grading, GPT-4o answering) at least 3 times with variance; give max_tokens; release generated items so downstream stages are reproducible even if the generator changes.

findings.title: EdX licensing/terms-of-use and third-party API processing are described only vaguely; redistribution plans unstated
findings.location: Page 2 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' (lines 157-162); Page 4 'Datasets' (lines 359-366)
findings.description: Inclusion requires 'permission for research use or availability under applicable terms', a phrase that names no license, no course-level terms, and no distinction between viewing, downloading audio, scraping SRT captions, and redistributing. EdX content is generally governed by course-specific licenses and platform terms that restrict download/redistribution; the paper does not say which courses were used, under which terms, or whether the 'cleaned' dataset (audio, captions, per-instructor labels) will be redistributed. It also does not disclose that EdX and M3AV transcript windows were transmitted to two commercial APIs (OpenAI, Google) for question generation, verification and QA, or under what data-use terms. M3AV's own license is likewise not stated.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'Inclusion requires continuous instructional speech, intelligible source audio, permission for research use or availability under applicable terms'. p.4: 'We use two publicly available corpora'. No license or ToS is cited anywhere.
findings.suggested_fix: Name the licenses/terms under which each EdX course and M3AV were used; state whether audio/captions were downloaded and whether anything will be redistributed (and how); disclose API data-processing terms; if redistribution is not permitted, commit to releasing only IDs and derived annotations.

findings.title: M3AV speaker selection is undisclosed and internally inconsistent; evaluated-set demographics not reported
findings.location: Page 2 lines 163-168; Page 3 lines 205-209; Page 4 lines 359-371; Table 1 (p.4)
findings.description: Three statements cannot all be true: p.2 says 'all M3AV ... recordings retained'; p.3 says speakers with unresolved background were 'excluded from the selected set (e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers)'; p.4 says M3AV was assembled 'targeting the same overall 75%/25% L2/L1 composition as EdX'. Since 228 NIH candidate speakers alone exceed the 123 M3AV videos used, a quota-driven subset was selected by inferred L1 status, but the sampling rule (random? convenience? by venue?) is never given. Selecting speakers to hit a demographic quota based on name-inferred labels is itself a governance concern. Separately, Table 1 reports EdX pre-exclusion counts (1,380 videos; 343/1,037), whereas the evaluation uses 1,232 videos; the L1/L2 composition and unique-speaker count of the evaluated set are not reported.
findings.evidence: p.2: '148 EdX recordings excluded on this basis; all M3AV (Chen et al. 2024) recordings retained'. p.3: 'speakers whose background could not be resolved this way are coded as unknown and excluded from the selected set (e.g., 16 of 228 candidate NIH speakers)'. p.4: 'targeting the same overall 75%/25% L2/L1 composition as EdX'; 'leaving 1,232 EdX and 123 M3AV videos'. Computed: 1,037/1,380 = 75.1%, 92/123 = 74.8%.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe the M3AV selection procedure step by step (candidate pool per venue, labeling, exclusion, sampling to quota) and reconcile the three statements; report Table 1 for the evaluated set (1,232 EdX) with unique speakers per group; release the video-ID lists.

findings.title: 'L2' treated as a monolithic, US-centric category; reference variety never named; no per-L1 breakdown
findings.location: Page 1 line 63 ('nonstandard accents'); Page 3 lines 198-209; Page 7 Limitations lines 732-734; Figure 2 (p.5); Table 5 (p.6)
findings.description: All disparity results collapse dozens of possible first languages and regional varieties into a single 'L2' bin (and all EdX evaluation into 27 people). The operationalization is US-centric: 'years of residence in the US' and 'year of arrival in the US' presuppose US-based speakers even though EdX hosts many non-US institutions, and there is no statement of how L1 English speakers of non-US varieties (Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean, British, Australian) are coded. The Limitations refer to 'the selected reference variety' but the paper never says which variety that is. This makes the 'L2' effect uninterpretable for any specific community, risks mislabeling L1 speakers of non-inner-circle Englishes as 'L2', and reproduces the deficit framing of 'nonstandard accents' relative to an unnamed standard.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US'; 'year of arrival in the US, and total years of US residence'. p.7: 'shaped by the listener sample and the selected reference variety' (variety unspecified). Figure 2 and Table 5 report only L1 vs L2.
findings.suggested_fix: Name the reference variety; report the distribution of L1 languages/regions and results by at least the largest L1 groups; state how non-US L1 English varieties were handled; replace 'nonstandard' with neutral terminology; discuss within-'L2' heterogeneity in Limitations.

findings.title: Dual-use risk to accented instructors is not discussed
findings.location: Page 7, 'Conclusions and Future Work' (lines 718-721) and 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' (lines 723-746)
findings.description: The study produces, for identifiable instructors, per-speaker ASR error rates, inferred L2 status, crowd-rated 'accentedness', and downstream QA loss, and the Conclusion frames the finding at the level of individual instructors. Such per-instructor accessibility scores could be used by platforms, departments, or students to deprioritize, rank, or penalize accented instructors (e.g., in course selection algorithms, teaching evaluations, or captioning-budget decisions), shifting the burden of a system failure onto speakers. The Limitations section contains no discussion of misuse, of aggregate-only reporting, or of the recommendation that remediation target ASR systems and captioning provision rather than instructors.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'they can make some instructors' knowledge less searchable, reviewable, and usable than others'.' The Limitations section discusses proxy validity, listener sample, causation, topic coverage, and pretrained knowledge, but no potential misuse.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a broader-impact paragraph: state that results should be used to improve ASR/captioning provision, not to evaluate instructors; commit to aggregate-only or de-identified release of per-speaker metrics and ratings; note the risk of institutional misuse.

findings.title: Key subjective and heuristic steps in BWER, normalization, and keyword filtering are unspecified
findings.description: BWER, the metric behind the 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates' claim and behind Tables 5-6, counts a keyword correct if 'its lexical form or an approved equivalent appears' - the approver and the equivalence list are not given. Normalization keeps 'content-bearing hyphens, acronyms, and symbols when their distinction matters to the lesson', a per-case judgment with no rule or annotator. EdX BWER is 'approximated as all non-function words' with no function-word list, making EdX and M3AV BWER non-comparable. The 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic', the 'automated filtering pipeline', and the 'automated in-audio explanation check' (applied only 'within the M3AV subset', so knowledge-intensity verification differs by corpus) are named but not described.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'A keyword is counted as correct only when its lexical form or an approved equivalent appears in the aligned ASR span.' p.3: 'We retain content-bearing hyphens, acronyms, and symbols when their distinction matters to the lesson.' p.2: 'via an automated in-audio explanation check applied to candidate keywords within the M3AV subset.'
findings.suggested_fix: Release the normalization code, the function-word list, the equivalence list and who approved it, and pseudo-code for the fragmentation/gluing heuristic and filtering pipeline; report BWER for EdX and M3AV as non-comparable or harmonize the keyword source.

findings.title: Limitations/Ethics section omits most items a responsible-research checklist requires
findings.location: Page 7, 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' (lines 723-746)
findings.description: Against an AAAI/ACL-style responsible-research checklist, the section addresses: proxy validity of QA LLMs, closed-form vs interpretive learning, missing visual channel, listener-sample dependence, correlation vs causation, topic generalization, and pretrained-knowledge leakage. It omits: ethics approval/consent for human raters and for profiling identifiable speakers; privacy of inferred national-origin/native-language labels; data licenses and redistribution; code/data availability; label noise and error in L1/L2 assignment; potential misuse against instructors; disclosure that copyrighted transcripts were sent to commercial APIs; rater compensation; and compute/hardware/energy. There is also no acknowledgment that the L2 effect is estimated from only 27 EdX individuals.
findings.evidence: The full section (lines 723-746) contains none of the words 'consent', 'IRB', 'ethics board', 'privacy', 'license', 'release', 'available', 'misuse', or 'compute'.
findings.suggested_fix: Expand the section (or add an Ethics Statement) covering each omitted item explicitly, even if briefly; where an item does not apply, say so and why.

findings.title: Deficit-framing statement attributes disparity to 'the recordings and speakers' and contradicts the Introduction
findings.location: Page 5, 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' (lines 455-459) vs Page 1 (lines 68-71)
findings.description: The Introduction correctly attributes disparities to 'imbalances in training data and modeling choices'. The Results then claim that because no ASR system reverses the L1/L2 ordering, 'the L1/L2 disparity is a property of the recordings and speakers rather than an artifact of any one ASR system's training distribution'. This locates the cause in speakers, and the inference is unsound: all seven systems were trained on predominantly L1-English data, so a shared ordering is exactly what a shared training-distribution bias would produce. The sentence should be reframed to avoid implying speaker deficiency.
findings.evidence: p.5: 'No system reverses this ordering for any speaker group, indicating the L1/L2 disparity is a property of the recordings and speakers rather than an artifact of any one ASR system's training distribution.' p.1: 'These disparities reflect imbalances in training data and modeling choices'.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite as: the disparity is consistent across systems, which is compatible with a shared training-data bias common to all current English ASR models; remove the attribution to speakers.

findings.title: Main-text claims rely on an appendix, 'Table 11', and an empty section reference that are not in the submission
findings.description: The submission is 9 pages with no appendix, yet the text defers to it the verified-subset accuracies, the McNemar tests for all seven ASR systems, the human-study design and quality control, and the non-BWER correlations. The multiple-choice drop figures used to argue that MC 'was masking part of the true effect' ('2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11') are not in any table in the paper, and 'see Section for details' is an empty cross-reference. A reviewer therefore cannot check several quantitative claims.
findings.evidence: p.6: '(10.3 to 14.0 percentage points (pt) versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11)'; p.6: '(see Section for details)'; p.6: 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.'
findings.suggested_fix: Include the appendix with the submission, or move the essential numbers (MC drops per model, rater protocol) into the main text; fix the empty section reference.

findings.title: Reference-transcript provenance: EdX captions are called 'independently verified gold-standard' without any verification evidence
findings.location: Page 2 lines 117-119 and 182-188; Page 4 lines 364-366
findings.description: The Methodology asserts each recording has 'an independently verified gold-standard reference transcript', but for EdX the reference is simply the platform-published SRT caption file, whose origin (professional captioning, instructor upload, or ASR with light editing) varies by course and is not audited here. No caption quality check, sample manual audit, or per-course provenance is reported, so WER/CER/BWER for EdX depend on an unknown reference quality that may itself correlate with instructor group.
findings.evidence: p.2: 'an independently verified gold-standard reference transcript'; p.2: 'Reference transcripts are not produced by the authors, but drawn from ... EdX's officially published caption files'.
findings.suggested_fix: Report how EdX captions were produced for the included courses, audit a random sample against audio, and drop or soften 'independently verified gold-standard'.

findings.title: How were 'year of arrival in the US' and PhD institution obtained, and what were the sources for the 27 instructors?
findings.location: Page 3 lines 198-209
findings.description: OpenAlex indexes works, authors, affiliations and institutions; it does not record PhD institution, native language, or year of arrival in a country. The paper should say which additional sources (CVs, lab pages, LinkedIn, interviews, Wikipedia) were consulted for M3AV speakers and for the 27 EdX instructors, who performed the lookups, whether two annotators agreed, and whether the compiled dossiers are stored and will be shared.
findings.evidence: p.3: 'verified for a subset of speakers via biographical lookup against academic metadata (OpenAlex ...), recording PhD institution and country, year of arrival in the US, and total years of US residence'.
findings.suggested_fix: Describe sources, annotators, agreement, storage and retention; state the size of the 'subset' verified.

findings.title: Do '27 unique instructors' equal Table 1's '27 courses', and does 'n' in Tables 5/7 count clips or speakers?
findings.location: Page 3 line 198; Table 1 (p.4, 'Groups: 27 courses'); Tables 5 and 7 (p.6-7)
findings.description: If each course has exactly one instructor, releasing course identifiers alongside L1/L2 labels de-anonymizes the instructors, which matters for the release plan. Tables 5 and 7 report 'n' without saying whether these are clips, ratings, or speakers, which affects both the statistics and the privacy exposure per speaker (e.g., NIH n=168).
findings.evidence: p.3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors'; Table 1: 'EdX 1,380 | 27 courses'; Table 5 header 'n' with L1 39, L2 196.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the instructor-course mapping and define n in each table; state how many distinct speakers underlie the human-study clips.

findings.title: Who generated and verified the questions for the human-study clips?
findings.location: Page 7 lines 640-646; Table 7
findings.description: The main pipeline says Gemini generates questions and GPT4o/Llama3 verify them, but the human-study paragraph says 'the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples'. It is unclear which model generated these items, whether the three checks (dependency, superficial-cue, answerability) were applied, and whether the same role-separation guarantee holds for Table 7.
findings.evidence: p.7: 'ASR results of sample clips were subjected to the same question generation criteria, but given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less, the QA LLMs were only able to generate questions for 194 of the clip samples'.
findings.suggested_fix: State the generator/verifier for the clip-level questions and confirm which checks were applied; correct the wording if Gemini, not the QA LLMs, generated them.

summary: The paper is readable and mostly well organized, with a clear RQ1-RQ3 framing, a complete reference list, and statistics that reproduce from the tabulated counts. However, presentation defects are numerous and several are substantive: the body text reports reference-condition QA accuracies (99.3/98.3/97.9%) that contradict the numbers printed on Figure 4's bars (0.954/0.940/0.935) and Figure 1's summary (94.3%); the text claims BWER exposes harder technical-vocabulary failures while Figure 3 and Table 2 show BWER below WER for every Whisper system; and the abstract/conclusion assert per-topic QA differences that no table or figure reports. The manuscript is not self-contained: it points to a non-existent "Table 11", an empty "see Section for details" reference, and five appendix pointers (including the entire human-study design) with no appendix supplied. Figure 4 uses a truncated y-axis, unreadable rotated labels, and a family-only legend that makes its "mirrors Table 2" claim unverifiable; Table 3's N is ambiguous about pooling across LLMs; Table 6's caption says "accuracy" for what are error correlations with undefined significance stars. Terminology (Wav2Vec2/Wav2Vec, GPT4o/gpt4o, "two-stage" meaning two different pairs of stages), undefined abbreviations (Whisper-L-t, Wav2Vec2-L-s, BWER formula, "fragmentation/gluing heuristic"), a bullet-list formatting failure, and an "Ethical Concerns" heading with no ethical content all need fixing.
strengths: Reference list is complete and not truncated: every one of the ~45 in-text citations resolves to an entry on pages 8-9, and entries are alphabetized (apparent artifacts like 'Y ang', 'T utoring', 'P .' exist only in the text extraction, not in the rendered PDF).

Reported statistics are internally reproducible: all six McNemar p-values in Table 3 and the open-ended test (toward=140, away=33, p=3.4e-17) reproduce exactly from the discordant counts via a one-sided binomial; the Cohen's h values in Table 4 (0.240, 0.253, 0.338) reproduce from the ref/asr proportions; dataset totals in Tables 1, 5 and 7 all sum correctly; Figure 2's Whisper-M L1/L2 WER (0.056/0.080) reproduces Table 2's pooled 0.074 at the stated 25/75 L1/L2 mix.
Results section opens with explicit research questions (RQ1-RQ3, p.4) and the three subsections map cleanly onto them, which makes the narrative easy to follow.
Figure 1 uses a concrete worked example ('base excision' -> 'basic session') that communicates the core failure mode immediately, and Table 3's caption defines 'Toward'/'Away' precisely.
Methodology is candid about the limits of role separation between question generator, verifiers and answerers (p.4, repeated in Experiment Settings) rather than overclaiming independence.
Anonymization is clean: 'Anonymous submission' byline, footnotes contain only Hugging Face URLs, no self-identifying citations or acknowledgments were found.
Limitations section (p.7) is substantive on proxies vs. real learners, missing visual channel, listener-sample dependence, and correlation vs. causation.

findings.title: Body text reference-condition QA accuracies contradict Figure 4 bar labels and Figure 1
findings.location: Page 5, 'QA Accuracy over ASR Transcriptions' paragraph; Figure 4 (page 5); Figure 1 bottom panel (page 2)
findings.description: The text states GPT4o reference accuracy is 99.3%, Llama3 98.3%, Qwen2.5 97.9%. The 'ref' bars in Figure 4 are labeled 0.954, 0.940 and 0.935. Their mean (0.943) matches Figure 1's 'Reference (Correct) 94.3%' and reproduces Cohen's h = 0.140 against Figure 1's 'ASR (Whisper) 90.6%' (h(0.943, 0.906) = 0.141), so the figures are mutually consistent and the body-text percentages are wrong (or refer to an unstated subset such as the GT-verified set deferred to the appendix). This is the headline QA number of the paper.
findings.evidence: Text: 'GPT4o is strongest in the reference case (99.3%), while Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%) show very similar performance.' Figure 4 bar labels read 0.954 (GPT4o ref), 0.940 (Llama3 ref), 0.935 (Qwen2.5 ref). Figure 1: 'Reference (Correct) 94.3% / ASR (Whisper) 90.6% / Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct the three percentages to match Figure 4 (95.4/94.0/93.5) or state explicitly which question subset the 99.3/98.3/97.9 figures come from and show it; add a small table of the exact accuracies so readers do not have to read 3pt bar labels.

findings.title: Dangling cross-references: 'Table 11', empty 'see Section for details', five appendix pointers with no appendix
findings.location: Page 6 'QA over Open-Ended Questions' (Table 11, 'see Section'); page 5 col. 2 and page 6 col. 1-2 (Appendix); page 6 'Human Study' and 'Relationship to ASR Performance'
findings.description: The paper contains only Tables 1-7 yet cites 'Table 11' for the multiple-choice drop range; a LaTeX \ref has failed leaving 'see Section  for details'; and five statements defer content to an Appendix that is not part of the submitted 9 pages: the verified-subset QA accuracies, the McNemar results over all ASR systems, the human-study design and quality control, and the non-BWER correlations. The human study in particular has no design description in the main text.
findings.evidence: '(10.3 to 14.0 percentage points (pt) versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt in Table 11)'; '(see Section for details)'; 'We further report the accuracies from the verified question subset in the Appendix.'; 'We further report the test results over all the ASR systems in the Appendix.'; 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.'; '(other correlations are available in the appendix)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'Table 11' with the correct table (or add a table of per-LLM multiple-choice drops), fix the broken \ref to 'Transcript-Conditioned QA', and either include the appendix or move the essential human-study design into the main text.

findings.title: Abstract and Conclusion claim per-topic QA differences that no result reports; knowledge-intensity classification never used
findings.location: Abstract (page 1); Conclusions (page 7); Methodology 'Recording Corpus' (page 2); Results pages 5-6
findings.description: The abstract promises 'substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material' and the conclusion repeats 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics'. No table or figure breaks QA accuracy down by topic or by the lower/higher knowledge-intensity label introduced on page 2; Figure 3 is ASR-only (Whisper-M). The results text actually says the LLMs 'show very similar performance'. The binary knowledge-intensity classification is defined and then never appears again.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'The results show substantial differences among QA LLMs and across recording topics, with the largest performance gaps occurring in knowledge-intensive material.' Page 2: 'segments are classified as lower or higher in knowledge intensity'. Page 5: 'Llama3 (98.3%) and Qwen2.5 (97.9%) show very similar performance.' Conclusion: 'downstream QA models differ substantially across topics.'
findings.suggested_fix: Either add a QA-accuracy-by-topic (and by knowledge-intensity) table/figure or rewrite the abstract and conclusion to claim only what Figures 2-4 and Tables 3-7 show.

findings.title: Text claims technical vocabulary is harder than function words, but Figure 3 and Table 2 show BWER below WER for all Whisper systems
findings.location: Page 5, 'ASR Errors Across Speakers and Domains' (two sentences); Figure 3 (page 5); Table 2 (page 4)
findings.description: Two sentences assert that BWER (restricted to rare/technical words) reveals larger errors than WER. The figure described immediately after shows the opposite: BWER is <= WER in every one of the eight domains (e.g., EdX Computer Science WER 0.081 vs BWER 0.072; EdX Engineering 0.093 vs 0.074; M3AV IPP 0.067 vs 0.039; M3AV NIH 0.083 vs 0.061). In Table 2 BWER < WER for all four Whisper checkpoints on both datasets; BWER exceeds WER only for the three Wav2Vec2 systems. The prose either describes a different quantity or is wrong.
findings.evidence: 'BWER exposes disparities that WER understates.' and 'We observe that topic-specific vocabulary presents a greater challenge than surrounding function words.' vs Figure 3 labels (WER/BWER): CS 0.081/0.072, Eng 0.093/0.074, Hum 0.047/0.047, Sci 0.044/0.043, SocSci 0.046/0.046, IPP 0.067/0.039, MLS 0.056/0.035, NIH 0.083/0.061; Table 2 Whisper-M EdX WER 0.074 vs BWER 0.064.
findings.suggested_fix: Either restrict the claim to Wav2Vec2 (where BWER > WER) and say so, or explain why a lower BWER still indicates that keyword errors matter more (e.g., per-error consequence rather than rate), and rewrite the Figure 3 discussion accordingly.

findings.title: Figure 4: truncated y-axis, unreadable bar labels, family-only legend; within-Whisper pattern does not visibly 'mirror Table 2'
findings.location: Figure 4 and its caption (page 5, top right); text 'This ordering closely mirrors the ASR error-rate ordering from Table 2'
findings.description: The y-axis starts at 0.75, visually exaggerating 1-10 pt gaps. Value labels are rotated 90 degrees in roughly 3pt type and are illegible at print size. The legend names only 'ref', 'Whisper family (asr)', 'Wav2Vec family (asr)' and the caption only says 'blue shades: Whisper; orange/red shades: Wav2Vec2', so a reader cannot tell which of the four Whisper or three Wav2Vec2 bars is which system. The text's claim that the ordering mirrors Table 2 is therefore unverifiable, and the visible pattern argues against it: for GPT4o the four Whisper bars read 0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945 (non-monotone); if the bars follow Table 2 order (S, M, L-t, L), the worst-WER system Whisper-L (WER 0.197) yields the highest QA accuracy.
findings.evidence: Caption: 'colored by family (blue shades: Whisper; orange/red shades: Wav2Vec2)'. Legend: 'ref / Whisper family (asr) / Wav2Vec family (asr)'. Y-axis ticks 0.75-1.00. GPT4o bars: 0.954 (ref), 0.933, 0.926, 0.944, 0.945, 0.896, 0.905, 0.906.
findings.suggested_fix: Label each bar with its ASR system (or use a 7-entry legend), start the y-axis at 0 or clearly mark the break, enlarge/horizontalize labels or move the values to a companion table, and reconcile the 'mirrors Table 2' sentence with the actual per-system values.

findings.title: Table 3 'N=1,107' is ambiguous: counts appear pooled over three LLMs (3,321 paired comparisons)
findings.location: Table 3 and caption (page 5); text page 6 'h = 0.140 on the full set'
findings.description: The caption says 'for all QA LLMs' and rows are labeled 'Full (N=1,107)', but there is no per-LLM breakdown. Arithmetic shows the counts must be pooled over 3 LLMs x 1,107 items: (160-37)/(3x1107) = 3.7 pt equals Figure 1's 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points', whereas (160-37)/1107 = 11.1 pt would contradict the '2.7 to 4.7 pt' multiple-choice drop stated on page 6. Readers cannot tell whether N denotes questions or paired tests, and per-model heterogeneity is hidden. Cohen's h is reported only for 'All' rows ('-' elsewhere) without explanation.
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Difference statistics results from McNemar's exact test and Cohen's h effect size for all QA LLMs over the Whisper-M ASR transcript.' Rows: 'Full (N=1,107) All 160 37 9.9x10^-20 0.140'. Page 6: 'versus 2.7 to 4.7 pt'. Figure 1: 'Accuracy Gap = 3.7 percentage points'.
findings.suggested_fix: State that discordant pairs are pooled across the three QA models (N = 3 x 1,107 comparisons) or split rows by LLM; define what N counts; either fill in h for the substitution/deletion rows or explain the dashes.

findings.title: Human study design is absent from the main text; comprehensibility scale direction and 'n' undefined
findings.location: Page 6 'Human Study of Perceived Accented Speech' and Table 5 caption; page 7 first paragraph
findings.description: The main text never states how many raters participated, their language background, how clips were selected, how long clips are (the '25 words or less' clip length surfaces only on page 7 in the QA discussion), or the rating instrument. Table 5 says Acc and Com are 'on a 9-point scale' but the text then says higher comprehensibility means harder to understand, which is counterintuitive and not stated in the caption. The 'n' column (39/196; 10/8/6/9/5; 15/14/168) is not defined as clips, speakers, or ratings. The clip sample is 84% M3AV-NIH (168 of 235) which is never noted.
findings.evidence: 'More design and quality control can be found in the Appendix.'; Table 5 caption: 'Accentedness (Acc) and Comprehensibility (Com) are on a 9-point scale'; text: 'the comprehensibility was also higher (i.e., raters identified L2 speech as more challenging to understand)'; page 7: 'given the small amount of content delivered in 25 words or less'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short design paragraph (raters, N, background, clip selection and length, scale anchors, e.g. '1 = no accent / very easy ... 9 = heavy accent / very hard'), define 'n', and note the NIH dominance of the human-study sample.

findings.title: 'Two-stage framework' means different stage pairs in Abstract vs Methodology vs Figure 1; Figure 1 misplaces Question Construction
findings.location: Abstract (page 1); page 2 'analysis proceeds in four linked steps'; page 3 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation'; page 4 'Transcript-Conditioned QA'; Figure 1 (page 2)
findings.description: The abstract defines the two stages as ASR transcription and LLM-driven QA. The Methodology and Figure 1 define Stage 1 as knowledge-centered question generation and Stage 2 as transcript-conditioned QA, with ASR as preprocessing. The same section also says the analysis 'proceeds in four linked steps'. Inside Figure 1, the 'Question Construction' box (which the text places in Stage 1) sits inside the 'Stage 2: Transcript-Conditioned QA' panel.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'a two-stage framework ... which includes ASR transcription and LLM-driven question-answering (QA) stages.' Page 3: 'The first stage converts each verified reference transcript into a set of questions'. Page 4: 'In the second stage, GPT4o, Llama3, and Qwen2.5 answer'. Figure 1 Stage 2 panel contains 'Question Construction' with the example MCQ. Page 2: 'The analysis proceeds in four linked steps.'
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one decomposition, use it in the abstract, Figure 1, and Methodology, and move the Question Construction box into the Stage 1 panel of Figure 1.

findings.title: Table 6 caption says 'ASR accuracy' but values are correlations with BWER; significance stars undefined; text misreports which models are below .30
findings.location: Table 6 and caption (page 6); text page 6 'Namely, Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t were below rs = .30'
findings.description: All correlations are positive with accentedness, which only makes sense if the ASR variable is an error rate (the text says 'Spearman correlations of BWER'), so the caption's 'ASR accuracy' is misleading. The *, **, *** markers are never defined (no alpha thresholds anywhere). The text singles out Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t as having Int(BWER) correlations below .30, but Whisper-S (0.215) is also below .30 and Whisper-L is 0.281; the sentence 'several models had significant but very low correlations' is not matched to the table.
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Correlation study of human ratings and ASR accuracy.' Table 6 Int (BWER) column: Whisper-S 0.215***, Whisper-M 0.353***, Whisper-L-t 0.195**, Whisper-L 0.281***. Text: 'Namely, Whisper-L and Whisper-L-t were below rs = .30.'
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle as 'Spearman correlations between human ratings and ASR BWER', add a table note defining * p<.05, ** p<.01, *** p<.001 (or whatever was used), and correct the list of models below .30.

findings.title: 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns' contains no ethical discussion despite biographical profiling of identifiable instructors
findings.location: Page 7 'Limitations and Ethical Concerns'; page 3 first paragraph (L1/L2 labeling procedure)
findings.description: The section heading promises ethical concerns but every sentence is a methodological limitation. Meanwhile the method assigns L1/L2 labels to 27 named EdX instructors by researching 'country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US, and accent/background' and to M3AV speakers via 'author name origin and affiliation' plus OpenAlex lookups. Inferring national origin/language status of identifiable public individuals from names and affiliations, consent, data release of these labels, and IRB/ethics approval for the human rater study are not mentioned. The limitations also omit the circularity of using LLMs to generate, verify, and judge questions.
findings.evidence: Page 3: 'each of the 27 unique instructors was individually researched for country of origin, native language, years of residence in the US, and accent/background'; 'an initial L1 hypothesis is formed from author name origin and affiliation'. Page 7 section contains no sentence about ethics, consent, privacy, or approval.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a paragraph addressing consent/privacy for speaker demographic inference, whether labels will be released, ethics-board approval for the rater study, and the name-based inference risk; or rename the section 'Limitations'.

findings.title: Undefined abbreviations and methods: Whisper-L-t, Wav2Vec2-L-s, BWER formula, 'approved equivalent', 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic', 'in-audio explanation check', Gemini version
findings.location: Page 2 col. 1-2 (model list, footnotes 1-3); page 2 col. 2 'in-audio explanation check'; page 3 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis'; page 4 'ASR and QA LLMs'
findings.description: Seven ASR systems are named by abbreviations but only Whisper-M and one wav2vec2 checkpoint have footnoted URLs; the suffixes '-t' and '-s' are never expanded, so Whisper-L-t and Wav2Vec2-L-s cannot be identified. BWER is introduced by citation only, with no formula, and the keyword-match rule relies on an undefined 'approved equivalent'. The 'fragmentation/gluing heuristic' and the 'automated in-audio explanation check' are named but never described. The question generator is 'Gemini' with no version or checkpoint, and the Llama/Qwen sizes appear only in a footnote URL and inside Figure 1 ('Llama-3.1-8B').
findings.evidence: 'four Whisper checkpoints: Whisper-S, Whisper-M 1, Whisper-L, and Whisper-L-t ... three wav2vec2 checkpoints: Wav2Vec2-B, Wav2Vec2-L, and Wav2Vec2-L-s'; 'Biasing Word Error Rate (BWER) (Chen et al. 2024)'; 'its lexical form or an approved equivalent'; 'we additionally apply a fragmentation/gluing heuristic'; 'via an automated in-audio explanation check'; 'Question generation uses Gemini (Gemini Team 2024)'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a model table (name, HF checkpoint, parameter count), give the BWER formula and the equivalence list source, describe the two heuristics in two sentences each, and name the Gemini model/version.

findings.title: Bullet list of keyword-priority criteria collapsed into a run-on paragraph with inline ' - ' separators
findings.location: Page 3, 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation', paragraph beginning 'A candidate receives a higher priority'
findings.description: The five criteria were clearly intended as an itemized list but render as a single justified paragraph with hyphens mid-line, which is hard to parse.
findings.evidence: '- it names the central object, process, theory, person, or operation discussed in the segment; - it is explicitly defined or contrasted with another concept; - it is discipline-specific ... ; - it participates in a causal, temporal, numerical, or taxonomic relation; - it recurs across the explanation'
findings.suggested_fix: Use a proper itemize environment (as done for the contributions on page 2).

findings.title: Garbled or self-contradictory sentences
findings.location: Page 3 col. 2 (LLM judge sentence); page 5 col. 1 (deletions sentence); page 5 col. 2 (Table 3 lead-in; 'verify this assumption')
findings.description: Several sentences do not parse or misstate what the analysis does. The LLM-judge sentence has no main verb structure; the 'Deletions of these erroneous knowledge-intensive terms' sentence is unclear (the terms are not erroneous); the Table 3 lead-in is ungrammatical; and the claim that McNemar's test verifies that disagreements 'concentrate in specific items' is a mismatch, since the test assesses directional asymmetry of discordant pairs, not concentration.
findings.evidence: 'Surviving candidates are triaged by an LLM judge, and the same commercial model used for question generation to keep separate from the three QA answering models for alignment quality and topic centrality.'; 'Deletions of these erroneous knowledge-intensive terms hurt the lessons when they appear only once.'; 'Table 3 shows the results from assuming differences in the QA accuracies indicate the reference being correct and ASR transcripts being incorrect.'; 'the small set of disagreements exists for knowledge-intensive terms. We thus use statistical tests to verify this assumption.'
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite each sentence; for the last, say the test checks whether disagreements favor the reference condition, and report the disagreement rate separately to support the 'concentrated' claim.

findings.title: Inconsistent model naming across text, tables, and figures
findings.location: Page 2 (wav2vec2), Tables 2 and 6, Figure 2 x-axis, Figure 4 legend, Table 4, Table 7 (page 7), reference list
findings.description: The same systems are named 'wav2vec2' (lowercase, page 2), 'Wav2Vec2-B/-L/-L-s' (Tables 2, 6), 'Wav2Vec-B/-L/-L-s' (Figure 2 axis) and 'Wav2Vec family' (Figure 4 legend). LLMs are 'GPT4o, Llama3, Qwen2.5' in text and Table 4 but 'gpt4o, llama, qwen' in Table 7; the reference entry is 'GPT-4o'. Figure 1 says 'Llama-3.1-8B'. The gold condition is 'reference (gold)' in text, 'ref' in Figure 4 legend and Table 4.
findings.evidence: 'three wav2vec2 checkpoints: Wav2Vec2-B'; Figure 2 labels 'Wav2Vec-B, Wav2Vec-L, Wav2Vec-L-s'; Figure 4 legend 'Wav2Vec family (asr)'; Table 7 header 'gpt4o llama qwen'; Figure 1 'Llama-3.1-8B'.

findings.title: Table 7 typeset in a much smaller font with code-style identifiers and spacing errors

The caption 'QA Accuracy with human study results' does not say what the rows are (clips grouped by whether all three LLMs answered correctly).

findings.title: Table 1 'Groups: 27 courses' conflicts with '27 unique instructors'; L1/L2 counts are pre-exclusion
findings.location: Table 1 (page 4); page 3 col. 1; page 4 'Datasets'

It is unclear whether groups are courses or instructors (or whether both happen to be 27). The L1/L2 columns (343 + 1,037 = 1,380) count videos before the 148 exclusions, whereas the ASR evaluation uses 1,232 EdX videos; the table does not say which population it describes.

findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the 'Groups' column, and either report post-exclusion L1/L2 counts or add a note that Table 1 describes the raw corpus.

findings.title: Punctuation, citation-format, and wording slips
findings.location: Page 6 col. 2; page 7 Related Work; page 6 col. 1; page 2 contributions; page 1 col. 2; section headings pages 4
findings.description: Missing period between sentences ('Table 6 The results'); doubled closing parenthesis after Dubois et al. 2024; a narrative citation without parentheses around the year ('Kuhn et al. 2023 found'); straight double quotes in conventionally "small" while curly quotes are used elsewhere; 'Experiment Settings'/'Experiment Results' rather than 'Experimental'; 'augmentation study' is an odd descriptor for a complementary human study; 'such a distinction' on page 1 has no clear antecedent after the intervening LLM paragraph.

findings.title: Citations attached to a claim they do not support; uncited policy claim
findings.location: Page 1, Introduction, first and second paragraphs
findings.description: Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench / LLM-as-a-judge) and Sidiropoulos et al. 2022 (ASR errors in passage retrieval) are cited as evidence that LLMs are 'ubiquitous for producing transcripts', which neither paper is about. The claim that 'many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech' has no citation.
findings.evidence: 'While Large Language Models (LLMs) become ubiquitous for producing transcripts (Shapira, Chazan, and Cohen 2025; Zheng et al. 2023; Sidiropoulos, Vakulenko, and Kanoulas 2022)'; 'many institutions have developed policies that demand 99% accuracy of transcribed speech.'
findings.suggested_fix: Move Zheng and Sidiropoulos to the QA/judging and downstream-task clauses where they belong (as done in Related Work), and cite a source for the 99% accuracy policy.

findings.title: Inconsistent heading levels and duplicated setup text between Methodology and Experiment Settings
findings.location: Page 2 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' (run-in) vs page 3 subsection headings; page 4 'Experiment Settings'
findings.description: 'Recording Corpus and Reference Transcripts' is a bold run-in paragraph heading while its sibling topics 'ASR Transcription and Error Analysis' and 'Knowledge-Centered Question Generation' are full subsection headings. The Experiment Settings section then restates material already in Methodology: the 148 excluded EdX recordings (page 2 and page 4), the gold-transcript sources, and the generator/verifier role separation (twice on page 4, once ending '(see Methodology for details)').
findings.evidence: Page 2: '(148 EdX recordings excluded on this basis; all M3AV ... recordings retained)'; page 4: 'A data-quality pass excluded 148 EdX videos'; page 4 col. 1 and col. 2 both describe that verifiers 'are drawn from the same pool of models used for downstream answering'.
findings.suggested_fix: Promote the corpus paragraph to a subsection and merge the duplicated sentences, keeping dataset counts in one place (Table 1 plus one paragraph).

findings.title: Related Work placed after Results, duplicating Introduction coverage
findings.location: Page 7, 'Related Work' (between Human Study and Conclusions)
findings.description: Related Work appears after all results and immediately before Conclusions, while the Introduction already cites most of the same disparity literature (Koenecke, Martin & Wright, Tatman, Dubois, Hirschi & Kang, Inceoglu, Kuhn). The late placement interrupts the flow from results to conclusions and repeats citations.

findings.suggested_fix: Move Related Work before Methodology or fold the unique parts (Accessibility and ASR Accuracy; QA LLMs) into the Introduction.

findings.title: Figure 1 text is illegible at column width and hard-codes results not stated in the body
